Seeded from the supplied Quick Revision and reference books, then every answer independently checked against the code or standard named in `verification.references`. Where the circulating printed key is wrong, `status` is 'key-corrected' and `notes` says exactly what was wrong — those notes are shown to the candidate.

questions.stem: Plaster of Paris is obtained by calcining:
questions.solution:
**Gypsum.**

Plaster of Paris is hemihydrate calcium sulphate, CaSO_{4}·½H_{2}O. It is made by heating (calcining) gypsum, CaSO_{4}·2H_{2}O, to about 120–160 °C, which drives off three-quarters of the water of crystallisation:

> CaSO_{4}·2H_{2}O  →(heat)→  CaSO_{4}·½H_{2}O + 1½H_{2}O

Why the others are wrong:
- **Limestone** (CaCO_{3}) calcines to quicklime, CaO — that is lime, not plaster of Paris.
- **Dolomite** (CaCO_{3}·MgCO_{3}) calcines to dolomitic lime.
- **Bauxite** is the ore of aluminium.

Exam hook: plaster of Paris sets in **5–10 minutes**, which is why retarders are added for practical plastering.

examTip.trap: Limestone is the tempting pick because it is the raw material for *cement*. Plaster of Paris has nothing to do with cement manufacture.
examTip.trick: Follow the chemistry: POP is a **sulphate** (CaSO₄·½H₂O) and gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O. Limestone is a **carbonate**. Only gypsum can lose water and stay a sulphate.
examTip.mnemonic: **G**ypsum → **G**ives POP. Calcining just drives off 1½ of the 2 waters.

questions.stem: The early strength of cement is mainly due to which compound?
questions.solution:
**Tricalcium silicate, C_{3}S (alite).**

The four Bogue compounds divide the work of hydration between them:

| Compound | Contributes | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| C_{3}S | **Early strength (up to ~7 days)** | Fast |
| C_{2}S | Ultimate / long-term strength | Slow |
| C_{3}A | Flash set; highest heat of hydration | Very fast |
| C_{4}AF | Little strength; gives colour | Fast |

C_{3}S makes up roughly 40–50% of ordinary Portland cement and hydrates quickly with a high heat of hydration, so it dominates the strength gained in the first week.

**Do not confuse:** C_{2}S gives the *ultimate* strength, and C_{3}A gives the *highest heat of hydration* — both are separate questions that appear in the same paper.

examTip.trap: C₂S is the classic wrong answer — it *does* give strength, but **late** strength (after 28 days), not early.
examTip.trick: The four compounds split cleanly by job: **C₃S** early strength, **C₂S** late strength, **C₃A** flash set and heat, **C₄AF** colour only.
examTip.mnemonic: **Higher number, faster action.** C₃S (3) beats C₂S (2) to strength. And C₃A, the highest-reacting of all, is so fast it must be restrained with gypsum.

questions.stem: The addition of gypsum to cement:
options: Increases the setting time of cement
Decreases the setting time of cement
Increases the ultimate strength of cement
Reduces the heat of hydration to zero
questions.solution:
**It increases the setting time** — gypsum is a *retarder*.

Without gypsum, the tricalcium aluminate (C_{3}A) in clinker reacts with water almost instantly and the cement suffers a **flash set**, becoming unusable within minutes. Gypsum (CaSO_{4}·2H_{2}O), interground at about **3–5%**, reacts with C_{3}A to form a thin ettringite layer around the grains, which blocks that runaway reaction and delays stiffening.

So gypsum buys the working time that makes cement practical: an initial setting time of **not less than 30 minutes** for ordinary Portland cement.

Note it does not change the *ultimate* strength appreciably — that is governed by C_{2}S and C_{3}S — and it reduces but does not eliminate the heat of hydration.

examTip.trap: "Decreases the setting time" feels right because an additive sounds like an accelerator. Gypsum is the opposite — it is a **retarder**.
examTip.trick: Ask what problem it solves. Without gypsum, C₃A makes cement **flash set** in minutes and it could never be placed. Gypsum exists purely to slow that down.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gypsum guards against the flash.** No gypsum, no working time.

questions.stem: The initial setting time of ordinary Portland cement shall not be less than:
questions.solution:
**30 minutes.**

IS 4031 (Part 5) measures setting time with the **Vicat apparatus**. IS 269 then requires, for ordinary Portland cement:

- **Initial setting time — not less than 30 minutes** (the cement must stay workable this long)
- **Final setting time — not more than 600 minutes**, i.e. 10 hours

Watch the direction of each limit: the initial time is a *minimum*, the final time is a *maximum*. Option (d), 600 minutes, is the final setting time — a very common distractor.

For comparison: rapid hardening cement also has a 30 minute initial set, while **low heat cement is allowed 60 minutes**.

examTip.trap: Candidates blur the two limits. Initial is a **minimum** (not less than 30 min); final is a **maximum** (not more than 600 min).
examTip.trick: Reason from purpose: you need *at least* half an hour to place and compact, and you want it hard within the working day.
examTip.mnemonic: **30 minutes to start, 10 hours to finish.**

questions.stem: The main compound formed on hydration of cement, responsible for its strength, is:
questions.solution:
**Calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) gel.**

When C_{3}S and C_{2}S hydrate they produce two things:

> Calcium silicate + water → **C-S-H gel** + Ca(OH)_{2}

The C-S-H gel is a poorly-crystalline, extremely fine solid that occupies most of the hardened paste volume and binds everything together — it is the source of essentially all of the strength.

**Calcium hydroxide** (Ca(OH)_{2}, portlandite) is the by-product. It contributes little strength, and is in fact the weak link: it is soluble, causes efflorescence and is what carbonates and lowers pH to allow reinforcement corrosion.

**Calcium sulphoaluminate** (ettringite) comes from the gypsum–C_{3}A reaction and controls setting, not strength.

examTip.trap: Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, is also produced on hydration and is a real product — but it contributes very little strength and is actually the weak, leachable phase.
examTip.trick: C-S-H is about **70% of the hydrated paste** and is what binds. If a question asks what gives concrete its strength, the gel is the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **C-S-H is the glue; Ca(OH)₂ is the by-product.**

questions.stem: The presence of sand in brick earth prevents:
options: Warping, shrinking and cracking of bricks
questions.solution:
**Warping, shrinking and cracking.**

Sand is the silica (SiO_{2}) component of brick earth, 50–60% of a good clay. Silica is non-plastic and dimensionally stable, so it acts as a skeleton that holds the shape while the brick dries and burns. Without enough of it the alumina-rich clay shrinks a great deal on drying and the brick warps and cracks.

The trade-off, and the usual follow-up question: **excess silica makes the brick brittle** and destroys cohesion.

The other ingredients have separate jobs:
- **Alumina** gives plasticity for moulding; in excess it *causes* shrinkage and warping.
- **Iron oxide** gives the red colour.
- **Lime** binds the particles and fuses the sand; in excess the brick melts and loses shape.
- **Alkalis (reh)** are what cause efflorescence.

examTip.trap: "Increases strength" is wrong in the way that matters — sand is a non-plastic filler and it actually *reduces* the fired strength slightly. Its job is dimensional control.
examTip.trick: Ask what pure clay does when it dries: it shrinks enormously and cracks. Sand is there to stop that.
examTip.mnemonic: Sand is the **shrinkage brake** in brick earth. Too little and it cracks; too much and it crumbles.

questions.stem: The indentation provided on the face of a moulded brick is called a:
questions.solution:
**Frog.**

The frog is the depression pressed into one face of the brick. It does two jobs: it keys the mortar so the bed joint develops shear resistance, and it carries the manufacturer's mark. A typical frog is 100 × 40 × 10–20 mm.

It is provided on hand-moulded and machine-pressed bricks, and is **laid facing upward** so it fills with mortar. Frogs are omitted on wire-cut bricks and on bricks used for flooring or paving.

The distractors are all *cut* bricks, not features of a whole one:
- **Bat** — a brick cut across its width (half bat, three-quarter bat).
- **Closer** — a brick cut along its length, used to close the end of a course and set the bond.
- **Queen closer** — a closer of half the brick's width.

examTip.trap: "Bat" and "closer" are offered because they are also brick terms — but both are *cut* bricks, not a feature moulded into a whole one.
examTip.trick: The frog has two purposes: it keys the mortar, and it is where the maker's stamp goes. It faces **upward** when laid.
examTip.mnemonic: **Frog on top** — so the mortar fills it and locks the course.

questions.stem: As per IS 1077, the minimum compressive strength of a first class brick is:
questions.solution:
**10.5 N/mm².**

IS 1077 grades common burnt clay bricks by class designation, where the number *is* the minimum average compressive strength in N/mm²:

| Class | Minimum compressive strength |
|---|---|
| First class | **10.5 N/mm²** (often quoted as class 10) |
| Second class | 7.0 N/mm² |
| Third class | 3.5 N/mm² |
| Common burnt clay (lowest) | 3.5 N/mm² |

The test uses the **frog filled flush with 1:1 cement–sand mortar** and the brick immersed for three days before loading, with load applied at 14 N/mm² per minute.

Note that N/mm² and MPa are the same unit, so 10.5 N/mm² = 10.5 MPa. Some circulating collections write this as "> 10.5" without units; the requirement is an average of not less than 10.5 N/mm².

examTip.trick: Remember the ladder for brick classes: **first class 10.5, second class 7.0, third class 3.5 N/mm²** — each roughly two-thirds of the one above.
examTip.mnemonic: **10.5 / 7 / 3.5** for first, second, third class.

questions.stem: For a first class brick, water absorption after 24 hours of immersion should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**20% by weight.**

IS 3495 (Part 2) immerses an oven-dried brick in cold water for 24 hours and computes

> Water absorption = (W_{wet} − W_{dry}) / W_{dry} × 100%

IS 1077 then limits it to:

| Brick | Limit (24 h cold immersion) |
|---|---|
| Class designation 12.5 and above | not more than **15%** |
| Class designation below 12.5 (incl. first class at 10.5) | not more than **20%** |
| Second class | not more than 22% |

A low absorption means a dense, well-burnt, durable brick; a high one means an under-burnt, porous brick that will spall in frost and carry damp.

**Correction to a widely-copied key.** Several circulating collections state this limit as "0.15". That is a mistyped **15%** — a water absorption of 0.15% is physically impossible for a burnt clay brick, and 15% is in any case the limit for the higher class designations, not for first class.

verification.notes: The printed key gives "0.15", which is a mistyped 15%. Even read as 15%, that is the limit for class designation 12.5 and above; for a first class brick (class 10.5) IS 1077 permits up to 20%. The answer here is 20% by weight.

examTip.trap: 15% is offered and looks plausible, but it is not a code figure for burnt clay bricks.
examTip.trick: Pair the strength limit with the absorption limit: a first class brick is **10.5 N/mm² and 20% absorption**; second class relaxes both.
examTip.mnemonic: **First class: 20. Second class: 22.** Absorption goes up as class goes down.

questions.stem: In the compressive strength test of a brick, the frog is filled with mortar of ratio:
questions.solution:
**1:1 (cement : sand).**

IS 3495 (Part 1) requires the frog and any voids in the bed face to be filled flush with a **1:1 cement–sand mortar** (clean coarse sand, 3 mm and down), after which the specimen is stored damp for 24 hours and then immersed in water for three days before testing.

The reason for such a rich mix is that the filling must be at least as strong as the brick. If a leaner mortar were used, the plug in the frog would crush first and the recorded figure would be the strength of the mortar, not of the brick.

Procedure in brief:
1. Remove any projections; fill the frog flush with **1:1** cement–sand mortar.
2. Store under damp jute for 24 h, then immerse in water for 3 days.
3. Place flat between plates, load at **14 N/mm² per minute** until failure.
4. Compressive strength = maximum load ÷ bed-face area; report the average of five bricks.

examTip.trick: The frog is filled so the load bears on a flat plane instead of a rim. A rich 1:1 mortar is used because it must reach strength in three days and must not be the weak link.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fill the frog 1:1** — the mortar must never be weaker than the brick under test.

questions.stem: The Vicat apparatus is used to determine:
options: Consistency and setting time of cement
questions.solution:
**Consistency (standard consistency) and setting time.**

The Vicat apparatus is a needle-and-plunger frame with interchangeable attachments, and IS 4031 uses it for both tests:

| Attachment | Test | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| 10 mm plunger | Standard consistency (IS 4031 Pt 4) | Plunger settles to 5–7 mm from the bottom |
| 1 mm² square needle | Initial setting time (Pt 5) | Needle penetrates to 5 ± 0.5 mm from the bottom |
| Needle with annular attachment | Final setting time (Pt 5) | Needle marks but the annulus does not |

Match each other test to its own apparatus, because these are asked as a set:
- **Soundness** → **Le Chatelier apparatus** (or the autoclave test)
- **Fineness** → 90 μm sieve, or Blaine air-permeability apparatus
- **Compressive strength** → 70.6 mm cement–sand mortar cubes in a compression machine

examTip.trap: Soundness is the standard wrong answer here, because both tests are cement tests done in the same laboratory session.
examTip.trick: Vicat uses **needles and plungers** pressed into a paste; Le Chatelier uses an **expanding mould** with indicator arms. Different apparatus, different property.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vicat = the needle** (consistency, initial and final set). **Le Chatelier = the arms** (soundness).

questions.stem: Soundness of cement is determined by the:
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier apparatus.**

Soundness measures a cement's resistance to **delayed expansion after setting**, caused by excess free lime, excess magnesia or excess sulphate. An unsound cement expands and cracks the hardened concrete, so it is a durability test, not a strength test.

The Le Chatelier mould is a split brass cylinder with two indicator arms. A paste of standard consistency is placed in it, kept in water at 27 °C for 24 h, then boiled for 3 hours; the increase in the distance between the arm tips is the expansion.

IS 269 limits:
- **Le Chatelier expansion — not more than 10 mm**
- **Autoclave expansion — not more than 0.8%**

The autoclave test is the one that detects unsoundness from magnesia; Le Chatelier detects free lime.

examTip.trap: Vicat is the mirror-image trap of the previous question. If you can tell the two apparatus apart you get both marks.
examTip.trick: Soundness means **freedom from delayed expansion** caused by free lime and magnesia. The Le Chatelier arms literally measure that expansion; the limit is 10 mm.
examTip.mnemonic: **Le Chatelier arms spread = unsound cement.**

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a non-destructive test on concrete?
questions.solution:
**The compression test on cubes** — it crushes the specimen, so by definition it is destructive.

A non-destructive test (NDT) assesses the material while leaving the structure fit for service. The standard family:

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Rebound hammer** (Schmidt) | Surface hardness → approximate compressive strength |
| **Ultrasonic pulse velocity** | Pulse speed → uniformity, voids, cracks, honeycombing |
| **Pull-out** | Force to pull an embedded insert → in-situ strength (semi-destructive but the member survives) |
| Cover meter / rebar locator | Cover depth and bar position |
| Half-cell potential | Likelihood of reinforcement corrosion |

The cube (or cylinder) compression test is the *reference* strength test precisely because it loads a specimen to failure — which is why it cannot be used on the structure itself.

examTip.trap: The word **NOT** is the whole question, and it is missed constantly. Underline it before reading the options.
examTip.trick: Non-destructive means the member survives. The cube test crushes the specimen, so it is destructive by definition.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rebound hammer, UPV and pull-out leave the concrete standing. The cube test does not.**

questions.stem: The bulking of sand is caused by:
options: The presence of moisture forming a film around the particles
The presence of clay and silt
An increase in the fineness modulus
questions.solution:
**A film of moisture around each particle.**

When sand is damp, surface tension holds a thin water film on every grain. The films keep the grains apart, so the same mass of sand occupies a larger **bulk volume**. That apparent increase is bulking.

The behaviour is not linear, and the shape of the curve is examined:

- Bulking rises steeply with moisture content and **peaks at about 4–6% moisture, where the increase in volume can reach 20–40%** (finer sand bulks more).
- Beyond that the films merge, the water starts to fill the voids instead of separating grains, and the bulking falls.
- **At full saturation the bulking is zero** — a fully inundated sand occupies the same volume as dry sand.

This matters on site because sand batched **by volume** must be corrected for bulking, or the mix will be sand-deficient and the concrete will be harsh and under-strength. The field test measures it by inundation: a sample is levelled, then flooded and re-levelled, and bulking = (h_{1} − h_{2}) / h_{2} × 100%.

examTip.trap: Candidates assume more water means more volume in a simple way — but **fully saturated sand shows no bulking at all**, because the films merge and collapse.
examTip.trick: Bulking peaks at about **4–6% moisture**, where volume can rise **20–30%**. Dry sand and drowned sand both sit at zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **Damp sand swells; dry and drowned do not.** This is why sand is batched by weight, not by volume.

questions.stem: The chemical classification of quartzite is:
questions.solution:
**Siliceous** — quartzite is almost entirely silica (SiO_{2}).

The chemical classification of rocks turns on the dominant compound:

| Class | Dominant compound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Siliceous** | Silica, SiO_{2} | **Quartzite**, granite, sandstone |
| Argillaceous | Clay / alumina | Slate, laterite, shale |
| Calcareous | Calcium carbonate | Limestone, marble, dolomite |

Quartzite is also worth knowing geologically: it is the **metamorphic form of sandstone**. Learn the parent–product pairs as a set, because they are asked every sitting:

| Original rock | Metamorphic form |
|---|---|
| Sandstone | **Quartzite** |
| Limestone | Marble |
| Shale / clay | Slate |
| Granite | Gneiss |

Being siliceous, quartzite is hard, very durable and acid-resistant, but difficult to dress — hence its use as road metal and rubble rather than for fine ashlar.

examTip.trick: Classify by the dominant chemistry: **siliceous** (quartz-rich — granite, quartzite, sandstone), **calcareous** (carbonate — limestone, marble), **argillaceous** (clay-rich — slate, laterite).
examTip.mnemonic: **Quartzite is quartz** — the name gives the answer away.

questions.stem: The drawback of electrical seasoning of timber is that it:
options: Cannot remove sap from the timber
Makes the timber susceptible to fungal attack
questions.solution:
**It causes splitting** (and can reduce the timber's strength), besides being the costliest method.

In electrical seasoning the green timber is placed in a high-frequency alternating field. Because moist wood is a poorer insulator than dry wood, the wet regions heat fastest and the water is driven off very quickly. That speed is exactly the problem: steep internal moisture gradients set up drying stresses, and the timber **splits and checks**. Prolonged heating also degrades the lignin and lowers strength.

Comparison worth carrying into the exam:

| Method | Speed | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|
| Natural / air | 2–4 years | Very slow; needs large yard |
| Kiln | Days | Costly; needs skill and plant |
| Water | Weeks | Reduces elasticity and durability |
| Boiling | Hours | Costly; reduces elasticity |
| Chemical (salt) | Moderate | Salts can corrode fasteners |
| **Electrical** | Fastest | **Splitting; strength loss; most expensive** |

Remember also the purpose of seasoning itself: **to reduce the moisture content** to equilibrium with the surroundings, giving dimensional stability, decay resistance and paintability.

examTip.trick: Rank the methods by speed against damage: **air seasoning** is slowest and gentlest; **kiln** is controlled and fastest in practice; **electrical and chemical** are quick but harsh and expensive.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fast seasoning splits.** Any method that drives moisture out quickly sets up a gradient, and the gradient cracks the timber.

questions.stem: The seasoning of timber is carried out primarily to:
questions.solution:
**To decrease the moisture content.**

Freshly felled timber holds 50% moisture or more. Seasoning brings it down to roughly **10–12% for interior work and 15–18% for exterior work**, in equilibrium with the service environment.

Why it must be done before use:
- **Dimensional stability** — unseasoned timber shrinks in service, opening joints and warping.
- **Decay resistance** — fungi need about 20% moisture; below that they cannot attack.
- **Strength and stiffness** increase as timber dries below the fibre saturation point.
- **Finishing** — paint, polish and preservatives will not adhere to wet timber.
- Lower weight, easier working, and better glue and fastener performance.

Note what seasoning does *not* do: it cannot remove **knots, shakes or other defects**, which are already present in the log — those are addressed by grading and conversion, not drying.

examTip.trap: "To increase strength" is a consequence, not the purpose — and picking it means missing that everything else follows from moisture removal.
examTip.trick: One cause, many effects: lower moisture gives **less shrinkage and warping, more strength, better paint adhesion, and resistance to decay and insects**.
examTip.mnemonic: Season down to about **12% for interior work, 15–18% for exterior.**

questions.stem: The constituent of paint that imparts colour to it is the:
questions.solution:
**Pigment.**

Each constituent of an oil paint has one job, and the examination asks for the mapping directly:

| Constituent | Typical material | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Base | White lead, red lead, zinc oxide, titanium oxide | Body and opacity; the bulk of the solid |
| Vehicle (binder) | Linseed oil | Carries the base; forms and binds the film |
| **Pigment** | Various | **Gives the colour**; adds hardness |
| Solvent / thinner | Turpentine | Makes the paint workable; evaporates |
| Drier | Litharge, manganese salts | Speeds drying by promoting oxidation |
| Extender / filler | Barytes, chalk | Bulks the paint out; reduces cost |

A point of care: the **base** also affects appearance and is itself often white or coloured, but the constituent added *specifically for colour* is the pigment.

Related single-fact question: **red lead is the pigment used for corrosion resistance** on structural steelwork, which is why a red-lead primer is the traditional first coat.

examTip.trap: "Vehicle" is the trap — it is a real paint constituent, but it is the *liquid carrier* that lets the pigment spread, not the colour itself.
examTip.trick: Learn the four by job: **pigment** colours and hides, **vehicle/base** carries, **drier** speeds oxidation, **thinner** adjusts consistency.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pigment = coloured Powder.**

questions.stem: Lacquer is a:
questions.solution:
**A spirit varnish.**

Varnishes are classified by the solvent that carries the resin:

| Varnish | Solvent | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Oil varnish | Linseed oil | Slow drying, hard, durable — best for exterior and heavy-wear surfaces |
| **Spirit varnish (lacquer, French polish)** | **Alcohol / spirit** | **Dries very fast by evaporation**; not durable; poor weather resistance |
| Turpentine varnish | Turpentine | Cheaper, dries faster than oil varnish, less durable |
| Water varnish | Water with shellac + ammonia/borax | For maps, pictures, book covers |
| Asphalt varnish | — | Blackens; for ironwork and fabrication |

Lacquer is shellac dissolved in alcohol, sometimes with a colouring pigment. Because it dries purely by solvent evaporation it hardens in minutes, which suits furniture and interior joinery, but the film is soft and is attacked by water and weather — so it is not used outdoors.

examTip.trick: Varnishes are named for their solvent: **oil** varnish (durable, slow), **spirit** varnish (fast, less durable — this is lacquer and French polish), **turpentine** varnish, **water** varnish.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacquer dries fast because spirit evaporates fast.**

questions.stem: Plastic bitumen is generally used for:
questions.solution:
**Crack filling** (and stopping leaks).

Plastic bitumen is bitumen blended with a thinner and a **filler** such as slate dust or asbestos, which gives it a stiff, putty-like body that stays where it is placed. That makes it right for filling cracks in masonry and concrete, sealing joints and stopping leaks — and, in pavements, for **crack sealing**.

Contrast the other bituminous applications:

| Product / use | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Plastic bitumen** | **Filling cracks, sealing joints, stopping leaks** |
| Tack coat | Thin bitumen sprayed to bond a new bituminous layer to an existing one |
| Prime coat | Low-viscosity bitumen sprayed to seal and bind a granular base before surfacing |
| Blown / oxidised bitumen | Roofing felt, pipe coating, joint filler |
| Cutback / emulsion | Cold-weather and patch work |

So both the pavement question ("primarily used for sealing cracks in asphalt pavement") and the materials question ("plastic bitumen is used for") resolve to crack filling.

examTip.trick: Match the bitumen to the job: **plastic bitumen** fills cracks, **cutback** is bitumen thinned with solvent for cold work, **emulsion** is bitumen dispersed in water, **blown** bitumen is stiff and used for roofing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plastic bitumen plugs cracks.**

questions.stem: The main alloying element in stainless steel is:
questions.solution:
**Chromium.**

Stainless steel is defined by containing at least about **10.5–12% chromium**. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form an extremely thin, adherent, self-repairing **chromium oxide (Cr_{2}O_{3}) passive film** on the surface, and it is that film — not the bulk metal — that resists corrosion. Scratch it and it reforms, which is why the protection is permanent.

Typical austenitic stainless (grade 304) is about **18% Cr and 8% Ni**. Nickel is important — it stabilises the austenitic structure and improves ductility, toughness and resistance to acids — but chromium is what makes the steel *stainless*.

Other alloying elements and what each buys:

| Element | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Chromium** | **Corrosion resistance** (passive film), hardness |
| Nickel | Toughness, ductility, austenite stability |
| Manganese | Hardness and wear resistance (Hadfield steel) |
| Tungsten | Hot hardness — high-speed tool steel |
| Molybdenum | Pitting resistance (grade 316), creep strength |
| Vanadium | Grain refinement, fatigue strength |

examTip.trap: Nickel is the near-miss — it *is* in most stainless steels and improves toughness, but it is chromium that makes the steel stainless.
examTip.trick: The threshold is **10.5% chromium**, which forms a self-repairing passive oxide film. Below that the steel is not stainless however much nickel it contains.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chromium = Corrosion resistance.** Both start with C.

questions.stem: The percentage of carbon present in steel is generally:
questions.solution:
**About 0.15% to 1.5%.**

Carbon content is what separates the three ferrous materials, and the boundaries are examined directly:

| Material | Carbon | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Wrought iron | ~0.05 – 0.25% | Very ductile, tough, forgeable; cannot be hardened |
| **Steel** | **~0.15 – 1.5%** | Strong and versatile; hardenable |
| Cast iron | ~2 – 4% | Hard, brittle, excellent in compression; not forgeable |

Within steel:
- **Mild steel** 0.15 – 0.30% — structural sections, reinforcement
- **Medium carbon** 0.30 – 0.60% — rails, shafts
- **High carbon** 0.60 – 1.50% — tools, springs

The trend to remember: as carbon rises, **hardness, strength and brittleness increase**, while **ductility, malleability and weldability decrease**. That is why structural steel is kept at the low-carbon end — it has to be welded and to deform before it fails.

examTip.trick: The carbon ladder decides the material: **wrought iron** under 0.05%, **steel** 0.15–1.5%, **cast iron** above about 2%.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under 2 it is steel, over 2 it is cast iron.** More carbon means harder and more brittle, less ductile and less weldable.

questions.stem: The property of a material by which it can be drawn out or elongated to an appreciable extent before rupture is called:
questions.solution:
**Ductility.**

The four are constantly interchanged in the options, so fix them by the *shape produced*:

| Property | Definition | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| **Ductility** | Can be drawn out / elongated appreciably before rupture | Drawn into **wire** |
| Malleability | Can be hammered or rolled without rupture | Beaten into **sheets** |
| Toughness | Resists fracture under impact; absorbs energy | Survives a **blow** |
| Hardness | Resists indentation, scratching, abrasion | Resists a **scratch** |

Ductility is measured in a tensile test as **percentage elongation** or percentage reduction in area. It is the property that matters most in structural design: a ductile member gives visible warning and redistributes load before it fails, which is why IS 1786 sets minimum elongation for reinforcement and why seismic design depends on it.

Also keep the opposites straight: **brittleness** is the absence of ductility, and **plasticity** is the ability to retain deformation permanently after the load is removed.

examTip.trap: Malleability is the deliberate near-miss, and the two are constantly swapped. Malleability is about being **hammered into sheets**, not drawn into wire.
examTip.trick: The question says "drawn out or elongated" — that is tension, and tension is ductility.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ductile → Drawn into wire. Malleable → Mallet into sheet.**

questions.stem: For formwork that is to be reused repeatedly in concrete construction, the preferred material is:
questions.solution:
**Steel.**

The deciding factor is the number of reuses, and steel is far ahead:

| Formwork | Approximate reuses |
|---|---|
| Timber | 8 – 10 |
| Plywood | 20 – 25 |
| **Steel** | **100 – 2000+** |

Steel also gives a smooth, uniform finish, is dimensionally stable (it does not absorb water, swell or warp as timber does), needs no propping against deflection at normal spans, and is easily fabricated into repeating panels for columns, walls and slabs.

The trade-off, which is why timber has not disappeared: steel has a high initial cost, is heavy to handle, corrodes if not oiled, and is uneconomical for one-off or irregular shapes. So steel is chosen precisely when the same shape is cast many times — the condition stated in the question.

examTip.trick: Choose formwork by number of uses: **timber** about 10–12 uses, **plywood** 20–25, **steel** **100+**. For repeated reuse the higher first cost is recovered easily.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steel formwork costs more once and pays back a hundred times.** It also gives a smoother finish and truer dimensions.

questions.stem: The arrangement made to support an unsafe structure temporarily is known as:
questions.solution:
**Shoring.**

These four are a classic matched set:

| Term | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Shoring** | **Temporary support to a structure that is unsafe, cracked, leaning, or has had a wall removed** |
| Underpinning | Strengthening or deepening an existing **foundation** |
| Scaffolding | Temporary **working platform** for workers and materials at height |
| Formwork (shuttering) | Temporary **mould** that holds wet concrete until it hardens |

Types of shoring, which is the usual follow-up question:
- **Raking (inclined) shore** — inclined members bearing against the wall, at 45°–75°, best near 45°
- **Flying (horizontal) shore** — spans horizontally between two parallel walls, leaving the ground clear
- **Dead (vertical) shore** — vertical props carrying the load down, used when rebuilding a wall or inserting an opening; works with needles through the wall

So shoring supports the *superstructure*, while underpinning treats the *substructure*.

examTip.trap: Underpinning and scaffolding are both offered and both are wrong for this definition — underpinning strengthens the **foundation**, scaffolding is a **working platform**.
examTip.trick: Shoring types: **raking** (inclined props to a wall), **flying** (spanning between two walls), **dead/vertical** (supporting from below).
examTip.mnemonic: **SHoring SHores up a wall. Underpinning goes UNDER the foundation.**

questions.stem: The process of roughening a surface before plastering is called:
questions.solution:
**Hacking.**

Hacking is the deliberate roughening of a smooth or dense background — typically a concrete surface — by chipping it with a hacking tool so that the plaster has something to grip. Without it, plaster applied to smooth concrete or to a very dense brick surface debonds and falls away in sheets.

The related terms, which appear as distractors:
- **Dubbing out** — filling deep hollows in the background with mortar *before* the first plaster coat, so the coat thickness stays even.
- **Keying** — the general principle of providing a mechanical grip; hacking is one way to achieve a key, as is raking out the mortar joints.
- **Rendering** — the name of the **first coat** of plaster (the base coat) on masonry.

Plaster coat names in order: **rendering coat** (first) → **floating coat** (second) → **finishing/setting coat** (final). For three-coat work the first is also called the scratch coat.

Before plastering, the surface must in general be **raked out, cleaned, roughened and thoroughly wetted**.

examTip.trick: The purpose is mechanical key. On concrete the same job is done by hacking; on smooth brickwork the joints are raked out instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hack it so the plaster has something to hold.**

questions.stem: In a stair flight, the number of treads is equal to:
options: The number of risers plus one
The number of risers minus one
questions.solution:
**The number of risers minus one.**

In a flight the risers and treads alternate, but the flight begins and ends on a riser — the last "tread" is the landing itself, which is not counted as a tread of the flight. So

> Number of treads = number of risers − 1

**Worked check.** A floor-to-floor height of 3.0 m with a 150 mm rise needs 3000 / 150 = **20 risers**, and therefore **19 treads** in that flight.

Related rules worth carrying in:
- **2R + T ≈ 600 mm** (or R + T ≈ 450 mm) for a comfortable stair
- Rise 150–190 mm and tread 250–300 mm for residential buildings
- A single flight should not have more than about 12–15 risers before a landing

So a question giving the floor height and rise is really asking you to divide, then subtract one.

examTip.trap: "Equal to the number of risers" is the instinctive answer and it is wrong by exactly one, every time.
examTip.trick: Picture a single step up onto a landing: one riser, no tread of its own. The top riser always lands on the floor above.
examTip.mnemonic: **One more riser than tread — always.** Check with 2R + T ≈ 600 mm for a comfortable stair.

questions.stem: The dressing of stone should be done:
options: After the stone has fully dried
questions.solution:
**Immediately after quarrying.**

Freshly quarried stone still holds its **quarry sap** — the natural moisture in its pores — and while that moisture is present the stone is comparatively soft and easy to cut, dress and carve. As the sap dries out the stone hardens, and dressing then costs far more effort and risks damaging the block.

Dressing at the quarry has a second advantage: waste is removed before transport, so haulage is cheaper.

The apparent contradiction to watch for: **seasoning of stone** *is* recommended — about 6 to 12 months of exposure so the quarry sap evaporates and the stone hardens before it is loaded in the work. The resolution is the order of operations: **dress first, while the stone is soft; then season the dressed stone before use.** Both statements are examined, and both are correct in their own place.

examTip.trick: Freshly quarried stone contains **quarry sap** — natural moisture that makes it markedly softer and easier to work. Once it dries out it hardens and dressing becomes slow and costly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dress it wet, before the sap dries.**

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a rectangular section of width b and depth d about a horizontal axis passing through its base is:
questions.solution:
**bd³/3.**

Start from the centroidal value and shift the axis with the parallel-axis theorem.

About the centroidal axis parallel to the width:

> I_{xx} = bd³/12

The base is a distance d/2 from the centroid, and the area is A = bd, so

> I_{base} = I_{xx} + A·h²
> I_{base} = bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)²
> I_{base} = bd³/12 + bd³/4
> I_{base} = bd³/12 + 3bd³/12 = **4bd³/12 = bd³/3**

The standard set to memorise:

| Section | About centroid | About base |
|---|---|---|
| Rectangle (b × d) | bd³/12 | **bd³/3** |
| Triangle (b × h) | bh³/36 | bh³/12 |
| Circle (dia. d) | πd⁴/64 | — |
| Semicircle (dia. d) | — | πd⁴/128 |

Note **db³/12** is the moment of inertia about the *vertical* centroidal axis (I_{yy}) — a deliberate distractor.

examTip.trap: bd³/12 is the reflex answer, but that is about the **centroidal** axis. The question asks about the **base**.
examTip.trick: Parallel axis theorem: bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)² = bd³/12 + bd³/4 = **bd³/3**. Note the base value is **four times** the centroidal one.
examTip.mnemonic: **12 at the centre, 3 at the base.**

questions.stem: The second moment of area of a hollow circular section with external diameter 20 cm and internal diameter 10 cm about its diametral axis is:
questions.solution:
**7363.11 cm⁴.**

For a hollow circular section about a diameter,

> I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64

Substituting D = 20 cm and d = 10 cm:

> D⁴ = 20⁴ = 160000 cm⁴
> d⁴ = 10⁴ = 10000 cm⁴
> D⁴ − d⁴ = 150000 cm⁴

> I = π × 150000 / 64
> I = 471238.9 / 64
> I = **7363.11 cm⁴**

**Traps in the options.** 14726.22 is twice the answer — that is the *polar* moment of inertia J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32, which applies to torsion, not bending. 1963.50 cm⁴ is πd⁴/64 for the 10 cm bore alone.

Companion formula for the same section:

> Section modulus, Z = I / (D/2) = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D)

examTip.trick: Hollow sections simply subtract: **I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 = π(20⁴ − 10⁴)/64 = π(160000 − 10000)/64 = 7363 cm⁴.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Fourth power.** Halving the inner diameter removes only one sixteenth of the material's contribution — which is why hollow sections are so efficient.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a triangular section about an axis through its vertex and parallel to the base is how many times that about an axis through its centroid parallel to the base?
questions.solution:
**9 times.**

For a triangle of base b and height h, the centroid lies at h/3 from the base, and therefore **2h/3 from the vertex**.

Centroidal value:
> I_{G} = bh³/36

Apply the parallel-axis theorem to shift to the vertex, with A = bh/2 and distance 2h/3:

> I_{vertex} = I_{G} + A·(2h/3)²
> I_{vertex} = bh³/36 + (bh/2)(4h²/9)
> I_{vertex} = bh³/36 + 4bh³/18
> I_{vertex} = bh³/36 + 8bh³/36 = **9bh³/36 = bh³/4**

Ratio:
> I_{vertex} / I_{G} = (bh³/4) / (bh³/36) = **9**

For completeness, the same triangle about its **base** (distance h/3 from the centroid):

> I_{base} = bh³/36 + (bh/2)(h/3)² = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = bh³/12

So the three values line up as bh³/36 (centroid) : bh³/12 (base) : bh³/4 (vertex) = 1 : 3 : 9.

examTip.trick: Three values for a triangle, all with bh³: **/36 about the centroid, /12 about the base, /4 about the vertex.** The ratio asked for is (1/4)/(1/36) = 9.
examTip.mnemonic: **36, 12, 4** — centroid, base, vertex. Each step up is a factor of 3.

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a solid hemisphere of radius r, measured from its plane base, lies at:
questions.solution:
**3r/8 from the base.**

This is a standard result for the *solid* hemisphere and is best memorised alongside its neighbours, because the options usually mix them:

| Body | Centroid, measured from the base |
|---|---|
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** |
| Hemispherical shell (surface) | r/2 |
| Semicircular lamina (area) | 4r/3π |
| Solid cone, height h | h/4 |
| Triangle, height h | h/3 |
| Solid pyramid, height h | h/4 |

Each distractor in this question is one of those neighbours: r/2 is the hemispherical *shell*, 4r/3π is the semicircular *lamina*, and 3r/4 is simply the complement of 3r/8 misremembered.

A quick sanity check: the hemisphere has more material near the base than near the pole, so its centroid must sit **below** the mid-height r/2. And 3r/8 = 0.375r < 0.5r, which is consistent.

examTip.trap: r/2 is the value for a **hollow** hemisphere and is the usual wrong pick.
examTip.trick: The solid hemisphere has more material near the flat base, so its centroid must sit **lower** than the hollow shell's. 3r/8 < r/2 ✓ — the inequality alone identifies the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid 3r/8, hollow r/2.** Solid sits lower.

questions.stem: The radius of gyration of a section is given by:
questions.solution:
**√(I/A).**

The radius of gyration k is defined so that, if the whole area A were concentrated at a distance k from the axis, it would give the same moment of inertia:

> I = A·k²  ⟹  **k = √(I/A)**

So k is proportional to the square root of the moment of inertia, and to the square root of the reciprocal of the area — which is exactly why all three of those phrasings appear as "correct" in some collections; they are the same statement.

Its units are those of length (mm, cm), not length⁴.

**Where it is used.** The radius of gyration is the shape parameter that governs buckling. In Euler's formula the critical stress depends on the **slenderness ratio** λ = l_{e}/k, so for a given area a section with a larger k (material pushed away from the axis, like a tube or an I-section) buckles at a higher load. That is the reason hollow sections are preferred for struts.

For a rectangle b × d about the centroidal axis:
> k = √((bd³/12)/(bd)) = **d/√12 = 0.2887 d**

examTip.trick: Check the units: I is in m⁴ and A in m², so √(I/A) has units of **metres** — a length, which a radius must be. Every other option fails dimensionally.
examTip.mnemonic: **k = √(I/A)**, and slenderness ratio is L/k. It is the distance at which all the area could be concentrated without changing I.

questions.stem: The perpendicular axis theorem is applicable to:
questions.solution:
**Plane laminae only.**

The perpendicular axis theorem states that for a **plane lamina**, the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane (the polar moment, I_{zz}) equals the sum of the moments of inertia about any two mutually perpendicular axes in the plane, meeting at the same point:

> **I_{zz} = I_{xx} + I_{yy}**

Its derivation uses r² = x² + y², which holds only because every element of the lamina lies in one plane — hence the restriction. It cannot be applied to a three-dimensional solid.

**Worked use, for a circular lamina of diameter d:**
> I_{xx} = I_{yy} = πd⁴/64
> I_{zz} = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = **πd⁴/32**

which is the familiar polar moment of inertia J used in torsion.

Do not confuse it with the **parallel axis theorem**, I = I_{G} + Ah², which shifts an axis to another *parallel* axis and applies to laminae and solids alike.

examTip.trap: "All bodies" is the trap. The perpendicular axis theorem applies **only to plane laminae**; the parallel axis theorem applies to everything.
examTip.trick: **I_zz = I_xx + I_yy** only works when all the material lies in one plane — the z-distances must be zero for the derivation to hold.
examTip.mnemonic: **Perpendicular = flat only. Parallel = anything.**

questions.stem: A plinth area estimate is prepared on the basis of:
options: The carpet area of the building
The plinth area of the building
The cubical contents of the building
The number of rooms in the building
questions.solution:
**The plinth area of the building, priced at a rate taken from a similar recently-built building.**

A plinth area estimate is an **approximate (preliminary) estimate**:

> Estimated cost = plinth area (m²) × plinth area rate (Rs/m²)

The plinth area rate is deduced from the actual cost of a comparable completed building of similar specification, height and locality, so the estimate is only as good as that comparison.

**Plinth area** is the built-up covered area measured at floor level to the **external face of the walls**, including internal walls but excluding open courtyards and cantilevered projections.

The family of approximate estimates:

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Plinth area** | Area at plinth level × rate |
| Cubical content | Plinth area × height, × rate per m³ — more accurate, since it accounts for storey height |
| Unit base / unit rate | Cost per unit (per bed for a hospital, per student for a school) |
| Service unit | Cost per functional unit (per kW, per km) |

Related numbers examined alongside this: **carpet area is about 50–65% of plinth area**, and the plinth area is roughly **60–75% of the total plot area** under typical bye-laws.

At a rate derived from a similar building.

examTip.trick: Rank the estimate types by precision: **plinth area** (roughest, per m² of plinth), **cubic content** (per m³), **approximate quantity**, then **detailed estimate** (most precise, item by item).
examTip.mnemonic: **Plinth area is the back-of-envelope figure** — used at the feasibility stage, never for tendering.

questions.stem: The process of determining the rate per unit of an item of work, including the cost of materials, labour, plant, overheads and profit, is called:
questions.solution:
**Rate analysis.**

Rate analysis builds up the rate for a unit of finished work (per m³ of concrete, per m² of plaster) from its constituents:

1. **Materials** — quantity per unit of work, at current market rates, plus wastage
2. **Labour** — the number of each class of worker per unit, at scheduled wages
3. **Plant and machinery** — hire or depreciation charges
4. **Overheads** — usually taken as a percentage (water charges, supervision, establishment)
5. **Contractor's profit** — commonly about **10–15%**

The sum is the rate that goes into the bill of quantities.

Distinguish the neighbours carefully — each is a separate exam item:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rate analysis** | **Working out the rate per unit of an item of work** |
| Detailed estimate | Quantities of every item × their rates, giving the total project cost |
| **Valuation** | Determining the *present worth* of an existing property |
| Specification | A written description of the materials, workmanship and quality required — it fixes *how*, not *how much* |

examTip.trick: Rate analysis builds the unit rate from its parts: **materials + labour + plant + overheads + profit** (contractor's profit usually 10–15%).
examTip.mnemonic: **Rate analysis answers "what does one cubic metre actually cost me?"** — as distinct from measuring how many cubic metres there are.

questions.stem: The standard specimen for the compressive strength test on concrete is a cube of side:
questions.solution:
**150 mm.**

The standard cube for the compressive strength test under **IS 516** is **150 × 150 × 150 mm**, cast in three layers, each compacted by 35 strokes of a 16 mm tamping rod or by a vibrating table.

| Detail | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Standard cube | **150 mm** |
| Smaller cube permitted | **100 mm**, when the nominal maximum aggregate size does not exceed 20 mm |
| Curing | Demoulded at **24 ± 0.5 h**, then in water at **27 ± 2 °C** |
| Test ages | **7 days** (an early check) and **28 days** (the specified strength) |
| Rate of loading | **140 kg/cm² per minute** |
| Number per sample | **3 cubes**; the average is the sample strength |

The 100 mm cube (option a) is the trap — it is *permitted*, but only for smaller aggregate, and it is not the standard specimen.

**Why 28 days.** Ordinary Portland cement reaches roughly **65–70% of its 28-day strength at 7 days**, and continues to gain slowly for years. Twenty-eight days is the practical compromise between representing the concrete's real strength and getting an answer before the next stage of construction is built.

**Why a cube rather than a cylinder.** Indian and Nepali practice uses the cube; American and European practice uses a **150 × 300 mm cylinder**. They are not interchangeable:

> **Cylinder strength ≈ 0.8 × cube strength**

because the cube is more heavily confined by platen friction over its shorter height, which restrains lateral expansion and raises the apparent strength. A grade written as M25 refers to the **cube**.

**The acceptance rule.** An individual result may fall below the grade strength; what must be satisfied is the running average of four consecutive samples together with a minimum for each individual result — so one low cube is investigated, not automatically a rejection.

examTip.trap: 100 mm is offered and is a real size — permitted when the maximum aggregate is 20 mm or less — but the **standard** specimen is 150 mm.
examTip.trick: Remember the companion figures: cylinder **150 × 300 mm**, and **cylinder strength ≈ 0.8 × cube strength** for the same concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **150 cube, 150×300 cylinder, 0.8 between them.**

questions.stem: The slump test on fresh concrete is a measure of its:
questions.solution:
**Workability.**

The slump test (**IS 1199**) measures the vertical subsidence of a fresh concrete cone after the mould is lifted — a simple index of how easily the mix can be placed and compacted.

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Mould | Frustum of a cone, **200 mm** bottom, **100 mm** top, **300 mm** high |
| Filling | **4 layers**, each rodded **25 times** |
| Result | The **subsidence in mm** after lifting the mould |

**Typical slump ranges by application:**

| Work | Slump |
|---|---|
| Road pavements, mass concrete | **20 – 50 mm** |
| Ordinary RCC — beams, slabs | **50 – 100 mm** |
| Heavily reinforced or congested sections | **100 – 150 mm** |
| Concrete placed by **tremie or pump** | **150 – 200 mm** |

**Its limitation, and why other tests exist.** The slump test is insensitive at both extremes — a very dry mix gives zero slump whatever its true workability, and a very wet mix simply collapses. Hence:

| Test | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Slump** | **Medium** workability; the site standard for its simplicity |
| **Compaction factor** | **Low** workability, dry mixes |
| **Vee-Bee consistometer** | **Very dry** mixes |
| **Flow table** | **Very wet** or flowing mixes |

**The types of slump are themselves diagnostic**, which is where option (c) comes in:

| Slump shape | Indicates |
|---|---|
| **True slump** | A satisfactory, cohesive mix |
| **Shear slump** | A **harsh, non-cohesive** mix — half the cone slides off; the mix is prone to **segregation** |
| **Collapse slump** | Far too wet |

So the test *reveals* a segregation tendency through the shape of the slump, but the quantity it **measures** is workability. Strength (a) needs the cube test and durability (b) the water–cement ratio and cover — neither is measurable on fresh concrete with a cone.

examTip.trap: "Strength" is the reflex wrong answer. Slump says nothing about strength — a high-slump mix from too much water is *weaker*, not stronger.
examTip.trick: Slump measures the **yield stress** of the fresh mix. Use the vee-bee or compaction factor test for very dry mixes where slump reads near zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **Slump is about placing, not about strength.**

questions.stem: The specific surface of ordinary Portland cement, determined by the air permeability method, shall not be less than:
questions.solution:
**225 m²/kg.**

Fineness is measured either as the **residue on a 90-micron sieve** (not more than 10% by mass) or, more precisely, as the **specific surface area** by the **Blaine air permeability** apparatus, for which the minimum is **225 m²/kg**.

The air permeability method works by timing the passage of a fixed volume of air through a compacted bed of cement of known porosity — the finer the cement, the greater the resistance and the longer the time.

**Why fineness matters.** Hydration proceeds from the **surface** of each grain inward, so a finer cement has more surface exposed to water at any moment:

| Finer cement | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Faster hydration** | Higher **early strength** |
| **Greater heat of hydration** | A risk of **thermal cracking** in mass concrete |
| **Better cohesion**, less bleeding | Improved workability retention |
| **More prone to shrinkage** | And to **air-setting** in storage |
| More expensive | Grinding is the costly stage of manufacture |

So fineness is not simply "more is better": **rapid hardening cement** is ground finer (about 325 m²/kg) precisely to gain early strength, while **low heat cement** is ground *coarser* to slow the heat release in a dam or raft.

**The related fineness limits:**

| Cement | Minimum specific surface |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland (33, 43, 53 grade)** | **225 m²/kg** |
| Rapid hardening | 325 m²/kg |
| Portland pozzolana | 300 m²/kg |
| Low heat | 320 m²/kg (but with a heat-of-hydration limit) |

**Do not confuse fineness with the other cement tests**, each of which has its own apparatus: **consistency and setting time** by the **Vicat** apparatus, **soundness** by **Le Chatelier** (or the autoclave test for delayed expansion), and **strength** on **70.6 mm mortar cubes** of 1:3 cement–standard sand.

examTip.trick: Specific surface is a measure of **fineness**. Finer cement hydrates faster, gains early strength faster, and also generates more heat and shrinks more.
examTip.mnemonic: **225 m²/kg minimum for OPC** — rapid hardening cement is finer still, at 325.

questions.stem: As per IS 383, fine aggregate for concrete is classified into how many grading zones?
questions.solution:
**Four.**

IS 383 groups sand into **Grading Zones I, II, III and IV**, from coarsest to finest, according to the percentage passing each standard sieve.

| Zone | Character | Suitability |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | **Coarsest** | Good, but needs a higher fine-aggregate proportion |
| **II** | Medium | **Most suitable for general concrete** |
| **III** | Fine | Usable, with the proportion adjusted |
| **IV** | **Finest** | **Not recommended** for reinforced concrete unless tested |

**Zone II is the reference.** Mix design tables are drawn up for Zone II sand, and using sand from another zone requires the fine-aggregate content to be corrected — increased for the coarser Zone I, reduced for the finer Zone III.

**The single number that summarises a grading** is the **fineness modulus**: the sum of the cumulative percentages retained on the standard sieves, divided by 100. It represents the average sieve on which the material is retained.

| Aggregate | Fineness modulus |
|---|---|
| **Fine sand** | 2.2 – 2.6 |
| **Medium sand** | 2.6 – 2.9 |
| **Coarse sand** | 2.9 – 3.2 |
| Coarse aggregate | 5.5 – 8.0 |

A **higher** fineness modulus means a **coarser** aggregate — the relation candidates most often invert.

**Why grading matters at all.** A **well-graded** aggregate has particles of many sizes, so the smaller ones fill the voids between the larger. That means fewer voids to fill with paste, hence **less cement and water for the same workability**, and therefore higher strength and lower cost. A **uniformly graded** (single-size) aggregate has the most voids; a **gap-graded** one omits intermediate sizes deliberately.

The demarcation itself: **fine aggregate passes the 4.75 mm sieve**, coarse aggregate is retained on it. All-in aggregate is the two together as dug, and is not accepted for structural concrete because its proportions cannot be controlled.

examTip.trick: Four zones, from **Zone I (coarsest) to Zone IV (finest)**. Zone II is the general-purpose sand for structural concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **Four zones, and the number rises as the sand gets finer.** Zone IV needs care — it demands more water and more cement.

questions.stem: The characteristic yield strength of Fe 500 reinforcing steel is:
questions.solution:
**500 N/mm².**

The grade designation of reinforcing steel **is** its characteristic yield strength (or 0.2% proof stress) in N/mm² — so Fe 500 means f_y = 500 N/mm². The number needs no memorising once that is seen.

**The grades under IS 1786 and IS 432:**

| Grade | f_y (N/mm²) | Minimum elongation | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **250** | 23% | **Mild steel**, plain round bars (IS 432) |
| **Fe 415** | 415 | 14.5% | HYSD / TMT |
| **Fe 500** | **500** | **12%** | HYSD / TMT — now the commonest |
| Fe 550 | 550 | 10% | HYSD / TMT |
| Fe 600 | 600 | 10% | HYSD / TMT |

Notice the trade-off in the third column: **as strength rises, ductility falls.** That is why the higher grades are not automatically better. A structure in a seismic zone must **deform without collapsing**, which requires ductility, so codes place limits on the grade used in earthquake-resisting members and specify **Fe 500D** (D for higher ductility) where high strength and ductility are both wanted.

That point is central for Nepal, which lies in a high seismic zone: the reinforcement must yield and absorb energy rather than fracture.

**In design, the value used is the factored one:**

> **Design yield strength = f_y / γ_m = f_y / 1.15 = 0.87 f_y**

so Fe 500 contributes **435 N/mm²** at the limit state of collapse; and for concrete, γ_m = 1.5 gives 0.67 f_ck/1.5 = **0.446 f_ck**. The two partial safety factors differ because steel is a manufactured product of far more consistent quality than site-made concrete.

**TMT versus cold-twisted.** **TMT (thermo-mechanically treated)** bars are quenched and self-tempered, giving a hard surface with a softer, ductile core — they are more ductile, more weldable and more corrosion-resistant than the older **CTD (cold-twisted deformed)** bars, which is why TMT has replaced CTD in practice.

The **surface deformations** (ribs) are what develop the bond with concrete; a plain mild steel bar relies on adhesion alone, which is why it needs **hooks and bends** at its ends.

examTip.trick: The grade number **is** the characteristic yield strength in N/mm². Fe250, Fe415, Fe500, Fe550 — no conversion needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **The number is the strength.** Design strength is then 0.87 × f_y, so Fe500 designs at 435 N/mm².

questions.stem: In the field sedimentation (bulk) test on sand, the silt content by volume should generally not exceed:
questions.solution:
**8% by volume.**

The field test is deliberately crude and needs no laboratory: a measuring cylinder is part-filled with a salt solution, sand added to a marked level, shaken, and left to stand for about three hours. The **silt settles as a distinct layer on top of the sand**, and its thickness is read as a percentage of the sand depth. The customary field limit is **8%**.

**Why silt is harmful.** Silt and clay are far finer than sand, so a given mass presents an enormous surface area. The consequences:

| Effect | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Higher water demand** | The fines must be wetted; more water means **lower strength** |
| **Weakened bond** | Clay coats the aggregate, so the paste bonds to the coating rather than to the stone |
| **More shrinkage** | Clay itself shrinks on drying |
| **Reduced durability** | A more porous, permeable concrete |

The second is the most damaging: a **clay coating** on an otherwise sound aggregate destroys the paste–aggregate bond, which is where concrete normally fails.

**Distinguish the field limit from the laboratory limits in IS 383**, which are by **mass** and separately stated — this is the distinction the question turns on:

| Deleterious material | Uncrushed sand | Crushed sand |
|---|---|---|
| **Material finer than 75 micron** | **3%** | **15%** |
| Clay lumps | 1% | 1% |
| Coal and lignite | 1% | 1% |
| Total deleterious (excluding fines) | 5% | 2% |

So **3%** (option a) and **15%** (option c) are both real limits — but for *crushed and uncrushed fines by mass* under IS 383, not for the field volumetric test. Both are offered here because a candidate who has memorised one table without noting which quantity it governs will pick the wrong one.

**The remedy** where sand exceeds the limit is **washing**, which is routine for river sand from a silty reach. Where washing is impractical, the mix must be redesigned for the higher water demand — never simply accepted.

**Bulking must not be confused with this.** Moist sand occupies a greater volume because surface moisture films push the grains apart — up to **20–40% at about 4–5% moisture** — which matters when batching **by volume**, and is corrected either by measuring the bulking or, far better, by **batching by mass**.

verification.notes: The 8% figure is the customary field volumetric limit; IS 383's tabulated limits are by mass (3% uncrushed, 15% crushed) and are stated in the solution so the candidate sees which quantity each governs.

examTip.trick: This is the jar test any site can run: sand and water in a measuring cylinder, left to settle, and the silt layer read off as a percentage of the sand column.
examTip.mnemonic: **8% by the field jar test, 3% by the laboratory sieve.** Excess silt coats the grains and destroys the cement–aggregate bond.

questions.stem: In Nepal, the certification mark showing that a product conforms to a Nepal Standard is the:
questions.solution:
**The NS mark.**

The **NS (Nepal Standard) mark** is administered by the **Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology (NBSM)** under the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, by authority of the **Nepal Standards (Certification Mark) Act, 2037 (1980)**.

| Mark | Body | Country / region |
|---|---|---|
| **NS** | **Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology** | **Nepal** |
| **ISI** | Bureau of Indian Standards | India |
| **CE** | European conformity marking | European Economic Area |
| **BIS hallmark** | Bureau of Indian Standards | India — for **precious metals** specifically |

**Why this matters for a civil engineer rather than being mere trivia.** For certain products the NS mark is **mandatory**, and **cement is the leading example** — a consignment without valid NS certification should not be accepted on site. The same applies to reinforcing steel bars, which must carry the manufacturer's mark and grade rolled onto the bar.

**How the Nepali and Indian standards relate in practice.** Nepal has its own **NS** series, but for many materials and design procedures Nepali practice **adopts or closely follows the Indian Standards** — IS 456 for concrete design, IS 800 for steel, IS 1200 for measurement. The codes with a distinctly Nepali character are those tied to local conditions:

| Nepali code | Governs |
|---|---|
| **NBC (Nepal National Building Code)** series | Building design and construction, including seismic |
| **NBC 105** | **Seismic design of buildings in Nepal** — revised 2020 |
| **Nepal Road Standard 2070** | Road geometry and classification |
| **Nepal Building Code / municipal bye-laws** | Setbacks, ground coverage, height |

**NBC 105:2020** is the one to know by name: it replaced the 1994 edition, introduced modern spectral shapes and ductility classes, and reflects what was learned from the **2015 Gorkha earthquake**.

A standard mark is a claim about **conformity**, not about **suitability** — an NS-marked cement is genuine 43-grade OPC, but whether 43-grade OPC is right for the work in hand remains the engineer's judgement.

examTip.trick: Keep the certification marks separate: **NS** is Nepal Standard, **ISI** is the Indian equivalent, and **CE** is European conformity.
examTip.mnemonic: **NS for Nepal**, administered by the Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology.

questions.stem: The aggregate impact value of aggregate used in concrete for wearing surfaces should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**30%.**

The **aggregate impact value (AIV)** measures resistance to **sudden shock or impact**, as distinct from a gradually applied load. A 15-hammer-blow test is performed and the AIV is the percentage of material passing a 2.36 mm sieve afterwards — so a **lower value means a tougher aggregate**.

**The limits under IS 2386 Part 4:**

| Application | Maximum AIV |
|---|---|
| **Wearing surfaces** — pavements, floors | **30%** |
| **Concrete other than wearing surfaces** | **45%** |
| Bituminous surface dressing | 30% |
| Bituminous macadam | 35% |

Both **30%** and **45%** are genuine limits, which is why they are both offered — the question specifies a **wearing surface**, so 30% governs. A candidate who has memorised only "45%" will answer wrongly.

**Why a wearing surface needs the stricter limit.** It is directly exposed to wheel impact, braking and abrasion, with no covering layer to distribute the load. Concrete beneath a screed or inside a beam never sees that.

**The strength and durability tests, each measuring a different thing** — the set these limits belong to:

| Test | Property | Typical limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | **30% / 45%** |
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradually applied load** | **30% / 45%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | Resistance to **wear** | 30% wearing, 50% other |
| **Soundness** (sodium/magnesium sulphate) | Resistance to **weathering** | 12% / 18% |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | 0.6% preferred; 2% maximum |
| **Specific gravity** | Quality | 2.6 – 2.9 |
| **Flakiness / elongation index** | **Shape** | 25% / 15% |

Note that the impact and crushing tests carry the **same numerical limits** but are not interchangeable: an aggregate can be strong under a slowly applied load yet brittle under impact. The impact test was developed as the **field alternative**, being quicker and needing no compression machine.

**The 10% fines value** (not option a here, but worth knowing) is the preferred test for **weaker** aggregates, where the crushing value becomes unreliable because the material crushes progressively rather than at a definable load.

examTip.trick: Two limits, and the tougher one applies where the surface is trafficked: **30% for wearing surfaces, 45% for other concrete.** The same 30/45 split applies to the aggregate crushing value.
examTip.mnemonic: **30 for wearing, 45 for the rest** — impact and crushing values both.

questions.stem: The characteristic compressive strength on which the grade designation M25 is based is the strength below which:
options: Not more than 10% of test results are expected to fall
Not more than 1% of test results are expected to fall
Not more than 5% of test results are expected to fall
questions.solution:
**Not more than 5% of test results are expected to fall.**

> **Characteristic strength** = the strength below which not more than **5%** of test results are expected to fall.

So M25 means a **28-day cube strength of 25 N/mm²** at the **5% fractile** — the letter M standing for *mix*, the number for that characteristic strength.

**Why it is defined statistically rather than as a minimum.** Concrete is made from natural materials, batched and compacted on site, so its strength is inherently **variable** — the results of many cubes from nominally identical concrete form an approximately **normal distribution**. Demanding that *no* result ever fall below 25 (option a) would require a mean so high as to be absurdly wasteful. Accepting a defined small proportion below the value is the honest and economical approach.

**This is what drives the mix design target:**

> **Target mean strength f'_ck = f_ck + 1.65 σ**

where the **1.65** is the standard normal deviate for the 5% fractile, and **σ** is the expected standard deviation. IS 10262 gives σ by grade — about **4.0 N/mm²** for M20–M25 and **5.0** for M30–M45.

**A worked illustration for M25:** target mean = 25 + 1.65 × 4.0 = **31.6 N/mm²**. The mix must be designed for roughly 31.6, not 25 — a point routinely missed, and the reason a mix designed "for M25" at exactly 25 fails acceptance about half the time.

**Note the consequence of better control.** A contractor with tight quality control has a smaller σ, so the same characteristic strength is achieved with a **lower target mean** — and therefore **less cement**. Good quality control pays for itself directly.

**The related definitions in the same family:**

| Term | Fractile |
|---|---|
| **Characteristic strength of concrete or steel** | **5%** below |
| **Characteristic load** | **5%** chance of being **exceeded** |

Both take the unfavourable 5% tail — low for strength, high for load — which is what makes the limit state method a consistent probabilistic framework rather than a set of arbitrary factors.

Grades run **M10 to M80** in IS 456, with **M20 the minimum for reinforced concrete** in normal exposure and higher minima for severe exposure conditions.

examTip.trap: "5% expected to exceed" is the reversed distractor and is very easy to pick under time pressure. Characteristic strength is the **lower** 5% fractile, so results fall *below* it.
examTip.trick: **f_ck = f_mean − 1.65σ.** The 1.65 is the standard normal value for 5%.
examTip.mnemonic: **Characteristic strength is the value 95% of results beat.** M25 means 25 N/mm², not an average.

questions.stem: The strongest bond in brickwork is:
questions.solution:
**English bond.**

English bond lays **alternate courses entirely of headers and entirely of stretchers**. Because a whole course of headers ties the two leaves of the wall together at once, it gives the best possible transverse bond and is the **strongest** arrangement.

**The bonds compared:**

| Bond | Arrangement | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **English** | Alternate **courses** of headers and stretchers | **Strongest**; the standard for load-bearing work |
| **Flemish** | Headers and stretchers **alternating within every course** | **Better appearance**, more economical in facing bricks, but **weaker** |
| **Stretcher** | All stretchers | Only for **half-brick** walls — partitions, and the leaves of a cavity wall |
| **Header** | All headers | Only for **curved** work and one-brick-thick footings |

The trade-off is the point worth carrying: **English bond for strength, Flemish for appearance.** Flemish is weaker because it uses more broken bricks (queen closers at every alternate course end) and its internal joints are less continuous.

**Why bonding exists at all.** The purpose is to **break the continuity of vertical joints** between successive courses. If vertical joints coincided, the wall would behave as a stack of independent narrow piers instead of one monolith, and a load applied at any point would not distribute sideways.

**The rules that follow from that purpose:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Vertical joints must **not coincide** in successive courses | Continuity of the wall |
| The lap should be **¼ brick** | The standard offset achieving it |
| **Queen closers** are placed **next to the quoin header** | To start the lap, never at the corner itself |
| **Brick bats** are avoided as far as possible | They weaken the work |
| Courses must be **truly horizontal** | The load must act normal to the bed |

**The closers**, whose names are examined constantly:

| Closer | Cut |
|---|---|
| **Queen closer** | Cut **lengthwise**, giving half the **width** |
| **King closer** | Cut **diagonally** across one end — half header, half stretcher |
| **Bevelled closer** | Bevelled along the length |
| **Mitred closer** | Cut at an angle across the width |

And note **Flemish bond has two varieties**: **double** Flemish, which presents the alternating pattern on *both* faces, and **single** Flemish, which shows Flemish bond on the face and English bond behind — combining appearance with strength, at the cost of more skilled labour.

examTip.trap: Flemish bond is the elegant wrong answer — it looks better and is often preferred for facework, but it is the **weaker** of the two.
examTip.trick: English bond alternates whole courses of headers and stretchers, giving no continuous vertical joint through the thickness. Flemish alternates within each course, which leaves more internal straight joints.
examTip.mnemonic: **English is strong, Flemish is fancy.**

questions.stem: The material most commonly used as a damp proof course in ordinary building construction is:
questions.solution:
**Bitumen or bituminous felt.**

A damp proof course (DPC) must be **impervious, flexible and durable**, and bitumen satisfies all three. It is laid as **hot-applied bitumen**, as **bituminous felt**, or as a **cement concrete course (about 1:1½:3, 40–75 mm thick) painted with hot bitumen** — the last being the commonest form in Nepali and Indian practice.

**Why flexibility matters.** A DPC sits at a plane where slight **differential settlement** and thermal movement occur. A rigid, brittle layer would crack, and a single crack destroys the continuity on which the whole barrier depends. That is why a plain rigid cement mortar (option a) is not a DPC on its own, even though it forms the *bed* on which one is laid.

**Where a DPC goes:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **At plinth level**, across the full wall thickness | Stops **rising damp** from the ground |
| Under the **floor** (as a membrane) | Stops damp through the floor slab |
| Over **parapets and copings** | Stops water entering from above |
| At **sills and lintels** of openings | Stops lateral penetration |
| In **cavity walls**, at the base and over openings | Directs water out rather than across |

**The mechanism it defeats — rising damp — is capillary action.** Water rises through the fine pores of masonry and mortar against gravity. It carries dissolved salts, which crystallise on the surface as **efflorescence**, and the persistent moisture causes plaster to blister, paint to peel, timber to rot and reinforcement to corrode. Since the water rises through the **material**, the remedy must be a **continuous impervious plane interrupting it** — which is why continuity is everything.

**The requirements a DPC must meet:**

> **Impervious** · **continuous over the whole area** · **flexible** enough to accommodate movement · **durable** for the life of the building · not **squeezed out** under the wall load

The last is a real failure mode: too soft a bitumen under a heavy wall extrudes at the face, thinning the layer where it is needed.

**Distinguish damp proofing from waterproofing.** Damp proofing resists moisture **without hydrostatic pressure** — as at plinth level. Waterproofing resists water **under pressure**, as in a basement below the water table or a water tank, and needs a more substantial system than a DPC.

examTip.trick: A DPC has one job: **break the capillary path**. Anything continuous and impervious works — bitumen felt, mastic asphalt, dense cement concrete, or a course of engineering brick.
examTip.mnemonic: **DPC goes 150 mm above finished ground level**, and must be continuous — one gap and the damp simply walks around it.

questions.stem: The horizontal member provided across the top of a door or window opening to support the wall above is a:
questions.solution:
**A lintel.**

A lintel spans the opening and carries the masonry above it, transferring that load to the **jambs** (the wall on either side). It is the simplest solution to the fundamental problem of an opening: the wall above has nothing to stand on.

**Distinguish the members of an opening**, all four of which appear as distractors in this family of question:

| Member | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Lintel** | **Across the top** of the opening | **Supports the wall above** |
| **Sill** | **At the bottom** of a window opening | Sheds water; finishes the opening |
| **Coping** | On top of a **parapet or wall** | Sheds water off the wall top |
| **Corbel** | Projects from a wall face | Supports a beam, truss or overhanging member |
| Jamb | The **vertical sides** of the opening | Receives the lintel's load |
| Soffit | The **underside** of the lintel or arch | — |

**Lintel or arch?** Both solve the same problem by opposite mechanisms, and the comparison is the substance of the topic:

| | **Lintel** | **Arch** |
|---|---|---|
| Action | **Bending** — flexural | **Compression** only |
| Suits | Materials strong in **tension** — RCC, steel, timber | Materials strong only in **compression** — brick, stone |
| Span | Economical to moderate spans | Larger spans possible |
| Support | Vertical reaction only | Vertical **and horizontal thrust** — abutments must resist it |
| Construction | Simple; no centering | Needs **centering** until complete |

The horizontal thrust is the arch's price: it must be absorbed by a sufficient mass of abutment, by a tie, or by an adjacent arch thrusting back. That is why a row of arches needs substantial **end** piers even though the intermediate ones are slender.

**Practical lintel rules.** The **bearing** at each end is at least **the depth of the lintel or 100 mm**, whichever is greater. Where the wall above is high, the load on the lintel is *not* the full height of masonry above it — an **arching action** develops in the brickwork, so only a triangular or limited portion is taken as acting on the lintel.

A lintel that projects to carry a **sunshade** over the opening is a **chajja**, cast monolithically with it as a cantilever.

examTip.trap: "Arch" is offered and also spans an opening — but an arch is curved and works in **compression**; a lintel is straight and works in **bending**.
examTip.trick: Position sorts them: **sill** at the bottom of the opening, **jamb** at the sides, **lintel** across the top.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lintel = Level beam over the opening.** Bearing at each end is normally 150 mm or the wall thickness.

questions.stem: The principal purpose of a cavity wall is to:
options: Reduce the number of bricks required
Increase the load carrying capacity of the wall
Prevent moisture penetration and improve thermal insulation
questions.solution:
**To prevent moisture penetration and improve thermal insulation.**

A cavity wall is two separate leaves with a continuous air gap between them, tied together but not bonded. Its two benefits follow directly from that gap:

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Damp resistance** | Water crossing the outer leaf runs **down the cavity face** and is drained out through weep holes; it cannot bridge the gap |
| **Thermal insulation** | The still air in the cavity is a **poor conductor** — a cavity wall insulates far better than a solid wall of the same thickness |
