| Sound insulation | The discontinuity interrupts the transmission path |
| Efflorescence reduced | Salts are not carried through to the inner face |

**Why it is not about strength.** Two half-brick leaves are **weaker** than one solid wall of the same total thickness, precisely because they are not bonded into a single monolith. Option (b) inverts the truth. Nor is economy the purpose (option a) — a cavity wall costs *more* than a solid wall for the same thickness of masonry.

**The construction rules, each with a reason:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Cavity width **50 – 100 mm** | Wide enough to interrupt capillarity, narrow enough for stable ties |
| Each leaf at least **100 mm** (half brick) | Minimum stable thickness |
| **Wall ties** at about 900 mm horizontally, 450 mm vertically | Hold the leaves together against wind |
| Ties **slope downward toward the outer leaf**, or carry a drip | So water runs **out**, never in along the tie |
| **Weep holes** at the base of the cavity | Drain the water that collects |
| A **DPC** at the base and stepped over openings | Directs water outward |
| The cavity must be kept **clear of mortar droppings** | Any bridge across it defeats the whole wall |

The last two rows are where cavity walls actually fail in practice: a **mortar bridge** or a **wrongly sloped tie** conducts water straight across the gap, and the wall then performs worse than a solid one because the defect is hidden.

**Effective thickness for slenderness** (IS 1905): for a cavity wall the effective thickness is taken as **two-thirds of the sum of the actual thicknesses of the two leaves, or the thickness of the thicker leaf, whichever is greater** — which formalises the fact that the two leaves do not act fully together.

Option (c) names a real incidental use — services are sometimes run in the cavity — but doing so risks bridging it, and it is never the reason a cavity wall is built.

examTip.trap: "To reduce cost" is wrong — a cavity wall uses more bricks and more labour than a solid wall of the same thickness.
examTip.trick: The **air gap** does the work twice over: it stops water crossing by capillarity, and still air is an excellent insulator.
examTip.mnemonic: **The cavity must stay clear.** Mortar droppings bridging the gap defeat the whole wall — which is why wall ties are laid to fall outward.

questions.stem: A raft (mat) foundation is most suitable when:
options: The safe bearing capacity of the soil is low and the loaded area is large
The foundation rests directly on sound rock
The load must be carried down to a deep hard stratum
The structure carries only a single heavy column
questions.solution:
**When the safe bearing capacity is low and the loaded area is large.**

A raft is a single slab covering the whole plan area, so it spreads the total building load over the greatest possible area. That reduces the intensity of pressure on the soil:

> **q = total load / total area**

With a weak soil, individual footings would each need to be so large that they would nearly touch — at which point it is cheaper and structurally better to cast one continuous slab.

**The rule of thumb:** a raft becomes economical when the footings would otherwise cover more than about **half the plan area**.

**Its second and often decisive advantage** is that a raft ties the whole structure together, so it reduces **differential settlement** — the raft settles more or less as one body. That matters more than total settlement: a building that settles 50 mm uniformly is undamaged, while one that settles 10 mm unevenly cracks.

**Why the other options point elsewhere:**

| Condition | Correct foundation |
|---|---|
| Sound **rock** at the surface | A simple **isolated footing** — the bearing capacity is ample |
| Load to be taken to a **deep** stratum | **Piles** or a well/caisson — depth, not spread, is the answer |
| A **single** heavy column | An **isolated footing**, sized for that column |
| Weak soil over a **large** loaded area | **Raft** |
| Two columns too close for separate footings, or one near a boundary | **Combined** or **strap** footing |

Option (c) is the important contrast: a raft is a **shallow** foundation and does nothing to reach a deeper stratum. Spreading load and transferring it downward are different strategies for different problems.

**The types of raft:**

| Type | Form |
|---|---|
| **Flat plate** | Uniform slab; for light loads and closely spaced columns |
| **Plate thickened under columns** | Where punching shear governs locally |
| **Beam and slab** | Slab stiffened by beams; for heavier or unequal loads |
| **Cellular / box** | Two slabs with intersecting walls — very stiff, and **buoyant** |

The **buoyancy raft** is worth noting for its ingenuity: excavating a deep basement removes a weight of soil, and if that removed weight approaches the building weight, the **net** increase in pressure at foundation level is near zero — a *floating* foundation, which can carry a heavy building on soil that would not otherwise support it.

A raft must also be checked for **uplift** where the water table is high, since an empty basement can float.

examTip.trick: The economic threshold: a raft pays when individual footings would cover **more than about half the plan area**.
examTip.mnemonic: **A raft SPREADS the load; piles TRANSFER it downward.** Different problems — a raft does nothing to reach a deeper stratum. Its second benefit is that it ties the structure together, cutting *differential* settlement.

questions.stem: In three-coat plastering, the first coat applied to the masonry surface is called the:
questions.solution:
**The rendering coat.**

The coats of plaster, in order of application:

| Order | Name | Purpose | Thickness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st** | **Rendering coat** | Levels the surface and **keys to the masonry** | **9 – 12 mm** |
| 2nd | **Floating coat** | Brings the surface to a true plane | 6 – 9 mm |
| 3rd | **Finishing (setting or skimming) coat** | The smooth final surface | **2 – 3 mm** |

So options (a), (b) and (d) all name the **same last** coat under its several names — which is exactly the trap. "Setting coat" and "skimming coat" are synonyms for the finishing coat, and a candidate who knows only that one term will be drawn to it.

**Number of coats by situation:**

| Coats | Where |
|---|---|
| **One** (12 mm) | Ordinary internal brick walls |
| **Two** (12 + 3 mm) | Better internal work; external walls |
| **Three** | Superior work, and uneven surfaces such as stone masonry |

**Why each coat must be thin and separately cured.** A thick single coat **shrinks** as it dries and cracks; a thin coat shrinks less and is restrained by the surface it keys to. Each coat is allowed to set and is kept damp before the next is applied, so that the later coat does not draw water from the earlier one.

**The preparation that decides whether plaster stays on:**

| Step | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Rake out the joints** to about 20 mm on brickwork | Gives a **mechanical key** |
| **Hacking** — roughening a smooth concrete surface | The same, where there are no joints to rake |
| **Clean and wet** the surface | Removes dust; stops the masonry sucking water from the mortar |
| **Screeds** (patches of plaster to level) | Establish the true plane |
| **Cure** for 7 – 10 days | Cement mortar needs water to gain strength |

**The wetting step is not a formality.** Dry brickwork absorbs water from the mortar so fast that the cement never hydrates at the interface, and the plaster later sounds hollow and falls off in sheets.

**Typical mortar mixes:** **1:4 to 1:6** cement–sand for cement plaster, **1:3** lime–sand for lime plaster. Richer mixes are not better — a mix richer than about 1:3 shrinks excessively and crazes.

Measurement, since it is an item-rate matter: plastering is measured **in m²**, with **no deduction for openings up to 0.5 m²** under IS 1200.

examTip.trap: "Finishing coat" is picked by anyone reading quickly — but that is the **third** coat, not the first.
examTip.trick: The three coats go in the order **rendering → floating → finishing**, getting thinner and finer each time (about 12 mm, 9 mm, 3 mm).
examTip.mnemonic: **Render, float, finish** — rough to smooth, thick to thin.

questions.stem: Single scaffolding, in which a single row of standards is erected away from the wall and the putlogs enter holes left in the masonry, is also known as:
questions.solution:
**Bricklayer's scaffolding.**

The two names go together because single scaffolding is used for **brick masonry**, where the putlog holes can be left in the joints as the work rises and filled in afterwards.

| Type | Rows of standards | Also called | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Single** | **One**, about 1.2 m from the wall; putlogs enter the **wall** | **Bricklayer's** scaffolding | **Brick** masonry |
| **Double** | **Two** — the scaffold is self-supporting, nothing enters the wall | **Mason's** scaffolding | **Stone** masonry |

**Why stone masonry needs the double type.** In stonework it is **not practicable to leave putlog holes** — the stones are large, irregular and dressed, and cutting a hole would damage the work and could not be neatly closed. So the scaffold must stand on its own, giving the second row of standards. This distinction, single↔brick and double↔stone, is the whole content of the question.

**The parts of a scaffold**, whose names are examined:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Standard** | The **vertical** member |
| **Ledger** | **Horizontal**, parallel to the wall, connecting standards |
| **Putlog** | **Horizontal, at right angles** to the wall — one end in the wall (single) or on a second ledger (double) |
| **Transom** | A putlog whose both ends rest on ledgers |
| **Bracing** | Diagonal members giving stability |
| **Board / batten** | The working platform |
| **Guard rail and toe board** | Fall protection |

**The other kinds, each for its own situation:**

| Scaffold | Where |
|---|---|
| **Steel (tubular)** | The general modern choice — strong, reusable, quickly erected, fire-resistant |
| **Cantilever / needle** | Where the ground cannot be used — over a road, or a projecting upper storey |
| **Suspended** | Hung from the roof on ropes — **painting and repointing** of tall buildings |
| **Trestle** | Movable tripods — **internal** work up to about 5 m |
| **Patented** | Proprietary systems with couplers and frames |

**Safety is the substance of the topic, not an afterthought.** Falls from scaffolding are among the commonest causes of construction death. The requirements: standards on **firm base plates or sole plates**, adequate **diagonal bracing**, platforms fully boarded with **guard rails and toe boards**, safe **access ladders**, no overloading, and **inspection before each use and after any alteration or bad weather**.

A scaffold is a **temporary structure that must nevertheless be designed** — which is precisely why it is so often the one that fails.

examTip.trick: Single scaffolding needs holes in the wall for the putlogs, so it suits **brickwork**, where holes can be left and filled later. Stone masonry cannot be holed, so it needs **double (mason's)** scaffolding with two rows of standards.
examTip.mnemonic: **Single = bricklayer's (holes allowed). Double = mason's (no holes in stone).**

questions.stem: An empirical rule for a comfortable stair is that the product of the rise and the tread, in centimetres, should lie between:
questions.solution:
**Between 400 and 450.**

The three classical empirical rules for a comfortable stair, with R the rise and T the tread in centimetres:

> **R × T = 400 to 450**
> **2R + T = 60 to 65**
> **R + T = 40 to 45**

They express the same thing three ways: a **large rise demands a small tread and vice versa**, because the human stride is roughly constant. The **2R + T** form is the most used, since a step costs twice as much effort to climb as to traverse.

**A worked check.** Take R = 15 cm and T = 28 cm: the product is 420 ✓, 2R + T = 58 (just below range but acceptable), R + T = 43 ✓. A comfortable residential stair.

Now take R = 20 and T = 20 — a steep stair: product 400, but 2R + T = 60. It satisfies the rules numerically while being unpleasant to use, which is why the rules are guides and the **dimensional limits** below govern.

**Typical dimensions:**

| Element | Residential | Public buildings |
|---|---|---|
| **Rise** | **15 – 19 cm** | **12 – 15 cm** |
| **Tread** | **25 – 30 cm** | **30 – 35 cm** |
| **Width of stair** | 90 cm minimum | **150 – 200 cm** |
| **Pitch** | Up to about **38°** | **25 – 33°** |
| Headroom | **2.1 m minimum** | 2.1 m minimum |
| Flight | **Not more than 12 steps** before a landing | Same |

Public stairs are **shallower and wider** because they must serve crowds, the elderly and children, and must work as an **escape route** under panic conditions.

**The rule that causes real accidents:** **every step in a flight must have the same rise.** A single odd riser — commonly at the top or bottom where a level was adjusted on site — is a genuine trip hazard, because a climber's stride becomes automatic after two or three steps and the foot arrives where it expects the tread to be.

**The terms:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rise** | Vertical distance between consecutive treads |
| **Tread** | Horizontal depth of the step |
| **Going** | Horizontal distance covered by a flight |
| **Nosing** | The projecting edge of the tread |
| **Winder** | A tapered step turning a corner |
| **Landing** | A level platform between flights |
| **Waist** | The thickness of the structural slab of an RCC stair |

In a straight flight, the **number of treads is one less than the number of risers**, because the top riser lands on the floor or landing above, which needs no tread.

examTip.trick: Two independent rules of thumb, and a good stair satisfies both: **R × T = 400–450 cm²** and **2R + T = 550–600 mm**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Product 400–450, sum 2R+T about 600.** A typical result is a 150 mm rise with a 300 mm tread.

questions.stem: A king post roof truss is economical for spans up to about:
questions.solution:
**About 8 m.**

The timber roof trusses, in ascending order of span — the sequence to memorise:

| Truss | Economical span | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Lean-to** | up to 2.5 m | Single slope against a wall |
| **Couple / couple close** | up to **4.5 m** | The simplest pair of rafters |
| **Collar beam** | up to 5 m | A tie raised above eaves level |
| **King post** | **up to 8 m** | **One** central vertical post |
| **Queen post** | **8 to 12 m** | **Two** vertical posts |
| Mansard / truncated | 12 to 18 m | Two slopes, usable attic |
| **Steel (Fink, Pratt, Howe)** | beyond 12 m | Timber becomes uneconomical |

The progression follows one idea: **as the span grows, more internal members are needed to keep every timber short enough to avoid excessive bending or buckling.** The king post has one central post; the queen post has two, which lets it reach half again as far.

**The members of a king post truss and what each does:**

| Member | Force | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Tie beam** | **Tension** | The bottom horizontal — resists the outward spread of the rafters |
| **Principal rafters** | **Compression** | The inclined members carrying the roof |
| **King post** | **Tension** | The central vertical — **holds the tie beam up**, preventing it sagging |
| **Struts** | **Compression** | From the foot of the king post to mid-rafter, shortening the rafter span |
| Purlins | Bending | Span between trusses, carrying the common rafters |

**The king post is in tension, not compression** — the single most-missed point in the topic. It does not "hold the ridge up"; it **hangs the tie beam** from the apex, so that the long tie does not sag under its own weight and the ceiling load. Calling it a post is misleading; it acts as a hanger.

**Why the tie beam is essential.** Two rafters leaning against each other push **outward** at their feet. Without a tie, that thrust would have to be resisted by the walls, which masonry cannot do. The tie converts the arrangement from a thrusting pair into a self-contained **triangle** — and a triangle is the only polygon that is stiff without rigid joints, which is the whole basis of trussing.

**Spacing:** timber trusses are placed at **3 to 4 m** centres, steel trusses at **4 to 5 m**, with purlins spanning between them.

examTip.trick: Learn the span ladder for timber trusses: **king post up to 8 m, queen post 8–12 m, mansard and truncated for more.**
examTip.mnemonic: **One king to 8, two queens to 12.** The king post has a single central vertical; the queen post has two, which is what lets it span further.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the formwork to vertical faces of walls, columns and the sides of beams may normally be removed after:
questions.solution:
**16 to 24 hours.**

The stripping times of IS 456:2000 (Table 11), for ordinary Portland cement:

| Formwork | Minimum period |
|---|---|
| **Vertical faces** of walls, columns, beam sides | **16 – 24 hours** |
| Soffit formwork to **slabs** (props left under) | **3 days** |
| Soffit formwork to **beams** (props left under) | **7 days** |
| **Props to slabs** — span up to 4.5 m | **7 days** |
| **Props to slabs** — span over 4.5 m | **14 days** |
| **Props to beams and arches** — span up to 6 m | **14 days** |
| **Props to beams and arches** — span over 6 m | **21 days** |

**The organising principle**, which makes the whole table follow from one idea: a **vertical** face carries **no load** — it merely holds the wet concrete in shape until it stiffens, so it can come off within a day. A **soffit** carries the **weight of the concrete itself**, and must stay until the member can support that weight; and **props** must stay longer still, because the member must also carry construction loads.

So the times increase with the **load the formwork is carrying** and with the **span** it must bridge — never arbitrary numbers to memorise.

**Note the distinction between removing the soffit form and removing the props.** Stripping the plywood soffit at 3 days while leaving the props standing lets the formwork be reused early without asking the young concrete to span. Missing this, and pulling the props with the form, is a genuine cause of collapse of newly cast slabs.

**Why early stripping is wanted at all.** Formwork is a large part of the cost of concrete construction — commonly **quoted at a third or more** of the total — and it is mostly the cost of *time*, since the material is reused. Every day earlier that a set of forms is released is a day it can be working elsewhere.

**Why it must nevertheless be resisted:**

| Stripping too early | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Concrete not yet strong enough | **Deflection, cracking, or collapse** |
| Surface not hard | **Damaged edges and honeycombing** |
| Curing interrupted | Lower final strength and durability |

**Where these times change:** they must be **extended** in cold weather and where **mineral admixtures or PPC** are used (both hydrate more slowly), and may be **shortened** on the basis of **actual cube results from site-cured specimens** — which is the professional way to accelerate a programme rather than guessing.

**Formwork requirements** in general: strong enough for the concrete plus construction loads, **rigid** so it does not deflect, **tight** so grout cannot escape, **smooth** and treated with a release agent, and **easily struck without damaging** the concrete. Steel and plywood dominate where reuse is repeated; timber where shapes are one-off.

examTip.trap: Candidates confuse this with the **soffit** figures, which are far longer — 7 days for slab props, up to 21 days for beam props spanning over 6 m.
examTip.trick: Vertical faces carry no load once the concrete has set; only **props under soffits** hold weight. That is the whole reason for the difference.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sides come off in a day; soffits stay for a week or three.**

questions.stem: The process of strengthening or deepening the foundation of an existing building is called:
questions.solution:
**Underpinning.**

Underpinning transfers the load of an existing structure to a **deeper or stronger stratum**, or increases the bearing area of the existing foundation.

**When it is needed:**

| Situation | Why |
|---|---|
| The building is **settling** | The existing bearing stratum is inadequate |
| A **basement is to be added** below | The foundation must go deeper than the new floor |
| A **deeper adjacent excavation** is planned | The neighbour's excavation would undermine this foundation |
| **Loads are being increased** — extra storeys | The existing foundation is now too small |
| The soil has **deteriorated** | Water table change, leakage, erosion |

The third is the commonest cause of dispute in dense urban building, and the one most relevant to Kathmandu: excavating for a new basement beside an existing house removes the lateral support of the soil beneath its footing.

**Distinguish the temporary-works terms**, which is what the distractors test:

| Term | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Underpinning** | **Strengthens or deepens a foundation** | **Below** the existing foundation |
| **Shoring** | **Temporarily supports** an unsafe or bulging wall | Against the **side** of a wall |
| **Scaffolding** | Provides a **working platform** for labour and material | Alongside the work |
| **Grouting** | Injects cement or chemical to **fill voids or improve soil** | Into the ground or a crack |
| Timbering | Supports the **sides of an excavation** | In a trench |

All four are used *around* an existing structure, which is why they are so easily confused. The discriminator is simple: **shoring supports sideways, underpinning supports from below, scaffolding supports workers, grouting fills voids.**

Note that **grouting** (option c) is a genuine method of *ground improvement* and is sometimes used **as part of** an underpinning scheme — but grouting names the technique, not the operation of deepening a foundation.

**The methods of underpinning:**

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **Pit (traditional)** | Work in **short alternate lengths** of 1.2–1.5 m, so the wall is never unsupported over a long stretch |
| **Pile** | Piles driven or bored on both sides, with needle beams through the wall |
| **Needle and pile / pier** | The wall carried on needles spanning between new piers |
| **Jacking / pretest** | Piles jacked in and preloaded, so settlement is taken out before transfer |
| Chemical or grout injection | Ground strengthened in place |

**The safety principle throughout** is the first row: **never remove support from a long continuous length at once.** Work proceeds in short alternate bays, each completed and loaded before the next is opened — the arch action of the masonry above spans the small gap. Ignoring this is how underpinning brings down the very building it was meant to save.

examTip.trap: "Shoring" is the near-miss — it supports the **superstructure** temporarily; underpinning works on the **foundation** permanently.
examTip.trick: Underpinning is needed when a new deeper basement is built alongside, when the existing foundation has settled, or when the building's load is being increased.
examTip.mnemonic: **Underpinning goes UNDER. Shoring holds the side.**

questions.stem: In modular brickwork, the nominal thickness of a one-brick load-bearing wall is:
questions.solution:
**200 mm.**

The **modular brick** of IS 1077 measures **190 × 90 × 90 mm**, and with a **10 mm mortar joint** the nominal (module) size becomes **200 × 100 × 100 mm**. Wall thicknesses therefore come in neat multiples of 100 mm:

| Wall | Actual | Nominal |
|---|---|---|
| **Half brick** | 90 mm | **100 mm** |
| **One brick** | **190 mm** | **200 mm** |
| One and a half brick | 290 mm | 300 mm |
| Two brick | 390 mm | 400 mm |

**Why the brick is 190 rather than 200.** So that brick **plus** joint equals the round module. This is the whole point of modular co-ordination: dimensions add up without cutting, and a designer can set out in 100 mm units knowing the brickwork will fit.

**The traditional (non-modular) brick** still widely used in Nepal and India is about **230 × 110 × 70 mm**, giving wall thicknesses of **115 mm, 230 mm, 345 mm** — so a "9-inch wall" is 230 mm and a "4½-inch wall" 115 mm. A candidate must note **which brick the question specifies**; this one says *modular*.

**The proportions of a brick are not arbitrary:**

> **length ≈ 2 × width + one joint**,  and the height is the width or less

This is what lets a header and a stretcher course course together in the same wall, and it is why bonding works at all.

**The other brick facts examined alongside this:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Weight of one brick | About **3 – 3.5 kg** |
| Bricks per m³ of brickwork | About **500** |
| Frog | **100 × 40 × 10–20 mm** depression, on the **top** face |
| Compressive strength, first class | **≥ 10.5 N/mm²** (IS 1077 minimum class 3.5) |
| Water absorption, first class | **≤ 20%** by weight after 24 h |
| Efflorescence | Not more than **slight** |

**The frog's purposes:** it forms a **key with the mortar** and carries the manufacturer's mark. It must be laid **upward** so that mortar fills it — laying a brick frog-down leaves a void, wastes the key, and weakens the wall.

**Why a minimum thickness matters structurally.** A wall's capacity is governed by its **slenderness ratio** — effective height (or length) divided by effective thickness — which IS 1905 limits to about **27 for load-bearing walls**. A half-brick wall is far too slender to be load-bearing over a normal storey height, so it serves only as a **partition** or as one leaf of a cavity wall.

examTip.trick: Modular brick is **190 × 90 × 90 mm**, and with a 10 mm joint the module becomes a clean **200 × 100 × 100**. That is the point of the modular system: the arithmetic is all in round numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brick 190, module 200.** Traditional (non-modular) brick is 230 × 110 × 70, giving a 240 mm wall instead.

questions.stem: The centroid of a semicircular area of radius r, measured from its diameter, lies at a distance of:
questions.solution:
**4r/3π ≈ 0.4244 r.**

By definition ȳ = (∫y dA)/A. Taking an elemental strip parallel to the diameter and integrating over the semicircle:

> ȳ = (2r³/3) / (πr²/2) = **4r/3π**

A useful sanity check: 4/(3π) = 0.424, which is a little **less than half the radius** — as it must be, since the area is widest near the diameter and narrows toward the top, pulling the centroid down.

**The standard centroids**, which must simply be known — and note carefully which are **areas** and which are **solids**, because the pairs are constantly confused:

| Shape | Centroid from the base / diameter |
|---|---|
| **Semicircular area** | **4r/3π** = 0.424 r |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** = 0.375 r |
| Quarter circle (area) | 4r/3π from **both** edges |
| **Semicircular arc** (a wire, not an area) | **2r/π** = 0.637 r |
| **Triangle** | **h/3** from the base |
| **Solid cone** | **h/4** from the base |
| Solid pyramid | h/4 from the base |
| Rectangle | d/2 |
| **Trapezium** of parallel sides a and b, height h | **h(2a + b)/(3(a + b))** from the side b |

Option (b), **3r/8**, is the deliberate trap — it is the **solid hemisphere**, a three-dimensional body, not the plane semicircular area. Option (d), 2r/3, belongs to neither.

**Why the arc differs so much from the area.** In the arc, every element of length is at the full radius r from the centre, so its centroid sits far out at 0.637 r. In the area, most of the material lies near the diameter where the shape is widest. The distinction between a **line, an area and a volume** is what the whole table turns on.

**Where this is used.** Composite sections are solved by taking moments of area about a convenient reference axis:

> **ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i) / ΣA_i**

with the areas of any **holes or removed portions taken as negative** — the standard method for a channel, an I-section with unequal flanges, or a circular section with a segment cut away.

And note the shortcut that saves most of the work: **if a section has an axis of symmetry, the centroid lies on it.** A section with two axes of symmetry has its centroid at their intersection, and needs no calculation at all.

examTip.trap: 3r/8 is the standard confusion — that is the **solid hemisphere**, a three-dimensional body. This question asks about a two-dimensional **semicircular area**.
examTip.trick: Keep the family straight: semicircular **area** 4r/3π ≈ 0.424r; semicircular **arc** 2r/π; solid hemisphere 3r/8; hollow hemisphere r/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **Area 4r/3π, arc 2r/π** — the area value is the arc value times 2/3.

questions.stem: By the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of an area A about an axis at a distance h from a parallel centroidal axis is:
questions.solution:
**I_G + A h².**

> **I_AB = I_G + A h²**

where I_G is the moment of inertia about the **centroidal** axis, A the area, and h the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.

**The term A h² can never be negative**, since both A and h² are positive. Three consequences follow immediately, and they are worth more than the formula itself:

1. The moment of inertia about any axis is **always greater** than about the parallel centroidal axis. So option (b) is impossible.
2. The moment of inertia is therefore **least about the centroidal axis** among all axes of that direction.
3. **Moving material away from the neutral axis increases I rapidly** — as the *square* of the distance.

That third point is the reason for the shape of nearly every structural section. An **I-section** places most of its material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, so the A h² term is large; a solid rectangle of the same area has much of its material uselessly close to the centre. It is also why a hollow tube is so much stiffer than a solid rod of equal weight, and why the depth of a beam matters far more than its width.

**The theorem's essential condition:** the two axes must be **parallel**, and one of them must pass through the **centroid**. Applying it between two arbitrary parallel axes, neither centroidal, is a standard error — the correct route is to go from the first axis to the centroidal axis and then out to the second.

**Its companion, the perpendicular axis theorem:**

> **I_ZZ = I_XX + I_YY**

which gives the **polar** moment of inertia about an axis normal to the plane, and applies to **plane laminae only**.

**The standard moments of inertia** used with the theorem:

| Section | About the centroidal axis | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **bd³/12** | **bd³/3** |
| **Triangle** b × h | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** |
| **Circle**, diameter d | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| Semicircle, radius r | 0.11 r⁴ | πr⁴/8 about the diameter |

Notice that each "about the base" value is exactly what the parallel axis theorem predicts. For the rectangle: bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)² = bd³/12 + bd³/4 = **bd³/3** ✓. For the triangle: bh³/36 + (½bh)(h/3)² = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = **bh³/12** ✓.

Working those two checks once is worth memorising four separate formulae, because it means only the centroidal values need to be remembered.

examTip.trick: The added term **Ah² is always positive**, so the moment of inertia about any parallel axis is always **greater** than about the centroidal one. That fact alone rejects any option with a minus sign.
examTip.mnemonic: **Move away from the centroid and I only ever grows.** Which is why the centroidal axis gives the minimum.

questions.stem: The section modulus of a section is given by:
questions.solution:
**Z = I / y.**

> **Z = I / y_max**

where I is the moment of inertia about the neutral axis and y_max the distance to the **extreme fibre**.

**Where it comes from.** The flexure formula is

> **M / I = σ / y**  ⟹  **σ = M y / I**

The stress is greatest at the extreme fibre, where y = y_max:

> **σ_max = M / (I / y_max) = M / Z**  ⟹  **M = σ_max · Z**

So Z is the single geometric property that converts a bending moment directly into the maximum bending stress. Its units are **mm³**, one power of length lower than I (mm⁴).

**Why it, and not I, governs strength.** Two properties of a section answer two different questions:

| Property | Governs | Question answered |
|---|---|---|
| **I** (mm⁴) | **Stiffness** — deflection | *How much will it deflect?* |
| **Z** (mm³) | **Strength** — bending stress | *Will it break?* |

A deep, thin section can have a large I but, because y_max is also large, a proportionately smaller Z — so a section chosen for deflection is not automatically the right one for stress. Both must be checked, and option (c), I/A, is neither: it is the square of the **radius of gyration**, which governs **buckling**.

**The standard section moduli:**

| Section | Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **bd²/6** |
| **Circle**, diameter d | **πd³/32** |
| Hollow circle | π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D) |
| Triangle, about the centroidal axis | bh²/24 (to the apex) |

Deriving the rectangle confirms the definition: I/y = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = **bd²/6** ✓.

**Note the d² in the rectangle.** Doubling the **depth** of a beam multiplies its moment capacity by **four**; doubling the **width** merely doubles it. That is why beams are deep rather than wide, and why laying a joist flat instead of on edge is such a serious error — turning a 50 × 200 mm joist on its side reduces its capacity to a quarter.

**For an unsymmetrical section** — a T-beam, a channel — the distances to the top and bottom fibres differ, so there are **two** section moduli, Z_top and Z_bottom. The **smaller** governs where the material is equally strong in tension and compression; but for a material such as cast iron or concrete, strong in compression and weak in tension, the section is deliberately shaped so that the **larger** y falls on the compression side.

examTip.trick: Z ties bending moment to stress: **σ = M/Z**. Units check it — I is m⁴ and y is m, so I/y is m³ ✓, which is what a section modulus must be.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z = I/y**, and for an unsymmetrical section there are two values — use **y to the extreme fibre in tension** for the critical check.

questions.stem: The polar moment of inertia of a solid circular section of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**πd⁴/32.**

By the perpendicular axis theorem, for a plane lamina:

> **J = I_ZZ = I_XX + I_YY**

A circle is symmetric, so I_XX = I_YY = πd⁴/64, giving

> **J = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32**

So the polar value is simply **twice** the diametral value — the fact worth carrying, since it means only one of the two need be remembered.

**The distinction the options test:**

| Quantity | Circle of diameter d | Units | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** about a **diameter** | **πd⁴/64** | mm⁴ | **Bending** |
| **J**, **polar** | **πd⁴/32** | mm⁴ | **Torsion** |
| **Z**, section modulus | **πd³/32** | mm³ | Bending **stress** |
| Z_p, polar modulus | πd³/16 | mm³ | Torsional **stress** |

Option (a) is the bending value and option (d) the section modulus — note that (d) has d³, one power short, so it can be eliminated on **dimensions alone** without recalling any formula. That habit of checking the power of length is worth more in an examination than memorising the table.

**Where J is used — the torsion equation:**

> **T / J = τ / r = G θ / L**

which gives the shear stress τ at radius r, and the angle of twist θ = TL/GJ. **GJ** is the **torsional rigidity**, exactly parallel to **EI** as the flexural rigidity.

**Why the shaft is the classic application.** In torsion the shear stress varies **linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface**, so material at the core carries almost nothing. A **hollow** shaft therefore transmits nearly the same torque as a solid one of the same outside diameter, at much less weight:

> **J_hollow = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32**

Removing the inner half of the diameter costs only 1/16 of the polar moment (since (½)⁴ = 1/16) while removing a quarter of the material. This is the same reasoning that puts the flanges of an I-beam far from the neutral axis — in both cases, **material far from the axis of action does the work**.

**A caution.** J = I_XX + I_YY holds only for a **plane lamina** about an axis perpendicular to its plane, and the torsion formula T/J = τ/r holds only for **circular** sections. Non-circular sections warp when twisted, and their torsional constant is not the polar moment of inertia at all.

examTip.trick: By the perpendicular axis theorem, **J = I_xx + I_yy = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32.** The polar value is exactly **twice** the diametral one.
examTip.mnemonic: **64 for a diameter, 32 for polar.** Halve the denominator, double the value.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a circular section of diameter d about a diameter is:
questions.solution:
**πd⁴/64.**

In terms of the radius this is **πr⁴/4**, since d = 2r gives π(2r)⁴/64 = 16πr⁴/64 = πr⁴/4. Both forms are worth holding, because problems are set in whichever is convenient — and mixing them up (using πr⁴/64) is the commonest slip in this topic.

**A dimensional check on the alternatives.** All four options here carry d⁴, so dimensions cannot discriminate; the value must be known. The neighbouring quantities:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **I about a diameter** | **πd⁴/64** = πr⁴/4 |
| **J**, polar | **πd⁴/32** = πr⁴/2 — exactly **twice** |
| **Z**, section modulus | **πd³/32** |
| **k**, radius of gyration | **d/4** |

The radius of gyration is a pleasing result worth verifying: k = √(I/A) = √[(πd⁴/64)/(πd²/4)] = √(d²/16) = **d/4**. So for a circle the radius of gyration is a **quarter of the diameter**, or **half the radius** — a fact used constantly in column design, since the slenderness ratio of a circular column is L/k = 4L/d.

**The hollow circular section**, which is what practical problems usually involve:

> **I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64**,  **A = π(D² − d²)/4**,  **k = √(D² + d²)/4**

The subtraction works because moment of inertia is **additive over areas**, so a hole is simply a negative area — provided both values are taken about the **same axis**. Where the removed portion is *not* concentric, the parallel axis theorem must be applied to it separately before subtracting.

**A worked illustration of why hollow sections are used.** Compare a solid 100 mm circle with a hollow one of 100 mm outside and 80 mm inside:

| | Solid | Hollow |
|---|---|---|
| Area | 7854 mm² | 2827 mm² — **36%** |
| I | 4.91 × 10⁶ mm⁴ | 2.90 × 10⁶ mm⁴ — **59%** |

The hollow section keeps **59% of the stiffness for 36% of the material** — a 64% improvement in stiffness per unit weight. That is the entire argument for tubes, pipes, hollow columns and box girders, and it follows directly from the h² in the parallel axis theorem: what matters is where the material sits, not merely how much there is.

examTip.trick: This is the base value from which the others follow: polar is twice it, and the section modulus is this divided by d/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **πd⁴/64 about a diameter.** Note the **fourth power** — doubling a shaft's diameter multiplies its stiffness by sixteen.

questions.stem: For a rectangular section of width b and depth d, the radius of gyration about the centroidal axis parallel to the width is:
questions.solution:
**d/√12 ≈ 0.2887 d.**

By definition k = √(I/A). About the centroidal axis parallel to the width, I = bd³/12 and A = bd, so

> k = √[(bd³/12)/(bd)] = √(d²/12) = **d/√12** = d/(2√3) ≈ **0.289 d**

Note that **b cancels** — the radius of gyration about this axis depends only on the depth, which is what makes it a purely *shape* property independent of scale in the other direction.

**Option (d), d/√3**, is the trap: that is the radius of gyration about the **base** (I = bd³/3), not the centroidal axis. And the values are worth comparing, because the relation between them is the parallel axis theorem in another guise:

| Axis | I | k |
|---|---|---|
| **Centroidal**, parallel to b | **bd³/12** | **d/√12** = 0.289 d |
| **Base** | bd³/3 | d/√3 = 0.577 d |
| Centroidal, parallel to d | db³/12 | b/√12 |

**What the radius of gyration means physically.** It is the distance from the axis at which the whole area could be concentrated without changing the moment of inertia:

> **I = A k²**

So it measures **how far the material is spread from the axis** — a purely geometric measure of efficiency. It is not a physical dimension of the section, and it is always **less than the extreme fibre distance**.

**Where it is used: columns.** The slenderness ratio is

> **λ = L_eff / k_min**

and it is the **minimum** k that governs, because a column buckles about its **weakest** axis. For a rectangle that is the axis parallel to the **longer** side — so a 200 × 300 mm column buckles about the axis giving k = 200/√12, not 300/√12. Overlooking that, and using the larger k, overestimates the capacity dangerously.

**Euler's formula** shows why:

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_eff² = π²EA/λ²**

The critical load falls as the **square** of the slenderness ratio. A column twice as slender carries a quarter of the load.

**The standard radii of gyration:**

| Section | k_min |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d (d > b) | **b/√12** |
| **Circle**, diameter d | **d/4** |
| Hollow circle, D and d | √(D² + d²)/4 |
| Square, side a | a/√12 |

And note why a **circular or square** column is efficient in compression: its k is the same in every direction, so there is no weak axis to govern. A rectangle wastes material, since the strong axis can never be used to capacity.

examTip.trick: Work it rather than recall it: **k = √(I/A) = √[(bd³/12)/(bd)] = √(d²/12) = d/√12 ≈ 0.289d.** Note that **b cancels** — the width is irrelevant.
examTip.mnemonic: **k ≈ 0.289 d.** The radius of gyration depends only on the dimension in the plane of bending.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a triangular section of base b and height h about its base is:
questions.solution:
**bh³/12.**

The two triangle values, and the relation between them:

| Axis | I |
|---|---|
| **Centroidal** axis parallel to the base | **bh³/36** |
| **Base** | **bh³/12** |
| An axis through the **apex**, parallel to the base | bh³/4 |

The parallel axis theorem ties them together, and checking it is the reliable way to recover whichever value is forgotten. The centroid lies at **h/3** from the base, so

> I_base = I_G + A(h/3)² = bh³/36 + (½bh)(h²/9) = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = **bh³/12** ✓

and from the base to the apex, at distance 2h/3 from the centroid:

> I_apex = bh³/36 + (½bh)(2h/3)² = bh³/36 + 2bh³/9 = **bh³/4** ✓

So all three options (a), (b) and (c) are genuine triangle values about *different* axes — the question turns entirely on reading **which axis** is asked for. Option (d), bh³/3, belongs to the **rectangle** about its base.

**Note the ratio.** I_base is **three times** I_G, and I_apex is **nine times** — reflecting how much more material sits far from an axis near the apex, where the triangle is narrow, than near the base where it is wide. That asymmetry is why the centroid is at h/3 and not h/2.

**The centroidal value bh³/36 is the one to memorise**, because every other axis follows from it by the theorem. The same discipline applies across the standard sections:

| Section | Centroidal I | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **bd³/12** | **bd³/3** (× 4) |
| **Triangle** b × h | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** (× 3) |
| **Circle** d | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| Semicircle r | 0.11 r⁴ | πr⁴/8 about the diameter |

**Where the triangle arises in practice.** Rarely as a whole section, but constantly as a **component of a composite one** — the fillets of a rolled section, a tapered cantilever, the triangular stress block of a partially cracked masonry section, and the varying-depth beams of a gantry or bridge. In every case the method is the same: split the shape into standard parts, find each part's centroidal I, transfer each to the common axis with I_G + Ah², and add — subtracting any holes as negative areas.

examTip.trap: bh³/36 is the reflex answer, but that is the **centroidal** value. The question asks about the **base**.
examTip.trick: Check with the parallel axis theorem: bh³/36 + (bh/2)(h/3)² = bh³/36 + bh³/18 = **bh³/12** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Triangle: 36 centroid, 12 base, 4 vertex.**

questions.stem: The product of inertia of a plane area about a pair of rectangular axes is zero when:
options: Both axes pass through the centroid
At least one of the axes is an axis of symmetry
questions.solution:
**When at least one of the axes is an axis of symmetry.**

The product of inertia is

> **I_xy = ∫ x y dA**

Unlike I_xx and I_yy it can be **positive, negative or zero**, because x and y are signed coordinates.

**Why symmetry makes it vanish.** If the y-axis is an axis of symmetry, then for every element at (+x, y) there is an identical element at (−x, y). Their contributions to ∫xy dA are (+x)(y)dA and (−x)(y)dA, which **cancel exactly**. Integrating over the whole area, every pair cancels and I_xy = 0.

Option (b) is the near miss: passing through the centroid is **not** sufficient. A **Z-section** or an **unequal angle** has centroidal axes about which I_xy is decidedly non-zero — which is precisely why those sections behave awkwardly. Option (c) fails for a different reason: a rectangle *is* symmetric, so I_xy is zero about its centroidal axes, but the reason is the symmetry, not the rectangularity — a rotated rectangle has a non-zero product of inertia about the original axes.

**What it is for: principal axes.** The axes about which I_xy = 0 are the **principal axes**, and about them the moments of inertia take their **maximum and minimum** values. Their orientation is

> **tan 2θ = 2 I_xy / (I_yy − I_xx)**

and the principal values are

> **I₁,₂ = (I_xx + I_yy)/2 ± √[((I_xx − I_yy)/2)² + I_xy²]**

The form is identical to the principal-stress equations, and Mohr's circle may be drawn for moments of inertia exactly as for stress.

**Why an engineer must care.** Simple bending theory — σ = My/I — is valid only when bending occurs **about a principal axis**. Load an **unequal angle** in its geometric plane and it does not deflect in that plane at all: it deflects sideways and twists, because the load is not aligned with a principal axis. This is **unsymmetrical bending**, and it is the reason:

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Angle sections used as **purlins** | Must be checked for unsymmetrical bending, or restrained |
| **Z-purlins** | Deliberately shaped, but the principal axes are inclined |
| A column of **unequal angle** section | Buckles about a principal axis, not a geometric one |
| **Doubly symmetric** sections (I, box, circle) | Geometric axes **are** principal — the simple theory applies directly |

The last row is why standard rolled sections are doubly symmetric wherever possible: it keeps design simple and behaviour predictable. And it also explains the earlier note that **I_xx + I_yy is invariant** with rotation of the axes — the sum is the polar moment of inertia, which cannot depend on how the in-plane axes are drawn.

examTip.trick: The product of inertia **I_xy = ∫xy dA** cancels to zero when the area is mirrored about either axis, because every element at +x is matched by one at −x.
examTip.mnemonic: **Symmetry kills the product of inertia** — and when it is zero, those axes are the **principal axes**, about which I is maximum and minimum.

questions.stem: The section modulus of a solid circular section of diameter d is:
questions.solution:
**πd³/32.**

From the definition Z = I/y_max, with I = πd⁴/64 about a diameter and y_max = d/2:

> **Z = (πd⁴/64)/(d/2) = πd³/32**

**Two of the options can be discarded on dimensions alone.** A section modulus has units of **length³**, so (c) and (d), both carrying d⁴, are moments of inertia and cannot be section moduli whatever their coefficients. That leaves only (a) and (b) to distinguish — and this habit of checking the power of length first should be automatic, because it halves the work on every question in this family.

**The remaining discrimination:** πd³/16 is the **polar** section modulus Z_p = J/r = (πd⁴/32)/(d/2), used for **torsional** shear stress τ_max = T/Z_p. So both survivors are real properties of the same circle, one for bending and one for torsion:

| Property | Circle of diameter d | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **Z**, section modulus | **πd³/32** | **σ_max = M / Z** — bending |
| **Z_p**, polar modulus | **πd³/16** | **τ_max = T / Z_p** — torsion |

The polar modulus is **twice** the section modulus, mirroring J being twice I.

**Where this is applied.** Designing a solid circular shaft or bar in bending:

> **d = ∛(32 M / (π σ_allow))**

A worked example: for M = 10 kNm and σ_allow = 150 N/mm²,

> d = ∛(32 × 10 × 10⁶ / (π × 150)) = ∛(679 000) ≈ **88 mm**

**Why a circular section is inefficient in bending**, despite being ideal in torsion. Compare a solid circle with a rectangle of the same **area**:

| Section | Area | Z |
|---|---|---|
| Circle, d = 100 mm | 7854 mm² | 98 × 10³ mm³ |
| Rectangle 60 × 131 mm | 7854 mm² | 172 × 10³ mm³ |

The rectangle gives **75% more** moment capacity for the same material, because a circle concentrates its area near the neutral axis where it contributes little. In **torsion** the situation reverses — the circle is optimal, since torsional shear is axisymmetric and no other shape avoids warping.

That contrast is the practical lesson: **circular sections for shafts and torsion members, deep rectangular or I-sections for beams in bending.**

examTip.trick: Derive it in one line: **Z = I/y = (πd⁴/64)/(d/2) = πd³/32.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Third power for section modulus, fourth power for I.** Z governs strength; I governs stiffness.

questions.stem: Among all axes parallel to a given direction, the moment of inertia of a plane area is least about:
options: Any axis lying in the plane of the area
questions.solution:
**The centroidal axis.**

The parallel axis theorem states I = I_G + A h². Since A is positive and h² can never be negative, the added term is **always ≥ 0**, and it vanishes only when **h = 0** — that is, when the axis passes through the **centroid**.

So among a family of parallel axes, the centroidal one gives the **minimum**, and I grows **quadratically** as the axis moves away.

**Why option (d) is the tempting wrong answer.** An axis of symmetry *does* pass through the centroid, so it *is* a minimising axis — but the word **"only"** makes the statement false. A section may have **no** axis of symmetry at all (a scalene triangle, an unequal angle) and still has centroidal axes about which I is least. Symmetry is a *sufficient* condition for an axis to be centroidal, never a necessary one.

Option (b) illustrates the opposite extreme: the base is typically the **farthest** common axis from the centroid, which is why I_base always exceeds I_G — bd³/3 against bd³/12 for a rectangle, a factor of four.

**Why this matters in practice, in three places:**

| Application | The consequence of the minimum |
|---|---|
| **Bending** | The **neutral axis passes through the centroid** in pure bending — so the I used in σ = My/I is the *centroidal* one, the smallest of the family. Using I about the base overestimates stiffness fourfold |
| **Column buckling** | A column buckles about the axis of **least** I — and among centroidal axes of different **orientation**, that is the **minor principal axis** |
| **Composite sections** | Every component's I must be **transferred to the common centroidal axis** before summing; adding centroidal values directly, without the Ah² terms, is the classic error and always **underestimates** I |

**Note the two distinct minimisations, which are easily conflated:**

> Among axes of the **same direction** → the minimum is the **centroidal** axis (parallel axis theorem)
> Among **centroidal** axes of different **orientation** → the minimum is the **minor principal** axis (where I_xy = 0)

This question asks the first. A column-design question asks the second, and the answer there is I_min, about the principal axis.

**And the sum is invariant.** For any pair of perpendicular axes through a given point, I_xx + I_yy is constant however the pair is rotated, since it equals the polar moment about that point. So rotating axes **trades** I_xx against I_yy without changing their sum — which is exactly why a section has both a maximum and a minimum principal value, and why they occur ninety degrees apart.

examTip.trick: Straight from the parallel axis theorem: **I = I_G + Ah²**, and Ah² can never be negative. So I is smallest when h = 0 — at the centroid.
examTip.mnemonic: **The centroidal axis always gives the minimum I.** Any parallel shift, in either direction, increases it.

questions.stem: The fundamental principle of surveying is:
options: Measuring every line in one direction only
questions.solution:
**Working from whole to part.**

A survey begins by establishing a **small number of control points to high accuracy** over the whole area, and only then fills in the detail between them.

**Why this order and not the reverse.** Errors in survey work **accumulate**. If detail were measured from one point to the next across an area, each small error would be carried into the next measurement and the total would grow without bound. By fixing an accurate framework first:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| Errors are **localised** | A mistake in detail affects only that detail, not the whole survey |
| Errors are **contained**, not accumulated | Each part is tied to already-correct control |
| Work can proceed **independently** in different parts | Several parties can survey simultaneously |
| A blunder is **detectable** | The detail must close onto known control |

That last row is the practical value: working from whole to part builds in a **check** at every stage. Working from part to whole (option a) offers no check at all until the very end, when it is too late to locate the error.

**The second principle** completes the pair:

> **To fix a point relative to two known points, at least two independent measurements are required** — two distances, two angles, or one of each.

The methods that follow from it — each a way of fixing a point from a known baseline:

| Method | Measurements |
|---|---|
| **Two distances** | From both ends of the base (trilateration) |
| **Two angles** | From both ends (triangulation) |
| **One distance and one angle** | Polar coordinates — what a **total station** does |
| **Perpendicular offset** | The distance along the base and the offset from it |

**How the principle appears in practice, at every scale:**

| Scale | The "whole" | The "part" |
|---|---|---|
| National | **Triangulation network** — GTS in the subcontinent | District and local surveys |
| Project | **Primary traverse** or GPS control | Secondary traverse, then detailing |
| Chain survey | The **main framework of well-conditioned triangles** | Chain lines and offsets |
| Levelling | **Permanent and GTS benchmarks** | Temporary benchmarks, then spot levels |

**A well-conditioned triangle** is the same idea applied to shape: no angle smaller than about **30°** nor larger than **120°**, because a point fixed by two nearly parallel rays is poorly determined — a small angular error then displaces it a long way. The ideal is close to equilateral.

examTip.trick: It exists to stop errors accumulating: establish a few points to **high accuracy** first (the framework), then fill in detail within them. Working part-to-whole lets a small early error propagate across the entire survey.
examTip.mnemonic: **Whole to part, and always check.** The companion principle is to fix a point by at least two independent measurements.

questions.stem: Ranging in chain surveying means:
options: Measuring the length of a survey line
Establishing intermediate points on a survey line
Testing the chain against a standard length
questions.solution:
**Establishing intermediate points on a survey line.**

When a line is longer than one chain, it must be measured in successive stretches — and every intermediate point must lie **exactly on the straight line** joining the two end stations. Ranging is the operation of fixing those points, marked by **ranging rods**.

**Why it cannot be skipped.** If an intermediate point strays off the line, the measured path is a **zig-zag**, and the sum of its parts is **always longer** than the straight distance. The error is systematic and always in the same direction — the measured length is too great, never too small — so it cannot cancel out over many measurements.

**The two kinds:**

| Method | When | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct ranging** | The two ends are **mutually visible** | The surveyor at one end signals the assistant to move the rod into line |
| **Indirect (reciprocal) ranging** | The ends are **not visible** — a hill or building intervenes | **Two** surveyors with rods align each other alternately, converging onto the line by successive approximation |

Indirect ranging is the elegant one: neither observer can see the far station, yet by each aligning the other in turn they converge onto the true line — a purely geometric solution requiring no instrument.

**The other operations of chain surveying**, which the distractors name:

| Operation | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Ranging** | **Fixing intermediate points on the line** |
| **Chaining** | Measuring the length along it |
| **Offsetting** | Measuring detail **perpendicular to** (or oblique to) the line |
| Testing / standardising | Checking the chain against a standard, since chains **stretch** with use |

**The correction for a chain of wrong length** is worth stating, as it is the commonest numerical question in the topic:

> **True length = measured length × (incorrect chain length / true chain length)**

So a chain that has **stretched** gives measurements that are **too small**, and correcting them makes them larger. The same ratio applies to areas as its **square**, and to volumes as its **cube** — which is where candidates most often go wrong, forgetting to square the ratio for an area.

**The corrections to a chained length** in general: standardisation (as above), **slope** (always subtractive, reducing the measured distance to the horizontal), **temperature**, **pull**, and **sag** (for a tape suspended in catenary, always subtractive). Slope and sag can only shorten the true horizontal distance; temperature and pull may act either way.

examTip.trap: "Measuring the line" is the plausible wrong pick — but ranging happens **before** any measurement.
examTip.trick: **Direct ranging** is used when the ends are intervisible; **reciprocal ranging** when a hill intervenes and two surveyors must signal each other into line.
examTip.mnemonic: **Range first, chain second.** You cannot measure a straight line until you have marked one.

questions.stem: If the whole circle bearing of a line is 200°, its reduced (quadrantal) bearing is:
questions.solution:
**S 20° W.**

A whole circle bearing of 200° falls in the **third quadrant** (180° to 270°), which is the **south-west** quadrant. In that quadrant the reduced bearing is measured **from south, toward west**:

> RB = WCB − 180° = 200° − 180° = **20°**, so the bearing is **S 20° W**

**The conversion rule, quadrant by quadrant** — the table to carry into the examination:

| WCB | Quadrant | Reduced bearing | Measured from |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0° – 90°** | I — **NE** | **RB = WCB** | **N, toward E** |
| **90° – 180°** | II — **SE** | **RB = 180° − WCB** | **S, toward E** |
| **180° – 270°** | III — **SW** | **RB = WCB − 180°** | **S, toward W** |
| **270° – 360°** | IV — **NW** | **RB = 360° − WCB** | **N, toward W** |

Notice the pattern that makes it memorable: quadrants **I and III subtract nothing and 180°** and are measured the natural way, while **II and IV subtract the WCB** from 180° and 360°. And the prefix letter alternates **N, S, S, N** while the suffix goes **E, E, W, W**.

**Why two systems exist at all.** The **whole circle** (azimuthal) system runs 0° to 360° clockwise from north and is used by the **prismatic compass** and by all computation, because a single continuous number is what trigonometry needs. The **quadrantal** (reduced) system is used by the **surveyor's compass** and in older records, and is more readable to a human — "S 20° W" conveys a direction at a glance in a way that "200°" does not.

**The bearings that must not be confused:**

| Bearing | Reference |
|---|---|
| **True bearing** | **True (geographic) north** |
| **Magnetic bearing** | **Magnetic north** — differs by the **declination** |
| Arbitrary / assumed bearing | Any convenient direction |
| **Fore bearing (FB)** | Taken in the direction of progress |
| **Back bearing (BB)** | Taken back along the same line |

> **BB = FB ± 180°** — using **+** when FB < 180° and **−** when FB > 180°

So for this line, FB = 200° gives BB = 200° − 180° = **20°**.

**And the declination relation:**

> **True bearing = Magnetic bearing + declination** (east declination positive, west negative)

Declination changes slowly with time and place, which is why a magnetic bearing must always be recorded with the **date** of observation — an old plan's magnetic bearings cannot be reused without correction.

examTip.trick: Learn the quadrant table and this question takes five seconds: **0–90° → N θ E; 90–180° → S (180−θ) E; 180–270° → S (θ−180) W; 270–360° → N (360−θ) W.** Here 200° sits in the third quadrant, so 200 − 180 = 20, giving **S 20° W**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quadrants run N-E, S-E, S-W, N-W clockwise from north.** 200° is just past south, heading west — so the letters must be S and W before you compute anything.

questions.stem: Local attraction at a station is detected when:
options: The magnetic bearing of a line differs from its true bearing
The length of a line measured twice does not agree
The difference between the fore and back bearings of a line is not 180°
The compass needle takes a long time to come to rest
questions.solution:
**When the difference between the fore and back bearings of a line is not 180°.**

For any line, geometry requires

> **BB − FB = ± 180°**

If the observed difference departs from 180° by more than the permissible instrumental error, then **at least one of the two stations is disturbed** — the needle there is not pointing to magnetic north.

**Why option (a) is wrong**, and it is the tempting answer: the magnetic bearing **always** differs from the true bearing, everywhere on earth, by the **magnetic declination**. That is a normal and predictable difference, not a defect. Local attraction is a **local** disturbance superimposed on it.

Option (d) describes a sluggish or dirty pivot — an **instrumental** fault, not a magnetic one.

**What causes it.** Any **magnetic material near the compass**:

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **Iron and steel objects** | Rails, pipes, poles, wire fences, reinforced concrete |
| **Iron ore** in the ground | The classic natural cause |
| **Electric current** — overhead lines, cables | Direct current is the worse offender |
| **The surveyor's own equipment** | Steel tape, chain, keys, spectacles, phone, even buttons |

The last row is worth taking seriously — a chain laid down beside the tripod is a frequent and entirely avoidable cause.

**How to locate and correct it.** Work through the traverse and find a line whose FB and BB **do** differ by exactly 180°. **Both** of its stations are free from local attraction, so their bearings are correct. Starting from that line, the correct bearings are carried forward around the traverse, and at each disturbed station the **error is the same for every bearing observed from it** — because the needle is deflected by one fixed amount there, whatever direction is being sighted.

That single fact is what makes the correction possible: local attraction affects **all bearings from a station equally**, so it can be isolated and removed station by station.

**The better remedies, in order of preference:**

1. **Shift the station** away from the disturbance — always the first choice.
2. Apply the correction as above, if the disturbance cannot be avoided.
3. Use a **theodolite** and measure **angles** rather than bearings, which does not depend on magnetism at all.

The third is why modern practice has largely abandoned the compass for precise work: a **total station** measures angles from a reference direction and is entirely immune to local attraction. The compass survives for reconnaissance and for filling in detail where speed matters more than precision.

examTip.trick: The test is arithmetic and needs no equipment: for any line, **FB − BB should be exactly 180°**. A discrepancy means the needle was deflected at one or both ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **Find the pair of stations whose difference IS 180° — those two are free of attraction**, and every other bearing is corrected from them.

questions.stem: In the rise and fall method of reducing levels, the complete arithmetic check is:
options: ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL, only
ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL
ΣIS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL
questions.solution:
**ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL.**

Three independently computed quantities must agree, which is what makes the rise and fall method self-checking:

| Quantity | From |
|---|---|
| **ΣBS − ΣFS** | The **observed staff readings** |
| **ΣRise − ΣFall** | The **differences** worked out between consecutive readings |
| **Last RL − first RL** | The **reduced levels** finally tabulated |

**Why the middle term is the whole point.** The **height of collimation** method has only the first and third checks available:

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL**

That verifies the **change points** — but it does **not** check the reduced levels of the **intermediate sights**, because those are computed directly from the plane of collimation and never enter the sum. An arithmetic error in an intermediate sight passes undetected.

The rise and fall method computes each level from the **one before it**, so every reading including every intermediate sight enters the ΣRise − ΣFall term, and any error breaks the check.

**The two methods compared:**

| | **Height of collimation** | **Rise and fall** |
|---|---|---|
| Computation | RL = HI − staff reading | RL = previous RL ± (rise or fall) |
| Speed | **Faster**, fewer steps | Slower |
| Intermediate sights | **Not checked** | **Fully checked** |
| Suits | **Many intermediate sights** — profile and cross-section levelling | **Precise** work, fly levelling |
| Checks | 2 | **3** |

So the choice is a real trade-off, not a matter of preference: use height of collimation for long runs of detail levels, rise and fall where accuracy must be demonstrable.

**The rule for rise or fall** is simple but reversed from intuition, and is where errors creep in:

> If the **later** staff reading is **smaller**, the ground has **risen** (the staff is higher, so less of it is above the line of sight).
> If **larger**, the ground has **fallen**.

**The terms:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Back sight (BS)** | The **first** reading after setting up — on a point of known RL |
| **Fore sight (FS)** | The **last** reading before moving the instrument |
| **Intermediate sight (IS)** | Any reading between them |
| **Change point** | A point on which both an FS and a BS are taken |
| **Height of instrument (HI)** | RL of the line of collimation = RL + BS |
| **Reduced level (RL)** | Elevation above the datum |

And the discipline that keeps a level run honest: **begin and end on a benchmark**, so the run **closes** and the misclosure is known. A levelling run that does not close proves nothing about its own accuracy, whichever reduction method was used.

examTip.trick: Three quantities must agree, and all three come from different columns of the field book — which is what makes it a genuine check rather than a repeat of the same arithmetic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rise and fall: three-part check. Height of instrument: two-part check** (ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL only). That extra leg is why the rise-and-fall method is preferred where accuracy matters.

questions.stem: A benchmark established by the national survey department, whose elevation is precisely determined with reference to mean sea level, is called a:
questions.solution:
**A GTS benchmark.**

**GTS** stands for **Great Trigonometrical Survey**. These are the highest-order benchmarks of the subcontinent's national network, their elevations established with reference to **mean sea level** and their positions precisely fixed, marked by permanent stones or plates and recorded in published tables.

**The hierarchy of benchmarks:**

| Type | Established by | Datum | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GTS** | **National survey department** | **Mean sea level**, precisely determined | The **primary** control for all levelling |
| **Permanent** | Government or other reliable agencies | Referred to a GTS benchmark | Regional and project control |
| **Temporary (TBM)** | The **surveyor**, at the end of a day's work | Referred to the nearest permanent BM | So the next day's work can resume and close |
| **Arbitrary** | The surveyor, with an **assumed** value | **Assumed** — commonly 100.000 m | Local work where only *relative* levels matter |

The distinction between the last two is worth noting: a **temporary** benchmark has a *correct* value tied into the national network, whereas an **arbitrary** one has an invented value. Levels from an arbitrary benchmark are internally consistent but cannot be compared with anyone else's — perfectly adequate for setting out one building, useless for a scheme that must connect to a road or a drain elsewhere.

**Why a common datum matters.** Mean sea level is used because it is a **single physical surface** available to everyone, so levels taken by different parties, in different years, in different districts, can be combined. Without it, no drainage scheme, canal, road or water supply crossing more than one survey could be designed — every gradient depends on levels that agree.

**Its practical importance in Nepal.** The country's benchmark network is maintained by the **Survey Department**, and the value of a GTS benchmark is what allows a project level in one valley to be referred to a level in another. It is also why the **2015 Gorkha earthquake** mattered to surveyors: co-seismic displacement altered the positions and heights of control points across central Nepal, so benchmarks in the affected region had to be re-established.

**Temporary benchmarks are not a formality.** At the end of every day's levelling the run should be closed onto a TBM whose value is recorded — so that if the following day's work reveals an error, only one day's readings are in doubt. A week of levelling with no intermediate closure can be wholly lost to a single undetected mistake.

**And a caution on "mean sea level".** It is a computed average of tidal observations over many years at a defined station, not the level of the sea on any given day. The datum for the subcontinent's network was historically fixed at **Karachi**, and modern GNSS heights are referred to an **ellipsoid** instead, requiring a **geoid model** to convert between the two — which is why a GPS receiver's raw height differs from a levelled RL.

examTip.trick: Rank benchmarks by permanence: **GTS** (national, precise, tied to mean sea level), **permanent** (established by other agencies), **arbitrary** (assumed value for a local job), **temporary** (a mark for one day's work).
examTip.mnemonic: **GTS is the national datum**, from the Great Trigonometrical Survey.

questions.stem: Contour lines of different elevations can cross one another only in the case of:
questions.solution:
**An overhanging cliff (or a cave).**

Contours normally **cannot cross**, because a crossing would mean one point on the ground has two different elevations. The single exception is where the ground surface **overhangs itself** — a cliff with an undercut, or a cave mouth — so that a vertical line through the overhang really does meet the surface at two heights. In such a case the lower contour is drawn **broken** to show it is hidden.

**The characteristics of contours — the full set, and each is examinable:**

| Characteristic | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Contours **close on themselves**, within or beyond the map | Every contour is a closed curve |
| **Close** contours | **Steep** ground |
| **Widely spaced** contours | **Gentle** slope |
| **Equally spaced** contours | **Uniform** slope |
| Contours **cannot cross** | Except at an **overhang** |
| Contours **cannot merge** | Except at a **vertical cliff**, where they coincide |
| A **closed contour with higher values inside** | A **hill** |
| A **closed contour with lower values inside** | A **depression** or pond |
| Contours cross a **ridge or valley at right angles** | The line of steepest slope is normal to the contour |
| **V pointing uphill** | A **valley** — the stream flows toward the V's opening |
| **U or V pointing downhill** | A **ridge** |

**The valley-versus-ridge test** in the last two rows is the one candidates most often invert. The reliable way to remember it: a **valley's contours point upstream**, because the low ground of the valley floor pushes the contour line *inland* toward higher country. Any watercourse on the map confirms it.

**A saddle** (option d) is the low point on a ridge between two summits — its contours form a distinctive figure-of-eight or hourglass, but they do **not** cross.

**Contour interval** — the vertical distance between successive contours — is chosen from the purpose and terrain:

| Situation | Interval |
|---|---|
| **Flat** ground, large-scale plan | **0.2 – 0.5 m** |
| Building site, urban survey | 0.5 – 1 m |
| Undulating country | 1 – 3 m |
| **Hilly / mountainous** | **5 – 25 m** |

The governing rule: the interval must be **constant across one map**, since the whole visual language of contour spacing — steep meaning close together — depends on it.

**What contour maps are used for** in civil engineering: selecting a **reservoir site** and computing its **capacity** (area within each contour, then the trapezoidal or prismoidal rule for volume), fixing a **canal or road alignment** to a chosen gradient, computing **earthwork**, delineating a **catchment boundary** (which follows the ridge line, always crossing contours at right angles), and finding whether two points are **intervisible**.

examTip.trap: "They never cross" is nearly right, and is the answer most candidates give — but the question is asking for the exception.
examTip.trick: Contours normally cannot cross because one point cannot have two elevations. An **overhanging cliff** is the case where the ground surface doubles back over itself, so a plan position genuinely does have two surface levels.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overhang and cave are the only crossings.** A vertical cliff makes contours coincide; only an overhang makes them cross.

questions.stem: Measuring a horizontal angle with the theodolite on both face left and face right eliminates the error due to:
options: Eccentricity of the horizontal circle centres
Maladjustment of the line of collimation and the trunnion axis
Slip of the vernier during the observation
questions.solution:
**Maladjustment of the line of collimation and of the trunnion axis.**

When the telescope is **transited** (turned over) to change face, any error arising from the line of sight not being perpendicular to the horizontal axis, or from the horizontal (trunnion) axis not being perpendicular to the vertical axis, **reverses its sign**. Averaging the two face readings therefore cancels it.

**Which errors are removed by which technique** — the discrimination the question is testing:

| Error | Eliminated by |
|---|---|
| **Collimation error** (line of sight not ⟂ trunnion axis) | **Both faces** — average FL and FR |
| **Trunnion axis error** (horizontal axis not ⟂ vertical axis) | **Both faces** |
| Vertical index error | Both faces |
| **Eccentricity of centres** | Reading **both verniers** (A and B), 180° apart, and averaging |
| **Imperfect graduation** | **Repetition** on different parts of the circle |
| Accidental reading errors | **Repetition** or **reiteration** |
| **Vertical axis not truly vertical** | **Nothing** — it must be corrected by **levelling the instrument** |

The last row is the one worth carrying: an out-of-plumb vertical axis is **not** removed by changing face, by reading both verniers, or by repetition. It is a genuinely uncorrectable error in the observations, and the only defence is careful levelling of the instrument before observing — which is why the plate bubble is checked in two perpendicular directions and re-checked after any movement.

**Face left and face right** simply mean the vertical circle to the observer's left or right of the telescope. Observing a full set on both faces is standard practice for any angle that matters.

**The related methods of improving a horizontal angle:**

| Method | How | Gains |
|---|---|---|
| **Repetition** | The **same** angle turned several times, accumulating on the circle | Reduces reading and graduation error; the accumulated total is divided by the number of repetitions |
| **Reiteration** | **Several** angles observed in succession round the horizon, closing back on the first | Detects error by the **closure of the horizon** |

**The fundamental relations** a theodolite must satisfy, in the order they are tested and adjusted:

1. The **axis of the plate bubble** must be perpendicular to the vertical axis.
2. The **line of collimation** must be perpendicular to the trunnion axis.
3. The **trunnion axis** must be perpendicular to the vertical axis.
4. The **axis of the altitude bubble** must be parallel to the line of collimation.

Adjustments 2 and 3 are what changing face cancels; adjustment 1 is what it cannot.

**The temporary adjustments at each setup**, distinct from the above permanent ones: **setting up** over the station, **centring** with the plumb bob or optical plummet, **levelling** with the foot screws, and **focusing** the eyepiece and objective to remove parallax. **Parallax** — the image not lying in the plane of the cross-hairs — causes a reading error that varies with the observer's eye position, and is eliminated by focusing the eyepiece on the cross-hairs first, then the objective on the target.

examTip.trick: Two-face observation reverses the instrument's geometry, so any error fixed in the instrument appears with **opposite sign** on the second face and averages out.
examTip.mnemonic: **Face left and face right cancel the instrument's own faults, but never the operator's.** It does not remove eccentricity of centring, nor a badly levelled plate bubble — those need a different remedy.

questions.stem: The Bowditch rule for balancing a closed traverse assumes that the errors in:
options: Linear and angular measurements are of the same order of accuracy
Neither linear nor angular measurement occur
questions.solution:
**That the linear and angular measurements are of the same order of accuracy.**

The **Bowditch (compass) rule** distributes the closing error in proportion to the **length** of each line:

> **Correction to latitude of a line = total error in latitude × (length of that line / perimeter)**
> **Correction to departure of a line = total error in departure × (length of that line / perimeter)**
