That proportioning is what implies equal weighting of the two kinds of measurement — appropriate to a **compass traverse**, where the bearings and the chained lengths are of comparable (and modest) reliability.

**The rules compared**, and this contrast is the substance of the topic:

| Rule | Assumes | Correction proportional to | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bowditch (compass)** | Linear and angular errors **comparable** | **Length** of the line | **Compass** traverse |
| **Transit** | **Angular** measurement **more precise** than linear | **Latitude / departure** of the line | **Theodolite** traverse |
| Axis method | Errors chiefly in **length** | — | Where bearings are reliable |
| Graphical | — | — | Rough or small traverses |

So the choice of rule is a statement about **which instrument was used** and therefore where the error is believed to lie. A theodolite measures angles to seconds, while a taped or stadia distance is far less certain — so the transit rule leaves the bearings largely alone and adjusts the lengths.

**The computation, in order:**

1. Compute **latitude** (L cos θ) and **departure** (L sin θ) for each line.
2. For a **closed** traverse, both should sum to zero. They do not, and the residuals are the **closing error** components ΣL and ΣD.
3. The **closing error** and its direction:

> **e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²)]**,  **tan θ = ΣD / ΣL**

4. Express the accuracy as a **relative error**, e / perimeter — the figure that says whether the traverse is acceptable:

| Relative closing error | Standard |
|---|---|
| 1 in 300 – 1 in 600 | Compass traverse |
| 1 in 1000 – 1 in 3000 | Theodolite traverse |
| 1 in 5000 and better | Precise work |

5. Distribute the corrections by the chosen rule, then recompute.

**A caution that matters more than the arithmetic.** Balancing a traverse **hides** error; it does not remove it. If the closing error exceeds the permissible limit, the correct response is to **re-observe**, not to distribute a large error smoothly and pretend the survey is closed. A gross blunder — a transposed digit, a missed whole degree, a line measured to the wrong station — produces a large misclosure, and spreading it around corrupts every station instead of the one at fault.

The useful diagnostic: the **direction** of the closing error often points at the offending line, because a single bad bearing displaces the traverse in a characteristic way.

**Latitude and departure conventions**, since sign errors are the commonest failure: **northing positive, southing negative; easting positive, westing negative.** For a closed traverse ΣN = ΣS and ΣE = ΣW, which is simply the statement that the traverse returns to where it began.

examTip.trick: Two rules, two assumptions: **Bowditch** assumes linear and angular precision are **comparable** (correction shared in proportion to leg length); **Transit** assumes the **angles are more precise** than the distances.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bowditch = Both equally good. Transit = Trust the angles.**

questions.stem: In the stadia method of tacheometry with the staff vertical and the line of sight horizontal, the horizontal distance to the staff is:
questions.solution:
**D = K · s + C.**

> **D = (f/i) · s + (f + d) = K · s + C**

where **s** is the staff intercept between the upper and lower stadia hairs, **f** the focal length, **i** the stadia hair interval, and **d** the distance from the objective to the instrument's vertical axis.

**The two constants:**

| Constant | Name | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| **K = f / i** | **Multiplying constant** | **100** |
| **C = f + d** | **Additive constant** | **0 to 0.3 m** |

A multiplying constant of **100** is deliberate: it makes the distance a simple matter of reading the intercept and shifting a decimal point — an intercept of 1.235 m means 123.5 m. That is the practical genius of the stadia method, and it is why K = 100 is near-universal.

**Modern instruments are anallatic**, meaning an additional lens is fitted so that **C = 0** and the relation reduces to the pure proportion

> **D = 100 s**

So option (b), f/i, names only the multiplying constant, and option (c) misuses the additive constant. Option (a) is a **fragment of the inclined-sight formula**, offered because that is the formula most candidates half-remember.

**The inclined sight, staff vertical** — the general case:

> **D = K s cos²θ + C cos θ**
> **V = K s (sin 2θ)/2 + C sin θ**

with the **RL of the staff station** then

> **RL = RL of instrument axis + V − central hair reading**

using **+V** for an angle of elevation and **−V** for depression. The **cos²θ** in the horizontal distance is what option (a) is torn from, and note that it appears **squared** — one cosine to reduce the intercept as seen obliquely, one to project the slope distance onto the horizontal.

**Why tacheometry exists.** It measures **distance and elevation together, without chaining**, from a single instrument setup. That makes it invaluable where chaining is impossible or unsafe:

| Situation | Why chaining fails |
|---|---|
| **Steep or broken hill country** | Slope corrections dominate; footing is dangerous |
| **Across a river or ravine** | The ground cannot be walked |
| **Marshy or wooded ground** | The tape cannot be laid straight |
| **Rapid contouring and detailing** | Chaining every point is far too slow |

Its accuracy — roughly **1 in 500 to 1 in 1000** — is lower than careful chaining, so it is used for **detail and contouring**, never for the primary control framework. That division of labour is the principle of working from whole to part again: precise methods for the framework, rapid ones for the fill-in.

**Determining the constants in the field.** Set the instrument on level ground, measure out known distances (say 50, 100, 150 m), read the intercept at each, and fit D = K s + C — two unknowns from two or more observations. The constants should be re-checked whenever the diaphragm is disturbed.

**The other tacheometric systems**, for completeness: the **movable hair (subtense)** method, in which s is fixed on a target and the hair interval varied, and the **tangential** method, using two vertical angles to two fixed targets and no stadia hairs at all.

examTip.trick: **K** is the multiplying constant, usually **100**, and **C** the additive constant, usually **0** for a modern internal-focusing telescope. So in practice the distance is simply **100 × staff intercept**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Multiply the intercept by 100.** A 0.5 m intercept means 50 m away.

questions.stem: A total station directly measures:
options: Horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance
Reduced levels, which need no further computation
questions.solution:
**Horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance.**

A total station is an **electronic theodolite** combined with an **electronic distance meter (EDM)** and an onboard processor. Those three quantities are what it *observes*; everything else it reports is **computed** from them:

| Observed | Computed from it |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal angle** | Bearings, coordinates |
| **Vertical angle** | Horizontal and vertical components of the slope distance |
| **Slope distance** | **Horizontal distance** = D cos θ; **vertical difference** = D sin θ |
| — | **Coordinates** (E, N, RL), areas, volumes, missing line dimensions |

So option (b) is wrong because the horizontal distance is derived, not measured; option (c) omits the EDM, which is the whole point of the instrument; and option (d) confuses observation with computation — a reduced level requires the **instrument height, the target height and a known starting RL** in addition to the observations.

That last distinction is the one worth carrying: **the instrument measures three raw quantities and computes the rest**, so an error in an entered instrument or target height corrupts every level it reports while leaving the angles and distances perfectly good.

**How the EDM works.** It emits an infrared or laser beam to a **prism (reflector)** and measures the **phase difference** of the returned signal, from which the distance follows. Accuracy is typically quoted as a fixed part plus a proportional part — of the order of **± (2 mm + 2 ppm)** — so at 1 km the proportional term contributes only 2 mm. Reflectorless models measure directly off a surface, at shorter range.

**Why it displaced the theodolite-and-chain:**

| Advantage | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Angle **and** distance in one observation | One setup does what previously took two operations |
| **Electronic recording** | No booking errors, no transcription errors |
| **Direct download** to CAD or GIS | No manual plotting |
| **Onboard computation** | Setting out by coordinates in real time |
| Immunity to **local attraction** | It measures angles, not magnetic bearings |

The **elimination of manual booking** is the least glamorous and most valuable of these: a large share of the errors in classical surveying were made in the field book and in transcription, not in the observations.

**Its principal field applications:** traversing, detail survey, contouring, **setting out** structures and road alignments from design coordinates, and **as-built** verification.

**Where GNSS is preferred instead.** A total station requires **line of sight** between instrument and target, so it cannot work through obstruction; GNSS needs **sky view** instead. That makes them complements, not rivals:

| Method | Needs | Fails in |
|---|---|---|
| **Total station** | **Line of sight** | Dense built-up areas, forest, around corners |
| **GNSS / RTK** | **Clear sky view** | Under canopy, in narrow urban canyons, indoors |

In Nepal's terrain and its dense older settlements, both are routinely used on the same project — GNSS to establish control, the total station to survey detail where the sky is blocked.

examTip.trap: "Coordinates" is the tempting answer because coordinates are what appears on the screen — but those are **computed**, not measured.
examTip.trick: A total station is a theodolite plus an EDM: the theodolite gives the two **angles**, the EDM gives the **slope distance**. Everything else is trigonometry done by the onboard processor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two angles and a distance measured; northing, easting and level computed.**

questions.stem: On the 30 m chord definition, the radius R of a circular curve of degree D is approximately:
questions.solution:
**R ≈ 1719 / D.**

The **degree of curve** D is the angle subtended at the centre by a chord of standard length. For a chord of length C:

> **sin(D/2) = (C/2) / R**

For small D the sine may be replaced by the angle in radians, giving

> **R ≈ 180 C / (π D) = 57.3 C / D**

**With C = 30 m:** R ≈ 57.3 × 30 / D = **1719 / D**.

**The whole family, from the one relation** — which is why the formula is worth deriving rather than memorising four numbers:

| Standard chord | Constant | Where used |
|---|---|---|
| **30 m** | **1719 / D** | **Metric practice — Nepal and India** |
| **20 m** | **1146 / D** | Metric, shorter chord |
| 100 ft (arc definition) | 5730 / D | American practice |
| 1 m | 57.3 / D | — |

All four options here are therefore **real constants** for different standard chords — the question is answered by knowing which chord goes with which, and 57.3 × 30 = 1719 settles it in one multiplication.

**A worked check.** A 4° curve on the 30 m chord definition has R = 1719/4 ≈ **430 m**. Exactly: R = 15/sin(2°) = 15/0.034899 = **429.8 m** ✓ — the approximation is good to well under a metre, and improves as D decreases.

**Why degree of curve rather than radius?** For **setting out**. Field work proceeds by laying off successive **standard chords**, and the deflection angle for each is simply **D/2**. Expressing sharpness as a degree therefore states directly what the surveyor must turn off at each peg, which a radius does not.

**The relations of a simple circular curve**, with Δ the deflection (intersection) angle:

| Element | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Tangent length** | T = R tan(Δ/2) |
| **Length of curve** | **L = πRΔ/180** |
| Long chord | 2R sin(Δ/2) |
| **Apex (external) distance** | R[sec(Δ/2) − 1] |
| Mid-ordinate | R[1 − cos(Δ/2)] |

**Setting out by deflection angles (Rankine's method)** is the classical procedure:

> **δ = 1718.9 C / R minutes**

The same 1719 appears again, now giving the **deflection angle in minutes** for a chord C — which is no coincidence, since it is the same relation rearranged.

**The important caution:** the **first and last sub-chords are shorter** than the standard chord, because the curve begins and ends at chainages that rarely fall on a round multiple. Their deflection angles must be computed separately from the same formula, and forgetting this is the commonest error in curve setting-out.

**A larger D means a sharper curve** — the two are inversely related, so a 1° curve is very flat (R ≈ 1719 m) while a 20° curve is tight (R ≈ 86 m).

examTip.trick: Two definitions exist and give different constants: **1719/D for the 30 m chord** definition, and **1746/D for the 30 m arc**. Nepali and Indian practice uses the chord definition.
examTip.mnemonic: **1719 over D.** A 1° curve therefore has a radius of about 1719 m — and the radius halves as the degree doubles.

questions.stem: The method of plane tabling used to determine the position of the plane table station itself is:
questions.solution:
**Resection.**

The four methods of plane tabling, distinguished by **what is being fixed**:

| Method | Fixes | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Radiation** | **Detail points**, from **one** station | Rays drawn to each point, distances **measured** and scaled off |
| **Intersection** | **Detail points**, from **two** stations | Rays from both; the point is where they **cross** — no distance measured |
| **Traversing** | A **series of stations** | The table is set at each in turn, forming a traverse |
| **Resection** | **The station itself** | Rays drawn **from** known plotted points **back** to the observer |

The first three fix **objects**; resection fixes **the observer**. That reversal is the whole distinction, and it is what makes resection so useful — the surveyor can set up anywhere convenient, without that point having been surveyed in advance.

**The methods of resection:**

| Method | Requires |
|---|---|
| By a **back ray** | One known plotted point and one known direction |
| **Two-point problem** | **Two** known plotted points, and an auxiliary station |
| **Three-point problem** | **Three** known plotted points — no auxiliary station needed |

**The three-point problem** is the classical one, solved by the **tracing paper method** (Bessel's), by the **graphical (Lehmann's) method** of trial orientation, or mechanically. Lehmann's rules for which way to shift the trial position, given the *triangle of error*, are the examinable part.

**The one configuration that must be avoided:** if the plane table station lies **on or near the circle passing through the three known points** — the **"danger circle"** — the three rays intersect at a common point for *any* orientation, so the position is **indeterminate**. The remedy is to choose a station well inside or well outside that circle.

**Why plane tabling is worth knowing despite being largely superseded.** Its distinguishing merit is that **plotting is done in the field, in view of the ground**:

| Advantage | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Plotted **on the spot** | Nothing is **omitted** — the surveyor sees what is missing |
| No field book | No **transcription** errors |
| Errors **visible immediately** | Checked against the ground while still there |
| **Rapid** for small-scale detail | Contours and topography |

Against which: it is **weather-dependent**, awkward to carry, unsuitable for precise work, and produces only the plotted sheet — there are **no recorded measurements** to re-plot at another scale or to re-check later. That last limitation is decisive in modern practice, where survey data must be reusable in CAD and GIS.

**The accessories**, examined by name: the **alidade** (the sighting rule, plain or telescopic), the **trough compass** for orientation, the **spirit level**, the **U-fork or plumbing fork** for centring the table over the station, and the **drawing sheet** itself.

**Orientation** — setting the table so that the plotted lines are parallel to the ground lines — is the operation on which everything depends, and is done either by the **trough compass** (quick, but subject to local attraction) or by a **back ray to a plotted point** (more reliable, and always preferred where a plotted point is visible).

examTip.trap: Intersection is the mirror-image method and is the usual confusion: intersection fixes an **inaccessible object** from two known stations; resection fixes the **station you are standing on**.
examTip.trick: Ask which point is unknown. If it is where you are, it is resection.
examTip.mnemonic: **RE-section = where I am. INTER-section = that thing over there.** Resection needs three known points (the three-point problem).

questions.stem: Reciprocal levelling is employed in order to:
options: Check that the levelling staff is of correct length
Measure the level difference on a very steep slope
questions.solution:
**To eliminate the errors of curvature, refraction and collimation when levelling across a wide obstacle.**

Ordinary levelling relies on placing the instrument **midway** between the two staff positions, so that the equal back and fore sight distances make the systematic errors cancel. Across a **wide river, ravine or valley** that is impossible — the instrument cannot stand in the middle.

**Reciprocal levelling restores the cancellation by symmetry in time instead of space:**

1. Set the instrument **near station A** and read on A (short sight) and on B (long sight).
2. Move to **near station B** and read on B (short sight) and on A (long sight).
3. The **true difference of level** is the **mean** of the two apparent differences.

Each setup has one short and one long sight, and the errors that scale with sight distance therefore enter with **opposite sign** in the two setups. Averaging removes them.

**What is removed, and what is not:**

| Error | Removed? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Curvature** of the earth | **Yes** | Depends on distance; reverses between setups |
| **Refraction** of the line of sight | **Largely** | Same, though it varies with time and weather |
| **Collimation** error of the instrument | **Yes** | Enters with opposite sign |
| Staff graduation error | **No** | Independent of geometry |
| Instrument not level | No | Must be corrected by levelling up |

**The magnitude of what is being removed:**

> **Combined curvature and refraction correction = 0.0673 d²** metres, with d in kilometres

where curvature alone is **0.0785 d²** (always making the object appear **lower**) and refraction restores about **one-seventh** of it (making objects appear **higher**). At 100 m the combined effect is under a millimetre; at **1 km it is 67 mm** — which is why the technique is needed only for long sights, and why balancing sight lengths is normally sufficient.

Refraction is the less trustworthy of the two, because it depends on air temperature and density gradients near the ground. That is why reciprocal levelling observations should be taken **at nearly the same time and in the same conditions from both ends** — or, better, **simultaneously with two instruments**, if the refraction is to cancel properly.

**Why the other options describe different operations:**

| Option | Actually |
|---|---|
| Establishing a benchmark | An ordinary levelling run closed onto existing control |
| **Checking the staff** | Comparison against a standard — a **standardisation** matter |
| Levelling a steep slope | Ordinary levelling in **short stages**, or trigonometric levelling |

**The family of special levelling methods**, each for its own obstacle:

| Method | For |
|---|---|
| **Simple / differential (fly) levelling** | The general case, in stages |
| **Reciprocal** | A **wide obstacle** that cannot be occupied |
| **Profile levelling** | Levels **along** a line — a road or canal centre line |
| **Cross-section levelling** | Levels **across** it, for earthwork |
| **Precise levelling** | High-order control, with special staves and procedures |
| **Trigonometric levelling** | Differences of level from **vertical angles** — inaccessible peaks |
| Check levelling | Verifying an earlier run |

And the discipline underlying all of them: **keep back sight and fore sight distances equal wherever possible**, close every run onto a benchmark, and never accept a run that has not closed within its permissible misclosure — commonly quoted as **± 12√K mm** for ordinary work, with K the circuit length in kilometres.

examTip.trick: Take a reading from each bank with the instrument close to each end in turn. The errors are **equal and of opposite sign** in the two sets, so averaging removes them exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Level from both banks and average.** Used across rivers and ravines, where you cannot set the instrument midway — which is the normal way of cancelling collimation error.

questions.stem: Simpson's rule for computing an area from a series of offsets requires that the number of ordinates be:
questions.solution:
**Odd.**

Simpson's rule fits a **parabola through every three consecutive ordinates**, so it consumes them in pairs of intervals. It therefore requires an **even number of intervals**, which — since the ordinates number one more than the intervals — means an **odd number of ordinates**.

> **Area = (d/3) [ (O₁ + Oₙ) + 4(O₂ + O₄ + …) + 2(O₃ + O₅ + …) ]**

that is, **(interval/3) × [first + last + 4 × sum of even ordinates + 2 × sum of the remaining odd ordinates]**.

**A memory aid:** the coefficients run **1, 4, 2, 4, 2, … 4, 1** — beginning and ending with 1, with 4 always in the even positions. Their sum is 3n for n intervals, which is why the whole is divided by 3.

**Compared with the trapezoidal rule:**

| | **Trapezoidal** | **Simpson's** |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary assumed | **Straight** between offsets | **Parabolic** through each three |
| Ordinates required | **Any number** | **Odd** (even number of intervals) |
| Accuracy | Lower | **Higher**, for a curved boundary |
| Formula | (d/2)[O₁ + Oₙ + 2(all intermediate)] | (d/3)[O₁ + Oₙ + 4(even) + 2(odd)] |

**What to do when the ordinates are even in number** — the practical question that follows immediately. Two accepted remedies:

1. Apply **Simpson's rule to the odd-numbered portion** and treat the **last strip as a trapezium**.
2. Apply the **trapezoidal rule throughout**.

The first is preferred, since it keeps the higher accuracy over most of the length.

**Which rule gives the larger answer** depends on the curvature of the boundary, and it is worth being able to reason it out rather than guess: where the boundary is **convex outward** (bulging away from the base line), the straight chords of the trapezoidal rule cut inside the true boundary and **underestimate** the area, while Simpson's parabola follows it. Where **concave**, the reverse.

**The volume analogues**, used for earthwork:

| Rule | Formula | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| **Trapezoidal (average end area)** | V = d[(A₁ + Aₙ)/2 + A₂ + … + Aₙ₋₁] | Any number of sections |
| **Prismoidal** | V = (d/3)[A₁ + Aₙ + 4(even A) + 2(odd A)] | **Odd** number of sections; more accurate |

The **prismoidal formula is Simpson's rule applied to areas instead of ordinates** — the same structure, one dimension higher. The difference between the two results is the **prismoidal correction**, and since the trapezoidal rule generally **overestimates** volume for the usual cutting and embankment shapes, the correction is normally **subtractive**.

**Where this arises in practice:** computing the area of an irregular plot from offsets to a chain line, the **capacity of a reservoir** from the areas enclosed by successive contours, the **earthwork** for a road or canal from cross-sections, and the discharge of a channel from a velocity–area survey. In each case the choice between the two rules is a choice about how the boundary between measurements is assumed to behave — never a mere formula preference.

examTip.trap: "Even" is a genuine trap because the number of **divisions** must be even — but the question asks about **ordinates**, which is one more than the number of divisions.
examTip.trick: Simpson's rule pairs the strips, so it needs an even number of strips, hence an **odd** number of ordinates. The trapezoidal rule has no such restriction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Odd ordinates, even divisions.** Simpson's is more accurate for a curved boundary; trapezoidal is safer when the shape is irregular.

questions.stem: The minimum number of satellites that must be observed to determine a three-dimensional position by GPS is:
questions.solution:
**Four.**

There are **four unknowns**, not three. The receiver must solve for its position — **X, Y and Z** — and also for the **receiver clock error**, because a satellite navigation fix is fundamentally a measurement of **signal travel time**, and the receiver's inexpensive quartz clock cannot keep time to the nanosecond accuracy required.

> **4 unknowns (X, Y, Z, Δt) ⟹ 4 observation equations ⟹ 4 satellites**

Each satellite gives one **pseudo-range** — so called precisely because it is contaminated by that unknown clock error:

> **Pseudo-range = true range + c · Δt**

**Why the clock is the fourth unknown, and why it must be solved rather than measured.** Light travels about **30 cm per nanosecond**, so a clock error of one microsecond corresponds to a position error of **300 m**. Fitting every receiver with an atomic clock is impossible; solving for the offset from a fourth satellite is both cheap and exact. A useful by-product is that GPS receivers are excellent **clocks**, which is why the system underpins time synchronisation in telecommunications and power networks.

**With three satellites** a **two-dimensional** fix is still possible if the height is assumed or held fixed — which is why a receiver may report a 2D position when the sky is partly blocked, and why such a position should not be trusted for levelling.

**The three segments of the system:**

| Segment | Comprises |
|---|---|
| **Space** | The satellite constellation — about **24–32** operational GPS satellites in **6 orbital planes**, roughly **20 200 km** altitude, 12-hour period |
| **Control** | Ground monitoring and master control stations, which track the satellites and upload corrected orbit and clock data |
| **User** | The receivers |

**The error sources, and how each is handled** — this is what distinguishes a 5 m handheld fix from a 10 mm survey fix:

| Error | Magnitude | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Ionospheric delay** | Largest | **Dual-frequency** receivers; models |
| **Tropospheric delay** | Moderate | Models |
| **Satellite clock and orbit** | Moderate | Broadcast corrections; precise ephemerides |
| **Multipath** — reflections off buildings | Variable | Antenna design; site choice |
| **Receiver noise** | Small | Averaging |
| **Poor satellite geometry (high DOP)** | Variable | Observe when more satellites are well spread |

**DOP (dilution of precision)** deserves note: even with many satellites, if they are **clustered in one part of the sky** the intersection of their ranges is poorly conditioned and the fix is weak — exactly the same geometric principle as the **well-conditioned triangle** in classical triangulation.

**The techniques, by accuracy:**

| Technique | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| **Single-point (autonomous)** | 5 – 15 m |
| **DGPS** — differential, with a base station | 1 – 3 m |
| **RTK** — real-time kinematic, carrier phase | **1 – 5 cm** |
| **Static** post-processed | **Millimetres** — geodetic control |

The leap from metres to centimetres comes from using the **carrier phase** rather than the code, and from **differencing** between a base station and the rover so that errors common to both cancel — the same cancellation-by-symmetry principle as reciprocal levelling.

**And a caution on heights.** GNSS gives **ellipsoidal** heights, whereas levelling gives **orthometric** heights above the geoid (mean sea level). The two differ by the **geoid undulation**, which in Nepal is large and varies across the country — so a GNSS height cannot be used as a reduced level without applying a geoid model.

examTip.trick: Three satellites would fix x, y and z — but the receiver's clock is a **fourth unknown**, and correcting it needs a fourth observation. A cheap quartz clock is the reason.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three for position, one for time.** Three satellites give a 2-D fix only, if the altitude is assumed.

questions.stem: In the centre line method of estimating, the quantity of an item is obtained by multiplying the total centre line length by:
options: The plinth area of the building
The breadth and depth of that item
The number of rooms in the building
questions.solution:
**By the breadth and depth of that item.**

The centre line method takes the **total length of the centre lines of all walls**, measured once, and multiplies it by the **cross-sectional dimensions** of each item — breadth × depth for excavation, foundation concrete, footings and superstructure masonry in turn.

> **Quantity = total centre line length × breadth × depth**

**Its great advantage** is that one length serves every item, since all the items of a wall share the same centre line. That makes it **quick** and internally consistent.

**The essential correction, and the reason candidates lose the mark.** At every **junction** of walls the centre line method **over-measures**, because the two intersecting walls each claim the shared corner. The rule:

> **Deduct half the breadth of the item, for each junction, per cross wall**

So a T-junction requires one deduction and a cross-junction two. A rectangular building with **no** internal walls needs **no** correction at all, since its centre line is a closed loop — which is why the method is exact and effortless for a simple building and requires care for a partitioned one.

**The two methods compared:**

| | **Centre line method** | **Long wall–short wall method** |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | One **total centre line** length | **Long walls** measured out-to-out, **short walls** in-to-in |
| Speed | **Faster** | Slower |
| Junctions | Need **deduction** of half breadth per junction | **Automatically** handled |
| Suits | Buildings with **walls of uniform thickness** | Walls of **differing thickness**, complex plans |
| Risk | Forgetting the junction deduction | Arithmetic slips over many items |

The long wall–short wall method is self-correcting because the long walls are measured **centre to centre plus the two half-breadths at each end** (i.e. out to out) while the short walls are measured **between** them — so the corners belong to the long walls only, once each.

**Where each is preferred in practice:** the centre line method for a straightforward building of uniform wall thickness, and the long wall–short wall method where thicknesses change between the footing, plinth and superstructure — because a change of thickness changes the out-to-out and in-to-in lengths but *not* the centre line, which is precisely when the centre line method's simplicity becomes a liability if the deductions are not tracked.

**The order in which items are taken up** in a detailed estimate of a building, since the same lengths are reused down the list: earthwork excavation → lime or cement concrete in foundation → footings and foundation masonry → DPC → superstructure masonry → RCC → doors and windows → flooring → roofing → plastering → finishing → services.

examTip.trick: The centre line method's advantage is speed — one length serves every item in a wall. Its trap is **junctions**: at every cross wall or T-junction the centre line must be **shortened by half the breadth** of the item, for each junction.
examTip.mnemonic: **One length, many items — but deduct at every junction.** Forgetting the deduction over-measures the work.

questions.stem: In a bill of quantities, reinforcement steel is measured in:
questions.solution:
**By weight — in quintals or tonnes.**

Steel is measured by **weight** because that is how it is bought and sold, and because bars of the same length but different diameter differ enormously in value. The length of each bar is computed from the bar bending schedule and converted using the **unit weight**:

> **Unit weight of a round bar = d² / 162 kg per metre**, with d in mm

**A worked check:** for a 12 mm bar, 144/162 = **0.888 kg/m** ✓. For 16 mm, 256/162 = **1.58 kg/m**; for 20 mm, **2.47 kg/m**.

**Where the constant 162 comes from**, since it is worth being able to reconstruct rather than merely recall:

> weight per metre = (πd²/4) × 7850 kg/m³ ÷ 10⁶ = d² × 0.00617 = **d²/162**

taking the density of steel as **7850 kg/m³**.

**Note that laps, hooks and bends are included** in the measured length — they are steel that must be bought and placed — but **binding wire, chairs and spacers are not** measured separately in ordinary practice, being covered by the rate.

**The units of measurement for the principal items** under IS 1200, which must simply be known:

| Item | Unit | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Earthwork excavation** | **m³** | On **authorised** dimensions, not as actually dug |
| **Concrete, brickwork, stone masonry** | **m³** | |
| **Half-brick walls, partition walls** | **m²** | Thin walls, so area with thickness stated |
| **Plastering, pointing, painting** | **m²** | |
| **Damp proof course** | **m²** | Thickness stated |
| **Flooring, roofing, ceiling** | **m²** | |
| **Reinforcement steel, structural steel** | **quintal / tonne** | **By weight** |
| **Skirting, dado, cornice, railing** | **running metre** | Linear items |
| **Doors and windows (frames)** | **m³** or number | Shutters in m² |
| Sanitary fittings, trees | **Number** | |

**The organising principle** behind the whole table: the unit follows the **dimension that governs the cost**. Where all three dimensions matter, m³; where thickness is fixed by specification, m²; where the section is fixed and only length varies, running metre; where the item is discrete, number; and where value depends on the mass of material, **weight**.

**The deduction rules** are the other half of measurement, and the two thresholds most often examined:

| Work | No deduction for openings up to |
|---|---|
| **Brickwork / masonry** | **0.1 m²** |
| **Plastering** | **0.5 m²** |

The plastering threshold is the larger because the labour of working around a small opening offsets the area saved — the measurement conventions are built to reflect real cost, not geometry alone.

examTip.trick: Convert by unit weight: **w = d²/162 kg per metre** with d in mm. So a 12 mm bar is 0.89 kg/m and a 20 mm bar is 2.47 kg/m.
examTip.mnemonic: **d²/162 kg per metre.** Steel is bought and measured by weight even though it is drawn and cut by length.

questions.stem: In a detailed estimate, the provision for contingencies is usually taken as:
questions.solution:
**3 to 5% of the estimated cost.**

Contingency covers the **small unforeseen items** that any real project throws up but which cannot be listed in advance — a slightly deeper foundation than the trial pits suggested, an extra manhole, minor changes during execution.

**Note what it is not for.** Contingency is **not** a provision for:

| Not covered by contingency | Handled by |
|---|---|
| **Design changes** or added scope | A **supplementary** estimate |
| A large **rate increase** | A **revised** estimate |
| Items **omitted by oversight** from the estimate | Correcting the estimate |
| **Price escalation** over a long contract | A separate escalation clause |

A contingency of 3–5% is deliberately small precisely because it is meant for genuinely minor items. Treating it as a general cushion for poor estimating is what leads to the cost overruns that then require formal revision.

**The other percentage provisions in a detailed estimate**, all commonly examined together:

| Provision | Typical rate | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Contingencies** | **3 – 5%** | Minor unforeseen items |
| **Work-charged establishment** | **1.5 – 2%** | Site supervisory staff engaged for that work |
| **Tools and plant (T&P)** | 1 – 1.5% | Departmental tools |
| **Petty supervision** | 1.5 – 2% | — |
| **Contractor's profit** (in rate analysis) | **10 – 15%** | The contractor's margin |
| Water charges | 1 – 2% | — |

Option (b), 10–15%, is the trap — that is the **contractor's profit** allowed within *rate analysis*, an entirely different provision at a different stage. A candidate who has memorised the percentages without noting what each attaches to will pick it.

**Work-charged establishment** deserves a note since the term is opaque: it means staff — an overseer, a work clerk — engaged **specifically for that work** and paid from its funds, as distinct from the permanent departmental establishment paid from the general budget.

**The types of estimate, and when each is prepared:**

| Estimate | When | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / approximate** | At the **conception** stage, for administrative approval | **Plinth area rate**, cubic content rate, or per unit (per bed, per km) |
| **Plinth area** | Early | Plinth area × rate from a similar completed building |
| **Cube rate** | Early | Volume × rate — better where storey heights differ |
| **Detailed** | Before **calling tenders** | **Item-by-item** measurement × rate |
| **Revised** | When the sanctioned figure is exceeded by more than **5%** | Fresh detailed estimate |
| **Supplementary** | When **additional work** becomes necessary during execution | Detailed, for the added items only |
| **Annual repair / maintenance** | Yearly | For upkeep |
| **Complete** | — | Including all ancillary costs — land, legal, supervision |

**Why an accurate estimate matters beyond the arithmetic.** It is the basis on which the work is **sanctioned**, on which **funds are allotted**, and against which tenders are judged. An estimate materially below the true cost stalls the work halfway for want of funds; one materially above it locks up money that could have been spent elsewhere. Both are professional failures, not merely clerical ones.

examTip.trick: The standard allowances in a detailed estimate: **contingencies 3–5%**, **work-charged establishment about 1.5–2%**, and **contractor's profit 10–15%** built into the rate analysis.
examTip.mnemonic: **3–5% for what you did not foresee.** It covers minor unforeseen items, not design changes — those need a revised estimate.

questions.stem: A revised estimate is required when the sanctioned estimate is likely to be exceeded by more than:
questions.solution:
**5%.**

A **revised estimate** is a fresh detailed estimate prepared for the **same work**, submitted for re-sanction when the original figure will be exceeded materially — conventionally by more than **5%**.

**Why 5% and not more.** The threshold has to be low enough that the sanctioning authority retains real control over public money. If a department could overspend by 20% without returning for approval, the sanction would mean little. It is set above zero only because minor variation is inevitable, and that minor variation is what the **3–5% contingency** provision is for.

So the two figures work together: **contingency absorbs small overruns; beyond about 5%, the estimate must be revised.**

**The grounds for a revised estimate:**

| Cause | Example |
|---|---|
| **Rates** have risen materially | Market change since sanction |
| **Quantities** differ substantially | Ground conditions unlike the investigation |
| The **original estimate** was defective | Items omitted or under-measured |
| **Material deviation** from the sanctioned design | — |

**Distinguish it sharply from a supplementary estimate** — this is the pairing the topic exists to test:

| | **Revised estimate** | **Supplementary estimate** |
|---|---|---|
| Covers | **The same work**, re-costed | **Additional work**, newly found necessary |
| Trigger | Sanctioned amount exceeded by **> 5%** | New work must be added to the original |
| Presented | As a **complete fresh estimate**, with a comparative statement of the original and revised figures against each item | As an estimate for the **added items only**, accompanied by the original |
| Question answered | *Why does the same work now cost more?* | *What is this new work and what does it cost?* |

The comparative statement is what a revised estimate must carry: item by item, the original quantity and rate against the new, with the reason for each variation. Without it the authority cannot tell an honest cost increase from an admission of poor estimating.

**Where this sits in the project cycle**, since the terms only make sense in sequence:

1. **Administrative approval** — sanction of the *proposal*, on the preliminary estimate.
2. **Technical sanction** — approval of the *detailed* estimate by the competent technical authority, confirming the design and the rates are sound.
3. **Expenditure sanction** — authority to spend.
4. **Tender and award.**
5. During execution — **variation orders**, and if needed a **revised** or **supplementary** estimate, followed by **re-sanction**.
6. **Completion report** and final bill.

**Technical sanction** is the engineer's own responsibility and the step most relevant professionally: it certifies that the quantities, the specifications and the rates are correct, and it is granted by an officer competent for that value of work. Signing a technical sanction for an estimate one has not checked is precisely the kind of casual certification that professional conduct rules exist to prevent.

examTip.trap: Do not confuse it with a **supplementary** estimate, which covers **additional work**. A revised estimate covers the **same work costing more**.
examTip.trick: Ask what changed. Scope unchanged but cost overrun → revised. New scope added → supplementary.
examTip.mnemonic: **Revised = same work, more money. Supplementary = more work.** The trigger is a 5% overrun.

questions.stem: The carpet area of a building is its plinth area less the area of:
options: The compound and open space around the building
Walls, verandahs, staircases, corridors and sanitary accommodation
Nothing — the two are the same
questions.solution:
**Less the area of walls, verandahs, staircases, corridors and sanitary accommodation.**

The three areas, in descending order of size — the sequence to hold:

| Area | Definition | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| **Plinth (built-up) area** | Area at floor level, measured **externally**, over the plinth | **Everything**, walls included |
| **Carpet area** | The **usable** floor area | Only the space one can actually lay carpet on |
| — | | |

> **Plinth area = carpet area + area of walls + circulation and service areas**

**What is excluded from the carpet area**, and the reason each is excluded: **walls** (not usable), **verandahs, staircases, corridors and lift wells** (circulation, not usable floor), **sanitary accommodation**, and shafts and ducts. What **is** included: the rooms, kitchen, and any store or usable enclosed space.

**Typical relationships**, worth knowing as a sanity check on any figure quoted:

> **Carpet area ≈ 50 – 70% of plinth area** for a residential building

The walls alone commonly account for **10 – 15%**, and circulation for the rest. A building whose claimed carpet area exceeds about 75% of its plinth area should be questioned.

**Why the distinction matters practically:**

| Area | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Plinth area** | **Estimating** — the plinth area rate; municipal **floor area ratio** and building permission |
| **Carpet area** | **Rent and sale** — what the occupier actually gets; the basis on which property must legally be sold in many jurisdictions |
| Super built-up area | A **marketing** figure — plinth area plus a share of common areas; not a technical term |

The last row is why the distinction became a consumer issue: quoting a **super built-up** area makes a flat sound larger than the space it delivers, and the remedy adopted in India (RERA) was to require sale on **carpet area**. An engineer asked to certify areas must state **which** area is being certified.

**How the plinth area estimate works.** It is the standard **approximate** estimate:

> **Approximate cost = plinth area × plinth area rate**

where the rate comes from a **recently completed building of similar type, specification and locality**. Its accuracy depends entirely on that similarity — the same plinth area of a school, a hospital and a warehouse cost very different amounts, since the rate embeds the specification.

**Measurement rules for plinth area**, which are examinable in their own right: measured **external** to the walls at floor level; a **courtyard, open verandah or open balcony is excluded**; a covered verandah is included; and areas of **different storey heights or specifications are measured separately**, because they attract different rates.

The **cube rate estimate** (plinth area × height × cube rate) is the refinement used where storey heights are unusual, since cost follows volume more closely than floor area when the height departs from the normal.

examTip.trick: Three areas in descending order: **plinth area** (everything at plinth level, measured externally), **carpet area** (only the usable floor), and between them the difference — walls, circulation and services.
examTip.mnemonic: **Carpet area is where you could actually lay a carpet.** It is typically 50–65% of the plinth area.

questions.stem: In earthwork, the term 'lead' refers to:
options: The horizontal distance through which excavated material is transported
The vertical height through which it is raised
The depth of the excavation below ground level
The width of the trench at its bottom
questions.solution:
**The horizontal distance through which excavated material is transported.**

**Lead and lift** are the paired terms of earthwork measurement:

| Term | Direction | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| **Lead** | **Horizontal** | The distance the material is **carried** |
| **Lift** | **Vertical** | The height it is **raised** |

Both affect the rate, because both cost labour and plant. The conventions:

> Lead is measured along the **shortest practicable route**, not as a straight line across obstacles.
> An **initial lead** (commonly 30 m) and an **initial lift** (commonly 1.5 m) are **included in the basic rate**; beyond those, **extra** is paid in stages.

So an item is quoted as, for example, "earthwork in excavation … including lead up to 30 m and lift up to 1.5 m", with separate items for every additional stage. This staging is why the same cubic metre of excavation carries several different rates on one project depending on where the spoil goes.

**Why the distinction is more than terminology.** For a deep foundation or a hill road, the **lift** can dominate the cost — raising spoil 6 m out of a pit is far more laborious than moving it 30 m on the level. And on a road project the **lead** dominates, since the haul from cut to fill may run to kilometres. Recognising which governs is how an engineer judges whether a quoted rate is reasonable.

**The related earthwork terms:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Borrow pit** | A pit from which **fill** material is taken, outside the works |
| **Spoil bank** | Where **surplus** excavated material is deposited |
| **Bulking** | The **increase in volume** of soil when excavated and loosened |
| **Shrinkage** | The **decrease** when it is compacted in an embankment |
| **Mass haul diagram** | A plot of cumulative volume against chainage, used to plan the **economical haul** from cut to fill |

**Bulking and shrinkage together are why three different volumes exist for the same soil** — and confusing them is the most consequential error in earthwork estimating:

| Volume | Where measured | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **Bank (in situ)** | In the ground, undisturbed | The base |
| **Loose** | In the truck | **Larger** — bulked, typically 20–30% for common soil |
| **Compacted** | In the finished embankment | **Smaller** than bank, typically by 10–20% |

So excavating 100 m³ in situ may yield 125 m³ to haul and produce only about 90 m³ of embankment — which means the **quantity to excavate is not the quantity to fill**, and a project balanced on paper by equating them will run short of material.

**Measurement of earthwork** itself: in **m³**, on the **authorised dimensions** shown on the drawing, **not as actually excavated**. If a contractor digs wider than specified for convenience of working, the extra is not paid for — the risk of over-excavation lies with the contractor, which is why side slopes and trench widths in the drawings matter commercially as well as technically.

Volumes are computed from cross-sections by the **trapezoidal (average end area)** or the more accurate **prismoidal** rule, the difference between them being the **prismoidal correction**.

examTip.trick: **Lead is horizontal; lift is vertical.** Both are paid for separately from the excavation itself, because both add cost without adding volume.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lead along, lift up.** The first 30 m of lead is usually included in the basic rate, with extra paid beyond it.

questions.stem: A bar bending schedule gives:
options: The sequence in which concreting is to be carried out
The rate per quintal of reinforcement steel
The total cost of the reinforcement in a structure
The shape, size, number, length and bending details of every bar
questions.solution:
**The shape, size, number, length and bending details of every bar.**

A bar bending schedule (BBS) is a **tabular statement** prepared from the structural drawings, listing for each distinct bar:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Bar mark** | An identifying number |
| **Diameter** | 8, 10, 12, 16, 20 mm … |
| **Shape / bending details** | Straight, cranked, L, U, stirrup, with a **sketch and dimensions** |
| **Cutting length** | The length of straight bar needed before bending |
| **Number** of bars | Including the count per member and the number of members |
| **Total length** | Number × cutting length |
| **Unit weight** | **d²/162** kg/m |
| **Total weight** | The quantity that goes into the bill |

**The cutting length is the whole difficulty**, and it is what distinguishes a BBS from a mere list. A bent bar is **shorter along its centre line than the sum of its outside dimensions**, because the bar curves around the bend rather than turning a sharp corner. So:

> **Cutting length = Σ(straight lengths) + Σ(hook and bend allowances) − Σ(bend deductions)**

with the standard allowances:

| Feature | Allowance |
|---|---|
| **Standard hook** (135°/180°) | **9d** per hook |
| **45° bend** | 1d deduction |
| **90° bend** | **2d** deduction |
| **135° bend** | 3d deduction |
| **Crank in a bar** (at 45°) | 0.42D extra, D being the vertical offset |
| **Lap length** (tension) | Typically **50d**, or as per the drawing |

A stirrup, having four 90° bends and two hooks, is a good exercise: cutting length = 2(a + b) + 2 × 9d − 4 × 2d = 2(a+b) + 10d, taking a and b as the outside dimensions less cover.

**Why the schedule matters on site**, and why it is a real engineering document rather than clerical work:

| Purpose | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Ordering** the right quantity of each diameter | Avoids both shortage and surplus |
| **Cutting and bending** before delivery to the pour | Bars arrive ready — no delay at the pour |
| **Minimising wastage** by cutting from standard 12 m lengths | Off-cuts are the largest avoidable waste in reinforcement |
| **Checking** the placed steel against the drawing | The bar mark identifies each bar unambiguously |
| **Measurement** for payment | Weight, from the same schedule |

**The last row is the link to estimating** — the BBS *is* the measurement of steel. So although option (c) is wrong, the schedule is the document **from which** the cost of reinforcement is derived: total weight × rate.

Option (a) names the **method statement or programme**, and option (b) belongs to **rate analysis**.

**A caution on cover, since it determines every cutting length.** The clear cover specified by IS 456 by exposure — **20 mm** for moderate, **40 mm** for severe, **50 mm** for very severe, and **40–50 mm** for a footing in contact with earth — must be deducted before the bar dimensions are computed. Getting the cover wrong makes every bar in the schedule the wrong length, and reinforcement placed with too little cover corrodes, which is the commonest cause of premature failure in concrete structures.

examTip.trick: The schedule is what the bar bender actually works from, and what the steel is ordered against. It also feeds the **cutting length**, which is the straight length plus hooks and bends less the bend allowances.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shape, size, number, length, bending.** A 90° bend allowance is 2d and a 135° hook is 3d for mild steel.

questions.stem: By the straight line method, the annual depreciation of an asset of initial cost C, salvage value S and useful life n years is:
questions.solution:
**(C − S) / n.**

The quantity to be recovered over the asset's life is not its whole cost but the part that will **not** be recovered on disposal:

> **Depreciable amount = C − S**,  and  **annual depreciation D = (C − S)/n**

Option (a) omits the salvage value and therefore over-depreciates; option (b) adds it, which makes no sense in any method.

**The book value** after m years follows directly:

> **Book value = C − m(C − S)/n**

which falls in a **straight line** from C to S — hence the method's name — and reaches exactly S at the end of the useful life.

**A worked illustration.** A concrete mixer costs Rs 500,000, has a salvage value of Rs 50,000 and a life of 10 years:

> D = (500,000 − 50,000)/10 = **Rs 45,000 per year**

and after 4 years the book value is 500,000 − 4 × 45,000 = **Rs 320,000**.

**The methods compared:**

| Method | Annual charge | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **(C − S)/n**, constant | **Uniform** |
| **Sinking fund** | (C − S) × i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1] | Uniform, but **credits interest** on the fund |
| **Declining balance** | A fixed **% of the reducing book value** | **Accelerated** — heavy early, light later |
| **Sum-of-years-digits** | (remaining life / Σ years) × (C − S) | Accelerated |
| **Production units** | (C − S) × (units this year / total units) | Follows **use** |

**Why the choice of method is not neutral.** Depreciation is not merely bookkeeping — it determines the **hire or ownership rate** charged for plant, and hence the rate analysis for every item of work the plant performs. It also feeds **replacement analysis**: the decision to keep or replace compares the equivalent uniform annual cost of the old machine (which **rises** as maintenance grows) against that of a new one, and the economic life is where they cross.

**Note that declining balance never reaches zero**, since a percentage of a positive number stays positive. That is mathematically inconvenient but physically realistic — most equipment retains some value indefinitely — and where a specific salvage value must be reached the rate is set as

> **k = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n)**

**The valuation terms that accompany depreciation**, routinely confused with one another:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Book value** | Cost **less accumulated depreciation** — an accounting figure |
| **Salvage value** | Worth at the end of life, sold **intact and working** |
| **Scrap value** | Worth of the **dismantled materials** — commonly taken as about **10%** of cost for a building |
| **Market value** | What a willing buyer would actually pay **today** |
| **Replacement value** | Cost of an **equivalent new** asset at current rates |
| **Sentimental / distress value** | Above or below market, for non-economic reasons |

Book value and market value can diverge sharply, and an engineer asked for "the value" of an asset must establish **which** value is wanted before answering — a fully depreciated machine with a book value of zero may still command a substantial market price.

Salvage value can even be **negative**, where dismantling, disposal or site restoration costs more than the materials fetch.

examTip.trick: Straight line depreciation writes off an **equal amount every year**, so the book value falls linearly to the salvage value at year n.
examTip.mnemonic: **(Cost − Scrap) ÷ Life.** Compare with the **declining balance** method, which writes off a fixed *percentage* and so depreciates faster early on — closer to how plant actually loses value.

questions.stem: The value of the dismantled materials of a building at the end of its useful life is its:
questions.solution:
**Scrap value.**

The distinction that the question rests on is **whether the asset survives as a working thing or only as material**:

| Value | The asset is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Salvage value** | Sold **intact and still usable**, perhaps by another owner | A mixer sold second-hand at the end of its useful life to this owner |
| **Scrap value** | **Dismantled** — worth only its **materials** | A demolished building's bricks, steel and timber |

So salvage assumes the thing continues to exist as a machine or structure; scrap assumes it does not. For a **building**, scrap value is conventionally taken at about **10% of the original cost**, and is **net of the cost of demolition** — which can make it small or even negative for a reinforced concrete structure, where breaking out and disposing of the concrete costs more than the recovered steel is worth.

**Why the option list is worth working through:**

| Option | Actually means |
|---|---|
| Salvage value | Worth at end of life, **intact** |
| **Scrap value** | Worth of the **dismantled materials** |
| **Book value** | Cost **less accumulated depreciation** — an accounting figure, unrelated to any market |
| **Market value** | What a willing buyer would pay **today**, for the property as it stands |

**Book value** is the one to be most careful with: it is a bookkeeping construct and may bear no relation to what anything is worth. A fully depreciated building with a book value of zero may still be worth a great deal, and a building whose book value is high may be unsaleable.

**Where scrap value enters a valuation.** In assessing a property by the **depreciation (cost) method**:

> **Present value = replacement cost − depreciation**, with the residual not falling below the **scrap value**

and in **depreciation calculation**, where scrap value plays the role of S in (C − S)/n for a building whose end state is demolition.

**The methods of valuing a property**, since the topic is broader than the terms:

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Rental (capitalised value)** | **Net income × year's purchase** | Income-producing property |
| **Cost / depreciation method** | **Replacement cost less depreciation**, plus land | Owner-occupied buildings, insurance |
| **Comparative (market) method** | Recent sales of **similar** property | An active market |
| **Development method** | Value after development, less cost to develop | Land ripe for development |
| **Profit-based** | Capitalised trading profit | Hotels, cinemas, business premises |

**The rental method's arithmetic**, since it is the one most often examined:

> **Net income = gross rent − outgoings** (taxes, repairs at about 1/12 of gross, insurance, management, sinking fund)
> **Year's purchase = 100 / rate of interest**, so at 8% YP = 12.5
> **Capitalised value = net income × year's purchase**

A building with a net annual income of Rs 240,000 at an 8% expected return is therefore worth 240,000 × 12.5 = **Rs 3,000,000**.

Note that **land does not depreciate** — it is valued separately and added — which is why the value of an old property in a good location is often almost entirely the land.

examTip.trap: **Salvage value** is the near-miss: salvage is what the asset fetches while still usable for its purpose; **scrap** is what the broken-up materials fetch.
examTip.trick: Scrap value is typically about **10% of the original cost**, and is what appears as S in the depreciation formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **Scrap = the value of the rubble.**

questions.stem: As per IS 1200, in plastering work no deduction is made for an opening whose area does not exceed:
questions.solution:
**0.5 m².**

The two thresholds of IS 1200 that are constantly examined together, and constantly interchanged:

| Work | No deduction for an opening up to |
|---|---|
| **Brickwork and masonry** | **0.1 m²** |
| **Plastering** | **0.5 m²** |

**Why plastering has the larger threshold — and this is the reasoning worth carrying rather than the numbers.** Measurement conventions are designed to make the *measured quantity* proportional to the *actual cost*, not to the geometric area. A small opening in a plastered wall:

- saves a trivial area of plaster, but
- **costs extra labour** — the plasterer must work carefully around the reveal, form neat edges, and finish the corners.

The two roughly cancel, so IS 1200 ignores small openings entirely. Above 0.5 m² the saved area dominates, and the deduction is made. Brickwork has no comparable edge-labour penalty, so its threshold is much lower.

**The plastering deduction rules in more detail**, since the topic goes beyond the single figure:

| Case | Rule |
|---|---|
| Opening **up to 0.5 m²** | **No deduction**; no addition for the reveal, jamb or soffit either |
| Opening **0.5 to 3 m²** | **Deduct on one face only**, whichever side is plastered; no addition for reveals |
| Opening **over 3 m²** | **Deduct on both faces**, and the reveals, jambs and soffits are **added** |
| Ends of joists, beams, posts | No deduction |

The middle row explains the neatness of the scheme: for a medium opening the deduction on one face and the omission of the reveals approximately offset, so the arithmetic stays simple while the cost stays fair.

**Plastering is measured in m²**, stating the thickness and the mortar mix, and is measured **on the finished face** — so a wall plastered on both sides is measured twice.

**The other measurement conventions worth holding as a set:**

| Item | Convention |
|---|---|
| **Brickwork** | m³; **no deduction for openings up to 0.1 m²**; no deduction for bearings of slabs or lintels up to a limit |
| **Reinforcement** | By **weight**; **laps, hooks and bends included** |
| **Earthwork** | m³, on **authorised** dimensions — over-excavation is not paid for |
| **Concrete** | m³; **no deduction for reinforcement**; deduct openings over 0.1 m² |
| **Painting** | m²; measured on the **actual surface** with multiplying factors for panelled doors, corrugated sheets, railings |
| **Flooring** | m²; deduct area covered by walls and columns |

**The multiplying factors for painting** are a neat parallel to the plastering rule: a panelled door is not measured on its developed surface but as its plain area × a factor (about 1.3 for one side of a panelled door), because that is easier to measure and reflects the labour more honestly.

**Why any of this matters commercially.** In an **item-rate contract** the contractor is paid on **measured quantity × tendered rate**, so the measurement rules directly determine payment. Site disputes are far more often about **how something was measured** than about the rate agreed — which is exactly why IS 1200 exists and why an engineer must be able to cite it rather than negotiate afresh on each project.

examTip.trick: The rule exists because measuring and deducting every tiny opening costs more in surveyor's time than the plaster is worth. The same 0.5 m² threshold appears in several IS 1200 rules.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under half a square metre, ignore it.** Between 0.5 and 3 m², deduct one face only; above 3 m², deduct both faces.

questions.stem: An estimate prepared for additional work found necessary while the original work is in progress is called a:
questions.solution:
**A supplementary estimate.**

It is a **detailed estimate for the additional work only**, submitted for sanction **together with** the original estimate, so that the authority can see the total effect on the project.

**Supplementary or revised?** The single discriminating question is **whether the scope has changed**:

| | **Supplementary** | **Revised** |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | **New work added** | **Same** work |
| Reason | Something further is **needed** | The **cost** of what was sanctioned has risen |
| Trigger | A decision to do more | Sanctioned amount exceeded by **> 5%** |
| Submitted | For the **added items**, with the original attached | As a **complete fresh estimate**, with a comparative statement |

So the test is: *is the work the same?* If yes, and only the money has changed, it is **revised**. If the work itself is different, it is **supplementary**. A single project may need both.

**The full family of estimates**, in the order a project meets them:

| Estimate | Prepared | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary / approximate** | At **conception**, for administrative approval | **Plinth area rate**, cube rate, or per unit — per bed, per km, per student |
| **Plinth area** | Early | Plinth area × rate from a similar completed building |
| **Cube rate** | Early | Volume × rate — better where storey heights are unusual |
| **Detailed** | Before **tender** | **Item by item**, measured and rated |
| **Revised** | During execution, when cost exceeds sanction by **> 5%** | Fresh detailed estimate |
| **Supplementary** | During execution, when **more work** is needed | Detailed, for the added items |
| **Annual maintenance / repair** | Yearly | Upkeep |
| **Complete** | — | Including land, legal, supervision — the whole cost of the project |

**Why a supplementary estimate must be prepared and sanctioned before the work is done**, not after. Executing unsanctioned work commits public money without authority, and if sanction is later refused the expenditure is irregular and the engineer personally answerable. The same principle governs **variation orders** in a contract: they must be issued **in writing and in advance**, valued at the contract rates where the work is of the same character, and at negotiated rates where it is not.

And there is a second reason for issuing them in advance, which is the contractor's protection: additional work justifies an **extension of time**, and without the written order there is no documentary basis for it — leaving the contractor exposed to **liquidated damages** for a delay the employer caused.

**A caution against habitual supplementary estimates.** They are legitimate for genuinely unforeseen needs, but a project that repeatedly requires them usually had an inadequate **investigation and design** stage. The professional remedy is better preliminary work — soil investigation, survey, and a properly interrogated brief — not smoother paperwork later.

examTip.trick: Match the estimate to the trigger: **revised** (cost exceeded by over 5%), **supplementary** (extra work added), **complete** (the original plus all supplementaries together).
examTip.mnemonic: **Supplementary = something extra turned up.** It is submitted with the original estimate so the sanctioning authority sees the total.

questions.stem: The capitalised value of a property is obtained by multiplying its net annual income by the:
questions.solution:
**The year's purchase.**

> **Capitalised value = net annual income × year's purchase**
> **Year's purchase (YP) = 100 / rate of interest** = 1 / i

The year's purchase is simply the **number of years' income that a buyer is willing to pay** for the property — hence the name. At an expected return of 8%, YP = 100/8 = **12.5**, so a property yielding Rs 200,000 net per year is worth 200,000 × 12.5 = **Rs 2,500,000**.

**Where the formula comes from.** For a perpetual income stream, the present value of Rs 1 per year for ever at interest i is **1/i**. A freehold property is treated as such a perpetuity, so its value is the annual income divided by the required rate of return.

**Note the inverse relation, which is the substance of the concept:**

| Expected return | YP | Effect on value |
|---|---|---|
| **5%** | **20** | **Higher** value |
| 8% | 12.5 | — |
| **10%** | **10** | **Lower** value |

A **higher** required return gives a **lower** valuation for the same income. This is not an accounting artefact but an economic truth: an investor who demands more return will pay less for a given income, and the rate chosen therefore reflects the **risk** of that income. A secure, well-let building is capitalised at a low rate and so valued highly; an uncertain income stream at a high rate and valued low. **Choosing the rate is the valuer's central judgement**, and it moves the answer more than any other input.

**Getting to the net income** is the other half of the work, and the outgoings must be deducted honestly:

> **Net income = gross rent − outgoings**

| Outgoing | Typical allowance |
|---|---|
| **Repairs and maintenance** | About **1/12 (8⅓%)** of gross rent |
| **Municipal and other taxes** | As assessed |
| **Insurance** | Premium |
| **Management and collection** | A percentage |
| **Sinking fund** | For eventual **rebuilding** |
| Loss of rent (voids) | An allowance for vacancy |

The **sinking fund** entry is the one candidates omit: since the building itself has a finite life, part of the income must be set aside to replace it, and only what remains is true return on capital. Where the lease is for a **limited term** rather than perpetual, the YP is not 1/i but the **present value of an annuity**, YP = [1 − (1+i)^−n]/i — sometimes with a **dual rate** allowing separately for the remunerative and the sinking fund rates.

**Why the other options are wrong** in an instructive way:

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| Rate of interest | The **reciprocal** of YP — multiplying by it would give a hundredth of the value |
| **Sinking fund factor** | **i/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]** — converts a **future** sum into an annual deposit; the opposite direction |
| Depreciation rate | Reduces the **cost-based** valuation, not the income-based one |

**Which valuation method to use** depends on what the property is:

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Rental / capitalised value** | **Income-producing** property — the method above |
| **Cost (depreciation) method** | Owner-occupied buildings; insurance valuation |
| **Comparative** | Where there is an active market in similar property |
| **Development method** | Land ripe for development |

And throughout: **land is valued separately and does not depreciate**, which is why an old building on a good site is often worth almost entirely its land value.

examTip.trick: **Year's purchase = 100 / rate of interest.** So at 8% the YP is 12.5, and capitalised value = net annual income × 12.5.
examTip.mnemonic: **YP is how many years' income the property is worth.** A lower interest rate means a higher YP and a higher valuation — which is why property values rise when interest rates fall.

questions.stem: An approximate estimate of a proposed building, prepared at the conception stage for administrative approval, is most commonly based on:
options: The plinth area rate of a similar completed building
Detailed measurement of every item of work
The bar bending schedule of the structure
The actual invoiced rates of all materials to be used
questions.solution:
**The plinth area rate of a similar completed building.**

> **Approximate cost = plinth area × plinth area rate**

The rate is drawn from a **recently completed building of similar type, specification and locality**, and the whole validity of the estimate rests on that similarity. The same plinth area of a warehouse, a school and a hospital cost very different amounts, because the rate silently carries the specification — the finishes, the services, the structural system.

**Why an approximate estimate is prepared at all, rather than going straight to a detailed one.** At the conception stage the design does not yet exist. A detailed estimate (option b) requires **complete drawings**, which cannot be produced until the project is approved and funded — so an approximate figure must come first, sufficient for the authority to decide whether to proceed and to allot funds. Options (c) and (d) require even more information than a detailed estimate.

The sequence is therefore: **approximate estimate → administrative approval → detailed design → detailed estimate → technical sanction → tender.**

**The methods of approximate estimating**, in increasing refinement:

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Plinth area rate** | Plinth area × rate per m² | **Buildings** — the standard method |
| **Cube rate** | Plinth area × **height** × rate per m³ | Buildings of **unusual storey height** |
| **Unit rate (service unit)** | Cost **per unit of function** | **Per bed** (hospital), per student (school), per seat (theatre), **per km** (road), per litre (reservoir) |
| Bay method | Cost of one **repeating bay** × number of bays | Factories, workshops, long sheds |
| Approximate quantity | Rough quantities of the **main items** only | The most accurate of the approximate methods |

**The unit rate method deserves note** because it is how public infrastructure is budgeted at policy level — a road at so much per kilometre, a school at so much per classroom. It is crude, but it is the only method available before any design exists at all, and it works because the *function* determines most of the cost.

**The cube rate refinement** exists for a specific reason: cost follows **volume** more closely than floor area once storey heights depart from the normal. A hall 6 m high costs far more per square metre of floor than a 3 m office, because the walls, columns and services all scale with height.

**What the accuracy actually is, and why that must be stated.** An approximate estimate is commonly reliable to within about **±10 to 15%** when based on a genuinely comparable building, and considerably worse when it is not. An engineer presenting one should say so — quoting an approximate figure to the nearest rupee, with no stated tolerance, invites it to be treated as a commitment. Many project cost overruns begin as an approximate estimate that was never described as approximate.

**The plinth area measurement rules**, since they determine the input: measured **externally at floor level**; **courtyards, open verandahs and open balconies excluded**; covered verandahs included; and areas of differing storey height or specification **measured separately**, because each attracts its own rate.

**And the complete estimate** is what the approval actually needs: the cost of construction is only part of the project cost, alongside **land acquisition, legal charges, supervision, contingencies, work-charged establishment and services**. An approximate estimate of construction alone, presented as the project cost, understates it substantially.

examTip.trick: At the conception stage there are no detailed drawings, so nothing can be measured. The only available basis is the cost of a **similar completed building** per square metre of plinth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Approximate estimate for administrative approval; detailed estimate for technical sanction and tendering.**

questions.stem: As per IS 1200, a damp proof course is measured in:
questions.solution:
**In square metres, stating the thickness.**

A DPC is a **thin layer of uniform, specified thickness**, so its cost varies with the **area** covered while the thickness is fixed by specification. The measurement convention therefore records the area and states the thickness alongside it — the same logic that governs plastering, flooring and painting.

**The general principle behind every unit in IS 1200**, which is worth more than the individual entries:

> **The unit of measurement follows the dimension that actually governs the cost.**

| If cost varies with | Unit | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **All three dimensions** | **m³** | Concrete, brickwork, earthwork, stone masonry |
| **Area**, thickness being specified | **m²** | **DPC**, plastering, flooring, painting, half-brick walls |
| **Length**, section being specified | **running metre** | Skirting, dado, cornice, railing, kerb, pipes |
| **The mass of material** | **quintal / tonne** | Reinforcement, structural steel |
| **Nothing but the count** | **number** | Sanitary fittings, manholes, trees, doors as units |

So a **DPC in m²** and **brickwork in m³** are not arbitrary conventions to be memorised separately — the DPC's thickness is fixed by the drawing while a wall's thickness varies with the item.

**A caveat worth knowing:** where a damp proof course is **thick enough to be a substantial course of concrete in its own right** — as when a cement concrete DPC is laid at appreciable thickness — it may be measured in **m³** like any other concrete, in accordance with how the item is described in the bill. The description in the bill of quantities always governs, which is why a well-drafted BoQ states the unit explicitly for every item.

**Typical DPC construction**, for context: cement concrete of about **1:1½:3** and **40–75 mm** thick, laid over the full width of the wall at plinth level and painted with **hot bitumen** at about 1.7 kg/m², or bituminous felt bedded in bitumen.

**Why the measurement rules deserve real attention rather than rote learning.** In an **item-rate contract** the contractor is paid **measured quantity × tendered rate**. That makes IS 1200 the arbiter of payment, and it explains the pattern of site disputes: arguments arise far more often about **how a quantity was arrived at** than about the rate that was agreed, because the rate is in the contract while the measurement is made afterwards.

**The general rules of measurement that apply across all items:**

| Rule | Effect |
|---|---|
| Measurements taken to the nearest **0.01 m** for linear dimensions | Consistent precision |
| Areas to **0.01 m²**, volumes to **0.01 m³** | — |
| Work of **different specifications measured separately** | Each carries its own rate |
| Work in **different situations** — below ground, above 3 m height — measured separately | Cost differs with access and lift |
| **Authorised dimensions** only | Over-excavation and over-thickness are not paid for |
| Measurements recorded in a **measurement book (MB)**, signed | The legal record for payment |

The **measurement book** is the last and most practical point: it is a formal, page-numbered record, entries in ink, corrections initialled and never erased, signed by both the measuring officer and the contractor. It is the document on which every running bill is paid and, in the event of a dispute, the primary evidence — so its discipline is a professional obligation, not clerical formality.

examTip.trap: "Cubic metres" is offered because a DPC clearly has thickness — but it is measured by **area**, with the thickness merely stated in the item description.
examTip.trick: The general IS 1200 rule: measure by the dimension that varies. A DPC's thickness is essentially constant, so area is what changes from job to job.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thin layers by area, thick work by volume, linear items by length.**
