questions.stem: In the SLUMP TEST on fresh concrete, a SHEAR slump (in which one half of the cone slides down an inclined plane) rather than a true slump indicates that:
options: The concrete has an unusually high strength
The test has been performed correctly and the result may be recorded as normal
The slump cone was filled in a single layer instead of three
The mix is lacking in cohesion and is prone to segregation
questions.solution:
**The mix is LACKING IN COHESION and is prone to segregation** — so the result is not a valid measure of workability and the test should be repeated, a shear slump on a second attempt indicating a deficient mix.

**The three forms the slumped concrete can take:**

| Form | Appearance | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** ← | **The mass subsides evenly, keeping its shape** ← | **A cohesive mix; the measurement is VALID** ← |
| **SHEAR slump** ← | **One half slides down an inclined plane** ← | **Poor cohesion; the measurement is NOT valid** ← |
| **COLLAPSE slump** ← | **The mass collapses completely** ← | **The mix is far too wet, or is a very high-workability mix for which the test is unsuitable** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S CONSEQUENCE IS THE PART MOST OFTEN MISHANDLED ON SITE AND IT MATTERS: a shear slump is not simply a large slump to be written down.**

> **The test assumes the concrete subsides as a coherent mass, and a mix that shears has not done so — the number measured is the height a sliding wedge happened to reach, which is not a measure of workability at all.**

> **So the correct action is to take a fresh sample and repeat the test.**

> **If the second sample also shears, the mix itself is deficient in cohesion and should be investigated rather than recorded, which usually points to too little fine aggregate, a poor grading or an excess of water.**

**THE TEST'S STANDARD PROCEDURE IS WORTH HAVING PRECISELY, SINCE DEPARTURES INVALIDATE IT:**

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Cone dimensions** | **200 mm bottom diameter, 100 mm top, 300 mm high** ← |
| **Filling** | **THREE layers, each approximately one third of the HEIGHT** ← |
| **Compaction** | **25 strokes of a 16 mm diameter, 600 mm long rounded rod per layer** ← |
| **Each layer's strokes** | **Distributed evenly; penetrating into the layer below for the upper layers** ← |
| **Lifting** | **Vertically, slowly, in 5 to 10 seconds, without twisting** ← |
| **Measurement** | **The DIFFERENCE between the cone's height and the highest point of the subsided specimen** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS A DETAIL THAT IS ROUTINELY GOT WRONG AND IT CHANGES THE RESULT: the three layers are each one third of the HEIGHT of the cone, not one third of its volume.**

> **Because the cone tapers, a third of its height is not a third of its volume — the bottom third holds far more concrete than the top third.**

> **So filling by equal volumes puts the layer boundaries in the wrong places and applies the wrong compactive effort to each part of the specimen.**

> **The distinction is easy to remember once noticed, and it is the kind of procedural detail that separates a test that means something from one that merely produces a number.**

**AND THE TEST'S LIMITATIONS DESERVE A CLOSING NOTE, SINCE IT IS OFTEN ASKED TO DO MORE THAN IT CAN:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It measures CONSISTENCY, not workability in full** ← | **Workability includes cohesion, compactability and finishability** ← |
| **It is insensitive for very dry mixes** ← | **Use the compacting factor or Vee-Bee test instead** ← |
| **And meaningless for very wet or superplasticised mixes** ← | **Use the flow table test** ← |
| **It says nothing about STRENGTH** ← | ← |
| **Its chief practical value is as a CONSISTENCY CHECK between batches** ← | ← |

> **The last row is what the test is genuinely good for and it is a considerable value: a slump measured on every load detects a change in the mix immediately.**

> **A batch that suddenly slumps 40 mm more than the previous ten has more water in it, and that is worth knowing before it is placed.**

> **So the slump test earns its place as a rapid, cheap, repeatable field check on CONSISTENCY rather than as a measure of quality in itself — and treating a single slump reading as a verdict on a mix asks it for something it was never designed to provide.**
tags: layers are one third of height

examTip.trick: **Poor cohesion and a tendency to segregate** — the reading is invalid, so repeat with a fresh sample.
examTip.trap: **Fill in three layers each one third of the HEIGHT, not the volume** — the cone tapers, so equal volumes put the boundaries in the wrong place.
examTip.mnemonic: **The slump test checks CONSISTENCY between batches** — a load slumping 40 mm more than the last has extra water. It says nothing about strength.

questions.stem: A DAMP PROOF COURSE (DPC) is provided in a masonry wall at plinth level principally to:
options: Prevent moisture rising from the ground into the wall above by capillary action
Increase the load-carrying capacity of the wall
Provide a level surface on which to build the superstructure
Allow the wall to expand and contract with temperature
questions.solution:
**Prevent moisture rising from the ground into the wall above by CAPILLARY ACTION** — which would otherwise dampen the wall, damage plaster and finishes, and promote decay.

**The mechanism the DPC interrupts:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Masonry and mortar contain fine interconnected PORES** ← | ← |
| **Water in the ground is drawn up those pores by capillary action** ← | **Against gravity — the finer the pore, the higher it rises** ← |
| **It can rise a metre or more in fine-pored brickwork** ← | ← |
| **Carrying dissolved SALTS with it** ← | ← |
| **Which crystallise at the surface as the water evaporates** ← | **Efflorescence, and spalling of the plaster** ← |
| **A DPC places an IMPERMEABLE barrier across the wall's full thickness** ← | **Breaking the capillary path** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE DAMAGE THAT MAKES RISING DAMP MORE THAN A COSMETIC PROBLEM AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the water itself evaporates and the salts it carried do not.**

> **They accumulate at the evaporation front, just behind the wall's surface, and crystallise there.**

> **Salt crystals occupy more volume than the solution they formed from, so they exert pressure that spalls the plaster and erodes the brick face.**

> **That is why rising damp damages a wall progressively rather than merely making it wet, and why simply drying a wall does not repair it — the salts remain and reactivate with each cycle of wetting.**

**THE REQUIREMENTS FOR AN EFFECTIVE DPC ARE SPECIFIC AND ITS FAILURES ARE USUALLY DETAILING FAILURES:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONTINUOUS across the wall's FULL thickness** ← | **A gap anywhere lets the moisture bypass it** ← |
| **Placed at least 150 mm above finished ground level** ← | **So splashing rain does not wet the wall above it** ← |
| **Properly LAPPED at joints and at corners** ← | **Commonly 100 mm, or the wall thickness** ← |
| **Continuous with the floor's damp proof membrane** ← | **Or moisture bypasses it through the floor slab** ← |
| **Not bridged by plaster, render, soil or a later path** ← | ← |
| **Made of a material that will not be punctured during construction** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF FAILURE IN AN OTHERWISE CORRECTLY BUILT WALL AND IT IS ENTIRELY AVOIDABLE: a DPC works only if there is no alternative path around it.**

> **Plaster carried continuously down the face of the wall past the DPC provides exactly such a path, and the moisture simply travels up through the plaster instead.**

> **So does earth banked against the wall above DPC level, a paving slab laid too high, or a later render.**

> **The remedy is to stop the plaster at the DPC and to maintain the 150 mm clearance permanently — which means the requirement belongs in the maintenance regime as well as in the construction, since a path can be created years afterwards by landscaping that nobody thought about.**

**THE COMMON MATERIALS ARE WORTH KNOWING WITH THEIR CHARACTERS:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen felt or bitumen-coated sheet** ← | **Common and economical; can be punctured or squeezed out under heavy load** ← |
| **Polythene or polymer sheet** ← | **Cheap, effective, easily damaged during construction** ← |
| **Mastic asphalt** ← | **Applied hot, forms a continuous layer** ← |
| **Cement concrete with a waterproofing admixture** ← | **Rigid, durable; a course of dense concrete at plinth level** ← |
| **Engineering brick or slate in cement mortar** ← | **Traditional, very durable, and rigid** ← |

> **The distinction that matters in selecting among them is RIGID against FLEXIBLE, and it follows from the structure's expected movement.**

> **A flexible DPC accommodates settlement and differential movement without cracking, and it can be squeezed or punctured.**

> **A rigid one carries load well and cracks if the wall moves, and a cracked rigid DPC is a DPC with a hole in it.**

> **So a building expected to settle unevenly — on variable ground, or of lightweight construction — is better served by a flexible DPC, and a heavily loaded wall on firm ground by a rigid one, which is a straightforward matching of the material's behaviour to the movement it must tolerate.**

examTip.trick: **Break the capillary path from the ground** — an impermeable barrier across the wall's full thickness.
examTip.trap: **BRIDGING defeats it** — plaster carried past the DPC, or soil banked above it, gives the moisture a way round. Keep 150 mm clear permanently.
examTip.mnemonic: **The salts stay when the water leaves** — crystallising and spalling the surface, which is why drying a wall does not repair it.

questions.stem: A rectangular section is 200 mm wide and 400 mm deep. Its moment of inertia about the centroidal axis PARALLEL TO THE WIDTH (the axis of bending for a beam of this orientation) is:
questions.solution:
**1.067 × 10⁹ mm⁴.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **I = b d³ / 12, with d measured in the direction of bending** | ← |
| **Here b = 200 mm and d = 400 mm** | ← |
| **d³** | **400³ = 64,000,000 = 6.4 × 10⁷ mm³** ← |
| **b d³** | **200 × 6.4 × 10⁷ = 1.28 × 10¹⁰** ← |
| **Divide by 12** | **1.28 × 10¹⁰ ÷ 12 = 1.0667 × 10⁹ mm⁴** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 2.67 × 10⁸ IS THE VALUE ABOUT THE OTHER AXIS AND IT IS THE ERROR THE QUESTION IS BUILT AROUND: I = db³/12 = 400 × 200³/12 = 2.67 × 10⁸ mm⁴.**

> **That is the moment of inertia about the axis parallel to the DEPTH, which governs if the beam is laid flat.**

> **The ratio between the two is (400/200)² = 4, so the section is four times as stiff standing up as lying flat — which is why beams are made deep and narrow and why a plank on edge carries far more than the same plank laid flat.**

> **The check is to ask which dimension is CUBED: the one in the direction of bending, which for a beam resisting vertical load is the depth.**

**THE CUBIC DEPENDENCE ON DEPTH IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT IN SECTION DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH FEELING RATHER THAN MERELY KNOWING:**

| Change | Effect on I |
|---|---|
| **Double the WIDTH** | **I doubles** ← |
| **Double the DEPTH** | **I increases EIGHT-fold** ← |
| **Increase depth by 10 per cent** | **I rises by 33 per cent** ← |
| **Increase width by 10 per cent** | **I rises by 10 per cent** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHY DEPTH IS THE VARIABLE TO SPEND MATERIAL ON AND IT DRIVES THE SHAPE OF EVERY EFFICIENT BENDING MEMBER: material placed far from the neutral axis contributes disproportionately.**

> **So an I-section concentrates its material in flanges as far from the centre as possible, joined by a web whose only job is to hold them apart and carry shear.**

> **A solid rectangle of the same area is far less stiff, because much of its material sits near the neutral axis where it contributes little.**

> **That single principle explains I-beams, box girders, hollow sections, ribbed slabs and the depth of every truss — the efficient answer is always to get the material away from the centre.**

**THE RELATED SECTION PROPERTIES ARE WORTH HAVING ALONGSIDE:**

| Property | Expression | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Moment of inertia I** | **b d³/12 for a rectangle** ← | **Deflection, and stiffness EI** ← |
| **Section modulus Z** | **I / y_max = b d²/6 for a rectangle** ← | **Bending STRESS: σ = M/Z** ← |
| **Radius of gyration r** | **√(I/A) = d/√12 for a rectangle** ← | **Buckling, through the slenderness ratio** ← |
| **Here: Z** | **200 × 400²/6 = 5.33 × 10⁶ mm³** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PROPERTY NEEDED FOR STRENGTH AND THE FIRST FOR STIFFNESS, AND CONFUSING THEM IS A COMMON ERROR: I governs how much the beam DEFLECTS and Z governs how highly it is STRESSED.**

> **A design may be governed by either — a long-span floor beam usually by deflection and a short heavily loaded one by stress — so both must be checked.**

> **Note that Z varies with d² while I varies with d³, so increasing depth helps deflection even more than it helps stress.**

> **That is why a beam that is strong enough but too flexible is almost always best cured by adding depth rather than width, and it is the first thing to try when a section fails its deflection check.**

material away from the neutral axis
I for stiffness Z for stress

examTip.trick: **I = bd³/12 = 200 × 400³/12 = 1.067 × 10⁹ mm⁴** — the depth is cubed.
examTip.trap: **2.67 × 10⁸ is the value about the other axis** — db³/12, for the beam laid flat. Four times less stiff.
examTip.mnemonic: **Double the depth, eight times the I** — which is why every efficient bending member moves material away from the neutral axis.

questions.stem: In levelling, the HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (collimation) method and the RISE AND FALL method differ in that the rise and fall method:
options: Requires fewer staff readings to be taken in the field
Provides a complete arithmetic check on every intermediate sight
Can be used only where the ground is level
Does not require a benchmark of known elevation
questions.solution:
**It provides a complete ARITHMETIC CHECK on every intermediate sight, because each reading is compared with the one before it** — whereas the height of instrument method checks only the backsights, foresights and the first and last reduced levels.

**The two methods compared:**

| Aspect | HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT | RISE AND FALL |
|---|---|---|
| **Method** | **HI = RL + BS; then RL = HI − any sight** ← | **Compare each reading with the PREVIOUS one to get a rise or a fall** ← |
| **Arithmetic check** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL** ← | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = Last RL − First RL** ← |
| **Are INTERMEDIATE sights checked?** | **NO** ← | **YES** ← |
| **Speed of reduction** | **FASTER, especially with many intermediate sights** ← | **Slower** ← |
| **Suits** | **Longitudinal sections, cross-sections, contouring — many intermediate sights** ← | **Precise levelling, where every reduced level must be verified** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE AND ITS CONSEQUENCE IS PRACTICAL: the height of instrument check will balance perfectly even if an intermediate sight has been reduced wrongly.**

> **That is because an intermediate sight never enters the check — the check involves only the backsights, the foresights and the two end levels.**

> **So an arithmetic error on an intermediate point passes undetected, and the error appears in the field as a wrong level for that one point.**

> **The rise and fall method catches it, because every reading participates in the rise-or-fall computation and therefore in the ΣRise − ΣFall total — which is why precise work uses it despite being slower.**

**THE THREE CHECKS IN THE RISE AND FALL METHOD MUST ALL AGREE AND THAT IS ITS STRENGTH:**

| Check | Expression |
|---|---|
| **1** | **ΣBS − ΣFS** ← |
| **2** | **ΣRise − ΣFall** ← |
| **3** | **Last RL − First RL** ← |
| **All three must be EQUAL** ← | ← |

> **THE REDUNDANCY IS THE POINT AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THE CHECK COMPLETE: three independently computed quantities that must agree.**

> **In the height of instrument method there are only two, and they omit the intermediate sights entirely.**

> **So the rise and fall method's extra labour buys genuine verification rather than merely a second opinion on the same numbers.**

> **It is worth noting that all three checks verify the ARITHMETIC only — none of them detects a misread staff, a disturbed instrument or a moved change point, which are field errors that no amount of computation will reveal.**

**THAT LAST POINT DESERVES DEVELOPING BECAUSE IT IS THE MORE IMPORTANT CAUTION:**

| Error | Detected by the arithmetic check? |
|---|---|
| **A mistake in reduction** | **YES (rise and fall); partly (HI)** ← |
| **A misread staff — 2.45 recorded as 2.54** | **NO** ← |
| **The staff not held vertical** | **NO** ← |
| **The instrument disturbed between sights** | **NO** ← |
| **A change point moved between foresight and backsight** | **NO** ← |
| **Collimation error in the instrument** | **NO** ← |

> **THE SECOND THROUGH SIXTH ROWS ARE ALL FIELD ERRORS AND THEY ARE CAUGHT BY FIELD PROCEDURE RATHER THAN BY COMPUTATION: closing the level run back to the starting benchmark, or on to another of known elevation, is what detects them.**

> **The misclosure so revealed is the real check on the work, and it is the reason a level run is always closed rather than left open.**

> **So the arithmetic checks confirm that the reduction was done correctly, and the closure confirms that the LEVELLING was done correctly — two different assurances, and a survey needs both.**

> **A run whose arithmetic balances perfectly and which was never closed has verified the easier half of the work and left the harder half unexamined.**

arithmetic checks do not catch field errors

examTip.trick: **Rise and fall checks EVERY reading; HI does not check intermediate sights** — hence three agreeing totals against two.
examTip.trap: **HI balances perfectly even with a wrong intermediate level** — that sight never enters the check.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic checks verify the REDUCTION; closing the run verifies the LEVELLING** — a misread staff passes every arithmetic test.

questions.stem: In preparing a detailed estimate, the CENTRE LINE METHOD of measuring quantities for a building's foundation, walls and plinth is preferred over the long wall–short wall method chiefly because it:
options: Gives a larger quantity, providing a margin for wastage
Can only be applied to buildings with a single room
Does not require the wall thicknesses to be known
Uses a single total centre-line length multiplied by the cross-sectional area at each level
questions.solution:
**It uses a SINGLE total centre-line length multiplied by the cross-sectional area at each level** — so the same length serves every layer regardless of its width, provided the correct DEDUCTION is made at each junction of walls.

**Why the centre line method is more economical of effort:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **In the long wall–short wall method, each wall's length changes with the width of each layer** ← | **The long wall lengthens and the short wall shortens as the layer widens** ← |
| **So lengths must be recomputed for the footing, the foundation concrete, the plinth and the superstructure** ← | ← |
| **The CENTRE LINE length does NOT change with the layer's width** ← | **The centre line is the same line at every level** ← |
| **So one length serves all layers** ← | ← |
| **And the quantity at each level is simply that length × that level's cross-section** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROPERTY THE METHOD EXPLOITS AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT HOLDS: widening a wall symmetrically about its centre line extends it equally on both sides.**

> **The outer face moves out and the inner face moves in by the same amount, so the line midway between them does not move at all.**

> **That is true at every level, which is why a single centre-line length is valid for the footing, the foundation, the plinth and the wall above.**

> **The long wall–short wall method must recompute because it measures to the faces, and the faces do move.**

**THE DEDUCTION AT JUNCTIONS IS THE METHOD'S ONE COMPLICATION AND IT IS WHERE ERRORS OCCUR:**

| Junction type | Deduction from the total centre-line length |
|---|---|
| **A CROSS (four walls meeting)** ← | **No deduction** ← |
| **A TEE junction** ← | **Half the layer's width, once, for each tee** ← |
| **A CORNER (two walls meeting at right angles)** ← | **The deduction is built in by measuring centre to centre** ← |
| **General rule for a simple rectangular building** ← | **Total centre line = 2 × (L + B) measured on the centre lines — no further deduction** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CASE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE AND THE REASON IS GEOMETRIC: at a tee, the centre lines of the three walls do not all meet at a single point in the way they do at a corner or a cross.**

> **The cross wall's centre line stops at the main wall's centre line, and the material in the overlap has been counted once too often.**

> **So half the width is deducted for each tee junction, at each level, using that level's width.**

> **Since the deduction depends on the layer's width, it is the one part of the calculation that does change level by level — which is the residual complication the method does not remove and the step most often forgotten.**

**THE PRACTICAL CHOICE BETWEEN THE METHODS DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE:**

| Situation | Preferred method |
|---|---|
| **A building with walls of UNIFORM thickness throughout** ← | **CENTRE LINE — fastest and least error-prone** ← |
| **Walls of DIFFERENT thicknesses in the same building** ← | **Centre line applied separately to each group, or long wall–short wall** ← |
| **Irregular plan with many offsets** ← | **Long wall–short wall, or measure by parts** ← |
| **Checking someone else's estimate** ← | **The OTHER method — an independent route to the same answer** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A GENUINELY USEFUL PRACTICE AND IT COSTS LITTLE: computing a quantity by a different method than the one originally used gives an independent check.**

> **If the two agree, the quantity is almost certainly right; if they differ, one of them contains an error that can then be found.**

> **That is far more informative than re-checking the original arithmetic, which tends to repeat the original mistake — a person re-adding their own column usually makes the same slip again.**

> **So for any quantity large enough to matter, a second computation by a different route is the check worth making, and it is the same independence principle that governs design checking and drawing review.**
tags: why the centre line does not move

examTip.trick: **One centre-line length × each layer's cross-section** — the centre line does not move as the wall widens.
examTip.trap: **Deduct half the width per TEE junction, using that layer's width** — the one part that still changes level by level.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check by the OTHER method** — re-adding your own column repeats the same slip; an independent route does not.
